title: Complete Android App Development Program (Kotlin)
description: A full 19-module program from beginner to job-ready Android developer: Kotlin, Android Studio, UI, navigation, data storage, Firebase, networking, media, Material Design, security, testing, publishing to Google Play, AI tools, freelancing, 10 real-world apps, an industry capstone and a Certificate of Completion.
outcomes: Program in Kotlin and use Android Studio confidently
Build Android UIs with XML layouts and Material Design
Handle navigation, activities, fragments and app lifecycle
Store data with SharedPreferences, SQLite, Room and Firebase
Consume REST APIs with Retrofit and add auth, media and device features
Test, secure, publish to Google Play, and build a portfolio to get hired
about: This is the complete TIH Android App Development Program, rebuilt into nineteen modules that take you from Kotlin basics to publishing full apps on Google Play.

Every content lesson has a video and formal detailed study notes with Kotlin code; ten real-world apps and an industry capstone build your portfolio, and you learn Firebase, networking, security, testing, publishing, AI tools and freelancing.

Software & tools: Android Studio, Kotlin, Firebase, Git & GitHub, Postman, Figma, SQLite & Room, Google Play Console and Material Design Components. You finish with a portfolio of apps and — after the graduation assessment — a Certificate of Completion.
requirements: A computer that can run Android Studio
No prior coding experience required — we start with Kotlin basics
Willingness to build and run every app in Android Studio

faqs.question: Do I need programming experience?
faqs.answer: No! We teach Kotlin from absolute scratch. If you completed our Computer Literacy course, you have everything needed to start this course.

faqs.question: What kind of computer do I need?
faqs.answer: Android Studio requires at least 8GB RAM (16GB recommended) and 4GB free disk space. Windows, Mac, and Linux all work. We provide an optimization guide for slower computers.

faqs.question: Can I publish apps to earn money?
faqs.answer: Yes! Google Play allows you to sell apps, use in-app purchases, and run ads. Many graduates earn income through their apps. We cover monetization strategies in the final module.

faqs.question: What comes after this course?
faqs.answer: We recommend our Advanced Android course covering Firebase, Jetpack Compose, and enterprise Android patterns. Or explore our Cross-Platform development course with Flutter.

📖 Welcome to the Course
From no code at all to an app published on Google Play.

}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Course Orientation. For Welcome to the Course, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

This course teaches Android development in Kotlin, the language Google has recommended since 2019, using Android Studio, the official development environment.

The order matters. Modules 2 and 3 give you the language and the tools; 4 to 11 build apps that do real work; 12 to 14 cover security, testing and publishing; 15 to 18 add AI tooling, freelancing and the projects that become your portfolio.

Key points

  • Kotlin is the primary language; Java still runs but new work starts in Kotlin.
  • Android Studio is the official IDE and is free.
  • You need a computer, not a phone, to develop — the emulator replaces a device.
  • Every module ends with a quiz you must pass to unlock the next.
  • Modules 17 and 18 are eleven real apps; they are the portfolio, not extras.
  • Type every example yourself. Reading code teaches far less than running it.

Example

A learner in Monrovia finishing this course has eleven working apps and a published Play Store listing. That listing is what a client or employer actually looks at — more than any certificate.

Why this matters

Android development is one of the few skills where the work can be done from anywhere and sold anywhere. The portfolio is what makes that possible.

lessons.title: 1.2 What is Android App Development?
lessons.html:
📖 What is Android App Development?
Writing software for the operating system on most of the world's phones.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

What is Android App Development?

What is Android App Development? is the focus of this Course Orientation lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

Android

Google’s mobile operating system and application platform.

Kotlin

A modern statically typed language officially supported for Android development.

Android Studio

The official integrated development environment for building Android apps.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

fun main() {
    println("My Android journey starts here")
}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Course Orientation. For What is Android App Development?, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Android is an open-source operating system built on the Linux kernel and used by the large majority of smartphones worldwide. Android development means writing applications that run on it.

A modern Android app is built from a few standard pieces: activities and screens the user sees, layouts that arrange them, code that responds to input, and often a network or database layer behind it.

Key points

  • Android is open source and built on the Linux kernel.
  • It holds the majority of global smartphone market share, especially outside North America.
  • Apps are distributed through Google Play and other stores, or installed directly.
  • Native Android means Kotlin or Java; cross-platform tools compile to it.
  • Each app runs in its own sandbox with its own permissions.
  • Devices vary hugely in screen size, Android version and performance.

Example

That variety is the defining constraint. An app that works on your emulator must also work on a five-year-old phone with a small screen and an intermittent connection — which describes a large share of the devices in Liberia.

Why this matters

Designing for that reality rather than for a flagship device is the difference between an app that gets used and one that gets uninstalled.

lessons.title: 1.3 Career Opportunities in Android Development
lessons.html:
📖 Career Opportunities in Android Development
Employment, freelancing, or your own product — and all three are remote-capable.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Career Opportunities in Android Development

Career Opportunities in Android Development is the focus of this Course Orientation lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

Android

Google’s mobile operating system and application platform.

Kotlin

A modern statically typed language officially supported for Android development.

Android Studio

The official integrated development environment for building Android apps.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

fun main() {
    println("My Android journey starts here")

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Course Orientation. For Career Opportunities in Android Development, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Android skills lead to three routes: employment with a company, freelance contract work, or building and publishing your own app. They demand different things, and you can move between them.

For someone in Liberia, freelancing is often the most accessible entry: it needs no relocation, no local employer, and the client cares about your portfolio rather than your address.

Key points

  • Employment: steady income, mentorship, slower start.
  • Freelance: accessible remotely; portfolio matters more than credentials.
  • Own product: highest ceiling, longest and least certain path.
  • Employers ask for published apps and readable code far more than certificates.
  • Related roles: QA, mobile UI design, technical support, app maintenance.
  • Maintenance contracts on existing apps are steady, underrated work.

Example

A common first freelance job is not building an app from nothing. It is fixing, updating or re-publishing someone's existing app — which is exactly what Modules 13 and 14 prepare you for.

Why this matters

Knowing the routes tells you what to build. If freelancing is the target, the portfolio in Modules 17 and 18 matters more than any other part of this course.

lessons.title: 1.4 Android Ecosystem Overview
lessons.html:
📖 Android Ecosystem Overview
The pieces around your code: the OS, the store, the services and the tools.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Android Ecosystem Overview

Android Ecosystem Overview is the focus of this Course Orientation lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

Android

Google’s mobile operating system and application platform.

Kotlin

A modern statically typed language officially supported for Android development.

Android Studio

The official integrated development environment for building Android apps.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

fun main() {
    println("My Android journey starts here")
}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Course Orientation. For Android Ecosystem Overview, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Your app sits inside a larger system. Android OS provides the runtime and APIs. Google Play distributes it. Play Services supply maps, sign-in, payments and more. Firebase offers a backend without you running servers.

API levels matter. Each Android release has a number, and your app declares the minimum it supports. Set it too high and you exclude older devices; too low and you cannot use newer features without extra work.

Key points

  • API level identifies the Android version your app targets.
  • minSdk is the oldest device you support; targetSdk is what you build against.
  • Google Play requires apps to target a recent API level to stay listed.
  • Play Services add maps, sign-in and payments beyond the base OS.
  • Firebase provides database, auth and storage without your own server.
  • Not every device has Play Services — some markets use alternative stores.

Example

Setting minSdk to a recent version is the easiest way to lock out exactly the users you most want to reach. Checking what devices your audience actually carries comes before choosing it.

Why this matters

Every technical decision in this course — layout choices, storage, network handling — is shaped by which devices you decided to support.

lessons.title: 1.5 Installing Android Studio
lessons.html:
📖 Installing Android Studio
One download, a long first run, and then you are set up for good.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Installing Android Studio

Installing Android Studio is the focus of this Course Orientation lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

Android

Google’s mobile operating system and application platform.

Kotlin

A modern statically typed language officially supported for Android development.

Android Studio

The official integrated development environment for building Android apps.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

fun main() {
    println("My Android journey starts here")
}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Course Orientation. For Installing Android Studio, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Download Android Studio from developer.android.com. The installer bundles the IDE, the Android SDK and an emulator image. The first launch downloads several gigabytes, so start it when you have the bandwidth.

It is demanding on hardware. 8 GB of RAM makes it comfortable; 4 GB works if you use a physical phone instead of the emulator, which is often the better choice on a modest machine anyway.

Key points

  • Download only from developer.android.com.
  • First run fetches the SDK and an emulator image — several gigabytes.
  • 8 GB RAM is comfortable; 4 GB works if you test on a real phone.
  • The emulator needs hardware virtualisation enabled in the BIOS.
  • Keep the SDK path free of spaces and non-English characters.
  • A physical Android phone over USB is faster and lighter than the emulator.

Example

On a 4 GB laptop, skip the emulator entirely: enable Developer Options on your own phone, connect it by USB, and run the app there. It is faster, uses no extra RAM, and shows you real device behaviour.

Why this matters

Getting the environment right once saves hours later. Most beginner problems in Module 3 trace back to an incomplete or interrupted first-run download.

📖 Setting Up the Development Environment
SDK components, a device to run on, and a project that builds.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Setting Up the Development Environment

Setting Up the Development Environment is the focus of this Course Orientation lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

Android

Google’s mobile operating system and application platform.

Kotlin

A modern statically typed language officially supported for Android development.

Android Studio

The official integrated development environment for building Android apps.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

fun main() {
    println("My Android journey starts here")
}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Course Orientation. For Setting Up the Development Environment, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

After installation, use the SDK Manager to confirm you have an SDK platform and the build tools, and the Device Manager to create an emulator or connect a phone.

To use a physical device: enable Developer Options by tapping Build Number seven times in Settings, then turn on USB debugging and accept the authorisation prompt when you connect.

Key points

  • SDK Manager installs platforms and build tools.
  • Device Manager creates emulators (AVDs).
  • Physical device: tap Build Number 7 times, then enable USB debugging.
  • Accept the USB debugging authorisation prompt on the phone itself.
  • Gradle sync must complete before anything will build.
  • Work offline where possible — Gradle caches dependencies after the first build.

Example

The first Gradle sync downloads dependencies and can take a long time on a slow connection. It is a one-off per project type; afterwards the cache makes builds much faster.

Why this matters

A working device and a green Gradle sync are the two things to confirm before writing any code. Almost every “my app will not run” question comes down to one of them.

Creating Your First Android Project is the focus of this Course Orientation lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

Google’s mobile operating system and application platform.

Kotlin

A modern statically typed language officially supported for Android development.

The official integrated development environment for building Android apps.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

    println("My Android journey starts here")
}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Course Orientation. For Creating Your First Android Project, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Create a new project in Android Studio using the Empty Views Activity template, with Kotlin and a minSdk of 24. Let Gradle finish syncing, then look at what was generated.

The goal is orientation, not comprehension. Find MainActivity.kt, activity_main.xml, AndroidManifest.xml and build.gradle.kts, and be able to say what each is for in one sentence.

Key points

  • Template: Empty Views Activity, Kotlin, minSdk 24.
  • Wait for the first Gradle sync to finish before touching anything.
  • Locate MainActivity.kt — the code for the first screen.
  • Locate activity_main.xml — its layout.
  • Locate AndroidManifest.xml — the app's declaration.
  • Change the app name in strings.xml and see it update.

Example

Deliverable: a project that builds, with the app name changed to something of your own and the change visible in the layout preview. Commit it to Git before you change anything else.

Why this matters

Everything in the course is built on this structure, and knowing which file to open is what makes the later modules navigable.

📖 Course Roadmap
What you will build, in what order, and why that order.

Key Words & Meanings

Course Roadmap

Course Roadmap is the focus of this Course Orientation lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

Android

Kotlin

A modern statically typed language officially supported for Android development.

Android Studio

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

    println("My Android journey starts here")
}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Course Orientation. For Course Roadmap, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

The course moves from language, to tools, to interface, to data, to publishing. Each stage assumes the last, which is why working out of order causes trouble.

Modules 2–3 are Kotlin and Android Studio. Modules 4–6 are the interface and navigation. Modules 7–9 are data: storage, Firebase and networking. Modules 10–14 add device features, design, security, testing and publishing. Modules 15–18 cover AI tooling, freelancing and the portfolio projects.

Key points

  • Language and tools first — everything else depends on them.
  • Interface and navigation before data, so you have somewhere to display it.
  • Storage, then Firebase, then networking — local before remote.
  • Security, testing and publishing before the portfolio projects.
  • Modules 17 and 18 build eleven apps that reuse everything prior.
  • Do the quizzes; they gate the next lesson deliberately.

Example

Learners who skip Module 2 to reach the interface faster usually return to it by Module 5, because layout code is Kotlin code. The order exists for that reason.

Why this matters

Knowing the shape of the course helps you judge progress and lets you tell a client what you can already do — useful well before you finish.

This is the placeholder for the capstone you build in Module 18. Do not start it now — but start thinking about the problem you want to solve, because a good one makes the whole project easier.

Choose something you understand. A problem you have watched someone struggle with produces better requirements than any invented brief, and you can explain your decisions convincingly in an interview.

Key points

  • The capstone is built in Module 18, not now.
  • Start collecting ideas as you work through the modules.
  • Choose a problem you genuinely understand.
  • Local problems make the strongest projects — you know the constraints.
  • Scope it to what you can finish and polish.

Keep a running list. Candidates that work well: a market stallholder's stock and sales tracker, a clinic appointment reminder, a school fee record, a transport fare calculator. Each is small, real and explicable.

The capstone is the piece an employer or client will actually look at, so the choice of problem matters as much as the code.

lessons.title: 2.1 Introduction to Kotlin
lessons.html:
📖 Introduction to Kotlin
Concise, safe, and designed to remove the mistakes Java made easy.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Introduction to Kotlin

Introduction to Kotlin is the focus of this Programming Fundamentals with Kotlin lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

variable

A named location or reference that stores a value.

function

A reusable block of Kotlin code that may receive parameters and return a result.

null safety

Kotlin’s type-system features for preventing unexpected null-value errors.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

fun total(price: Double, quantity: Int): Double {
    require(quantity > 0)
    return price * quantity
}
val amount = total(5.0, 3)

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Programming Fundamentals with Kotlin. For Introduction to Kotlin, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Kotlin is a statically typed language that runs on the Java Virtual Machine and interoperates fully with Java. Google made it the preferred Android language because it is shorter to write and removes whole categories of bug.

The headline feature is null safety: the type system distinguishes values that can be null from those that cannot, so the null pointer exception that dominates Java crash reports is caught at compile time instead.

Key points

  • Statically typed, JVM-based, fully interoperable with Java.
  • Null safety is built into the type system.
  • Type inference means you rarely write the type twice.
  • Semicolons are optional and conventionally omitted.
  • Far less boilerplate: a data class replaces dozens of Java lines.
  • Everything in this course is Kotlin, but you will read Java in older projects.

Example

In Kotlin, var name: String can never hold null; var name: String? can. The compiler forces you to handle the second case before you can use it, which is where the crash used to happen.

Why this matters

Null safety alone removes the single most common cause of Android app crashes, which is why the language change was worth making.

lessons.title: 2.2 Variables and Data Types
lessons.html:
📖 Variables and Data Types
val for things that will not change, var for things that will.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Variables and Data Types

Variables and Data Types is the focus of this Programming Fundamentals with Kotlin lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

variable

A named location or reference that stores a value.

function

A reusable block of Kotlin code that may receive parameters and return a result.

null safety

Kotlin’s type-system features for preventing unexpected null-value errors.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

fun total(price: Double, quantity: Int): Double {
    require(quantity > 0)
    return price * quantity
}
val amount = total(5.0, 3)

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Programming Fundamentals with Kotlin. For Variables and Data Types, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

val declares a read-only reference; var declares one you can reassign. Prefer val by default — it makes intent clear and prevents accidental modification.

Kotlin infers types, so val count = 5 is an Int without saying so. Declare the type explicitly when it aids readability or when the value comes later.

Key points

  • val = read-only; var = reassignable. Default to val.
  • Types: Int, Long, Double, Float, Boolean, Char, String.
  • Type inference: val n = 5 is an Int without annotation.
  • val means the reference cannot change, not that a list's contents cannot.
  • String templates: "Hello, $name" inserts a value directly.
  • Kotlin does not implicitly convert numeric types — use toInt(), toDouble().

Example

val list = mutableListOf(1, 2) then list.add(3) is legal. val prevents reassigning list to a different list; it does not freeze the contents. That distinction catches many beginners.

Why this matters

Choosing val wherever possible is the cheapest way to make Android code easier to reason about, particularly once several screens share state.

lessons.title: 2.3 Operators
lessons.html:
📖 Operators
Arithmetic, comparison, logic — plus a few Kotlin adds.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Operators

Operators is the focus of this Programming Fundamentals with Kotlin lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

variable

A named location or reference that stores a value.

function

A reusable block of Kotlin code that may receive parameters and return a result.

null safety

Kotlin’s type-system features for preventing unexpected null-value errors.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

fun total(price: Double, quantity: Int): Double {
    require(quantity > 0)
    return price * quantity
}
val amount = total(5.0, 3)

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Programming Fundamentals with Kotlin. For Operators, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Kotlin has the usual arithmetic (+ − * / %), comparison (== != < > <= >=) and logical (&& || !) operators.

Two are worth singling out. == compares values in Kotlin (unlike Java, where it compares references), and ?:, the Elvis operator, supplies a default when the left side is null.

Key points

  • == compares values; === compares references.
  • Integer division truncates: 7 / 2 is 3, not 3.5.
  • % gives the remainder: 7 % 2 is 1.
  • Elvis ?: supplies a fallback: name ?: "Guest".
  • Safe call ?. returns null instead of crashing on a null receiver.
  • && and || short-circuit — the right side may not run.

Example

val display = username ?: "Guest" gives a usable value whether or not username is null. Combined with ?. it removes most of the defensive null checking Java required.

Why this matters

The safe call and Elvis operators together are how idiomatic Kotlin handles absent data, and you will use them constantly once network responses appear in Module 9.

questions.explanation: Integer division truncates toward zero, so the result is 3.

questions.question: In Kotlin, what does == compare?
questions.explanation: Kotlin's == compares values; === compares references.

lessons.title: 2.4 User Input
lessons.html:
📖 User Input
Reading what the user typed — and never trusting it.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

User Input

User Input is the focus of this Programming Fundamentals with Kotlin lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

variable

A named location or reference that stores a value.

function

A reusable block of Kotlin code that may receive parameters and return a result.

null safety

Kotlin’s type-system features for preventing unexpected null-value errors.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

fun total(price: Double, quantity: Int): Double {
    require(quantity > 0)
    return price * quantity
}
val amount = total(5.0, 3)

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Programming Fundamentals with Kotlin. For User Input, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

In a console exercise you read input with readLine(). In an Android app you read it from an EditText via its text property, then convert it to the type you need.

Conversion is where apps crash. toInt() throws if the text is not a number; toIntOrNull() returns null instead, which you can handle. Always use the safe variant on user input.

Key points

  • Console: readLine(). Android: the EditText's text property.
  • Input arrives as a String and must be converted deliberately.
  • Use toIntOrNull(), not toInt() — it returns null rather than crashing.
  • Check for empty input before converting.
  • Set inputType on the field to bring up the right keyboard.
  • Validate and show a clear message; never fail silently.

Example

val age = input.toIntOrNull() then if (age == null) showError() handles a user typing “twenty” gracefully. Using toInt() instead closes the app.

Why this matters

Unhandled input conversion is one of the most common causes of crashes in beginner apps, and the safe variants remove it entirely.

questions.explanation: inputType selects the keyboard layout, which reduces but does not remove the need for validation.

lessons.title: 2.5 Conditional Statements
lessons.html:
📖 Conditional Statements
if, else and when — and in Kotlin they return values.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Conditional Statements

Conditional Statements is the focus of this Programming Fundamentals with Kotlin lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

variable

A named location or reference that stores a value.

function

A reusable block of Kotlin code that may receive parameters and return a result.

null safety

Kotlin’s type-system features for preventing unexpected null-value errors.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

fun total(price: Double, quantity: Int): Double {
    require(quantity > 0)
    return price * quantity
}
val amount = total(5.0, 3)

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Programming Fundamentals with Kotlin. For Conditional Statements, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

if / else works as expected, but in Kotlin it is an expression: it produces a value you can assign. when replaces Java's switch and handles ranges, types and arbitrary conditions.

when is the idiomatic choice for more than two branches. It reads more clearly than a chain of else-ifs and the compiler can check that an enum is handled exhaustively.

Key points

  • if is an expression: val max = if (a > b) a else b.
  • when replaces switch and handles multiple branch types.
  • when matches ranges (in 1..9), types (is String) and conditions.
  • else is required when when is used as an expression.
  • Prefer when over three or more else-if branches.
  • No fall-through: only the matching branch runs.

Example

val grade = when (score) { in 80..100 -> "A"; in 70..79 -> "B"; else -> "F" } assigns directly. The equivalent if-chain is longer and easier to get wrong.

Why this matters

Because both forms return values, Kotlin code tends to assign once rather than declaring a variable and mutating it, which is easier to follow.

questions.question: Which construct handles multiple branches most cleanly in Kotlin?

options: It is an expression that returns a value
questions.explanation: if returns a value, so it can be assigned directly to a variable.

questions.question: When is 'else' required in a when block?
options: When when is used as an expression
questions.explanation: Used as an expression, when must be exhaustive, which usually means an else branch.

lessons.html:
📖 Loops
Repeat over a range, over a collection, or until a condition changes.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Loops

Loops is the focus of this Programming Fundamentals with Kotlin lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

variable

A named location or reference that stores a value.

function

A reusable block of Kotlin code that may receive parameters and return a result.

null safety

Kotlin’s type-system features for preventing unexpected null-value errors.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

fun total(price: Double, quantity: Int): Double {
    require(quantity > 0)
    return price * quantity
}
val amount = total(5.0, 3)

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Programming Fundamentals with Kotlin. For Loops, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

for iterates over ranges and collections. while repeats while a condition holds. do-while runs at least once before testing.

Kotlin's ranges are expressive: 1..5 counts up, 5 downTo 1 counts down, 1..10 step 2 skips, and until excludes the upper bound.

Key points

  • for (i in 1..5) includes 5; for (i in 1 until 5) stops at 4.
  • downTo counts backwards; step changes the increment.
  • Iterate a collection directly: for (item in list).
  • forEach is the functional equivalent and reads well for short bodies.
  • break exits the loop; continue skips to the next iteration.
  • Avoid modifying a collection while iterating over it.

Example

for (i in 1 until list.size) is safe for index access; 1..list.size would run one past the end and crash. The until form exists precisely to avoid that off-by-one.

Why this matters

Off-by-one errors on list indices are among the most common runtime crashes, and Kotlin's range syntax makes the correct version the shorter one.

questions.explanation: downTo produces a descending range.

questions.question: What should you avoid while iterating a collection?
questions.explanation: Structural modification during iteration causes a concurrent modification error.

📖 Functions
Name a block of work, give it inputs, get a result.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Functions

Functions is the focus of this Programming Fundamentals with Kotlin lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

variable

A named location or reference that stores a value.

function

A reusable block of Kotlin code that may receive parameters and return a result.

null safety

Kotlin’s type-system features for preventing unexpected null-value errors.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

fun total(price: Double, quantity: Int): Double {
    require(quantity > 0)
    return price * quantity
}
val amount = total(5.0, 3)

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Programming Fundamentals with Kotlin. For Functions, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

A function is declared with fun, takes typed parameters, and declares a return type. If it returns nothing the type is Unit and can be omitted.

Kotlin adds two conveniences worth using: default parameter values, which remove the need for overloads, and named arguments, which make calls with several parameters readable.

Key points

  • fun add(a: Int, b: Int): Int { return a + b }.
  • Single-expression form: fun add(a: Int, b: Int) = a + b.
  • Default values: fun greet(name: String = "there").
  • Named arguments: greet(name = "Musu").
  • Return type Unit means it returns nothing and may be omitted.
  • Keep functions short and single-purpose; they are easier to test.

Example

fun createUser(name: String, isAdmin: Boolean = false, sendEmail: Boolean = true) called as createUser("Musu", sendEmail = false) is clear at the call site. Three boolean positional arguments would not be.

Why this matters

Named arguments and defaults remove most of the overloading and builder patterns Java needed, which keeps Android code considerably shorter.

📖 Arrays
A fixed-size, indexed sequence of values.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Arrays

Arrays is the focus of this Programming Fundamentals with Kotlin lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

variable

A named location or reference that stores a value.

function

A reusable block of Kotlin code that may receive parameters and return a result.

null safety

Kotlin’s type-system features for preventing unexpected null-value errors.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

fun total(price: Double, quantity: Int): Double {
    require(quantity > 0)
    return price * quantity
}
val amount = total(5.0, 3)

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Programming Fundamentals with Kotlin. For Arrays, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

An Array holds a fixed number of elements of one type, accessed by a zero-based index. Its size is set at creation and cannot change.

In practice Android code uses List far more often, because most data has a size that varies. Arrays remain useful for fixed collections and when interoperating with Java APIs that expect them.

Key points

  • Zero-based indexing: the first element is arr[0].
  • Size is fixed at creation; arr.size reports it.
  • arrayOf(1, 2, 3) creates one; IntArray(5) creates a sized one.
  • Accessing an out-of-range index throws an exception.
  • Prefer List when the number of items can change.
  • arr.indices gives a safe range for iteration.

Example

arr[arr.size] is always out of bounds, because the last valid index is size - 1. Iterating with for (i in arr.indices) avoids the mistake entirely.

Why this matters

Index errors are a frequent source of crashes; using indices or iterating the elements directly removes the arithmetic that causes them.

variable

function

A reusable block of Kotlin code that may receive parameters and return a result.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

fun total(price: Double, quantity: Int): Double {
    require(quantity > 0)

val amount = total(5.0, 3)

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Programming Fundamentals with Kotlin. For Lists, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

listOf() creates a read-only list; mutableListOf() creates one you can add to and remove from. Most app data — contacts, messages, products — is a list.

Kotlin's collection functions do most of the work you would otherwise loop for: filter, map, sortedBy, first, any, sumOf.

Key points

  • listOf() read-only; mutableListOf() supports add and remove.
  • filter { } selects; map { } transforms.
  • sortedBy { } orders; find { } returns the first match or null.
  • isEmpty() and isNotEmpty() are clearer than checking size.
  • list[0] on an empty list crashes; firstOrNull() does not.
  • Lists feed the RecyclerView in Module 4 — the standard way to display them.

Example

products.filter { it.price < 100 }.sortedBy { it.name } replaces a loop, a temporary list and a comparator in one readable line.

Why this matters

Almost every screen you build displays a list. These functions are what turn raw data into what the screen should show.

lessons.title: 2.10 Object-Oriented Programming Basics
lessons.html:
📖 Object-Oriented Programming Basics
Bundle data with the behaviour that belongs to it.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Object-Oriented Programming Basics

Object-Oriented Programming Basics is the focus of this Programming Fundamentals with Kotlin lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

variable

A named location or reference that stores a value.

function

A reusable block of Kotlin code that may receive parameters and return a result.

null safety

Kotlin’s type-system features for preventing unexpected null-value errors.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

fun total(price: Double, quantity: Int): Double {
    require(quantity > 0)
    return price * quantity
}
val amount = total(5.0, 3)

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Programming Fundamentals with Kotlin. For Object-Oriented Programming Basics, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Object-oriented programming organises code into classes that hold data (properties) and the operations on it (methods). An object is one instance of a class.

Android is built this way: an Activity is a class, a View is a class, your data model is a class. Understanding the four ideas — encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction — is what makes the framework legible.

Key points

  • Class = blueprint; object = one instance of it.
  • Encapsulation: keep data private, expose controlled access.
  • Inheritance: a class extends another and reuses its behaviour.
  • Polymorphism: different classes respond to the same call differently.
  • Abstraction: expose what something does, hide how.
  • Kotlin classes are final by default; mark them open to allow inheritance.

Example

class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() is inheritance in the very first line of every Android screen you write. Your class gets the whole lifecycle from the parent and overrides only what it needs.

Why this matters

You cannot read Android's own code without this vocabulary, and every screen, view and adapter in the rest of the course is an application of it.

function

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

fun total(price: Double, quantity: Int): Double {

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Programming Fundamentals with Kotlin. For Classes and Objects, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

A Kotlin class declares its constructor parameters in the header: class User(val name: String, var age: Int). That single line creates the properties and the constructor together.

For classes that only carry data, data class additionally generates equals, hashCode, toString and copy. Most model classes in an Android app should be data classes.

Key points

  • Primary constructor sits in the class header.
  • val parameters become read-only properties; var ones are mutable.
  • data class generates equals, hashCode, toString and copy.
  • init { } blocks run when an instance is created.
  • Create an instance without new: val u = User("Musu", 30).
  • copy() makes a modified duplicate: u.copy(age = 31).

Example

data class Product(val id: Int, val name: String, val price: Double) is a complete model class. Comparing two products, printing one, or copying one with a changed price all work without another line of code.

Why this matters

Data classes are what make Kotlin model layers so short, and they are the shape everything in Modules 7 to 9 stores, sends and receives.

This lesson consolidates Module 2. Work each exercise in Android Studio's Kotlin playground or a scratch file, and run it — reading code teaches far less than watching it fail and fixing it.

Aim to write, not to recognise. If you can only follow an example when it is in front of you, you have not learned it yet.

📖 Android Studio Interface
Four panels do almost everything.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Android Studio Interface

Android Studio Interface is the focus of this Android Studio Basics lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

IDE

Software that combines code editing, building, running, and debugging tools.

Android SDK

Libraries and tools used to compile, test, and package Android applications.

Gradle

The build system that manages dependencies and produces Android app packages.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

// Module-level build.gradle.kts
dependencies {
    implementation("androidx.core:core-ktx:1.13.1")
}
// Sync the project, then Build > Make Project

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Android Studio Basics. For Android Studio Interface, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

The Project panel shows your files; the editor holds your code; Logcat shows what the running app reports; and the toolbar selects a device and runs the app.

Two habits pay off immediately: learn the Run and Debug buttons, and keep Logcat open. Almost every question about why an app misbehaves is answered there.

Key points

  • Project panel — files, switchable between Android and Project views.
  • Editor — code, with red underlines for compile errors.
  • Logcat — runtime output and crash stack traces.
  • Build panel — compile errors and Gradle output.
  • Run (green triangle) installs and starts; Debug attaches the debugger.
  • Ctrl+Shift+F / Cmd+Shift+F searches the whole project.

Example

A red underline in the editor is a compile error — the app will not build. A crash after the app starts is a runtime error, and its explanation is in Logcat, not the editor.

Why this matters

Distinguishing compile errors from runtime crashes is the first debugging skill, and it determines which panel to look at.

The build system that manages dependencies and produces Android app packages.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

// Module-level build.gradle.kts
dependencies {
    implementation("androidx.core:core-ktx:1.13.1")
}
// Sync the project, then Build > Make Project

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Android Studio Basics. For Project Structure, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

An Android project separates code from resources. Kotlin lives under app/src/main/java; layouts, images and strings live under app/src/main/res; and AndroidManifest.xml declares the app's components and permissions.

The res folder's subdirectory names are meaningful. layout, drawable, values and mipmap each have a defined purpose, and Android selects among qualified variants automatically by device.

Key points

  • java/ — Kotlin and Java source (the folder name is historical).
  • res/layout/ — XML layouts. res/drawable/ — images and shapes.
  • res/values/ — strings, colours, dimensions, styles.
  • res/mipmap/ — launcher icons only.
  • AndroidManifest.xml — components, permissions, app metadata.
  • build.gradle — dependencies and build configuration.

Example

Putting user-visible text in res/values/strings.xml rather than hard-coding it means translating the app later is a matter of adding one file, not editing every layout.

Why this matters

The structure is a convention the build system relies on. Files in the wrong folder either fail to build or silently fail to be found at runtime.

lessons.title: 3.3 Emulator Setup
lessons.html:
📖 Emulator Setup
A virtual device for testing, and when to use a real one instead.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Emulator Setup

Emulator Setup is the focus of this Android Studio Basics lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

IDE

Software that combines code editing, building, running, and debugging tools.

Android SDK

Libraries and tools used to compile, test, and package Android applications.

Gradle

The build system that manages dependencies and produces Android app packages.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

// Module-level build.gradle.kts
dependencies {
    implementation("androidx.core:core-ktx:1.13.1")
}
// Sync the project, then Build > Make Project

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Android Studio Basics. For Emulator Setup, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

The Device Manager creates an Android Virtual Device: choose a phone profile, a system image (an API level), and start it. It behaves like a real device for most purposes.

It is heavy. On a machine with limited RAM, a physical phone connected over USB is faster, uses no extra memory, and shows you genuine performance — which matters when your users are on modest hardware.

Key points

  • Create an AVD in Device Manager: profile + system image.
  • Choose an API level matching the devices you intend to support.
  • The emulator needs hardware virtualisation and a lot of RAM.
  • A physical device over USB is faster and more representative.
  • The emulator can simulate location, network speed and incoming calls.
  • Test on at least one low-end configuration, not only a flagship profile.

Example

The emulator lets you throttle the network to simulate a slow connection. Testing your app that way, rather than on fast Wi-Fi, reveals loading states you would otherwise never see.

Why this matters

Whichever you use, testing on something resembling your users' actual devices is what stops an app that feels fine in development from being unusable in the field.

questions.question: What does the Device Manager create?
questions.explanation: Device Manager configures emulators from a device profile and system image.

questions.question: Why might a physical phone be better than the emulator?
options: It is faster, uses no extra RAM and shows real performance
It is more accurate for colours
questions.explanation: Real hardware avoids the emulator's memory cost and reflects genuine device performance.

questions.question: Which emulator feature helps test poor connectivity?
questions.explanation: Throttling the network reveals loading and error states hidden by a fast connection.

lessons.html:
📖 Running Your First App
See your own code running on a real device.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Running Your First App

Running Your First App is the focus of this Android Studio Basics lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

IDE

Software that combines code editing, building, running, and debugging tools.

Android SDK

Libraries and tools used to compile, test, and package Android applications.

Gradle

The build system that manages dependencies and produces Android app packages.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

// Module-level build.gradle.kts
dependencies {
    implementation("androidx.core:core-ktx:1.13.1")
}
// Sync the project, then Build > Make Project

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Android Studio Basics. For Running Your First App, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Enable Developer Options and USB debugging on an Android phone, connect it, and run the app from Android Studio. Then change the text, run again, and watch it update.

Use a physical device if you have one. Emulators are slower on modest hardware, and a real phone shows you what users actually experience — including how the app looks in sunlight.

Key points

  • Enable Developer Options: tap Build Number seven times.
  • Turn on USB debugging and accept the prompt on the phone.
  • Prefer a real device to the emulator on a modest computer.
  • Change a string, run again, and confirm the change appears.
  • Read the Build output when it fails — the message names the problem.
  • Try it on the cheapest device you can find.

Example

Deliverable: a screenshot of your app running on a real phone, with text you wrote. Note the device model and Android version — you will want that record when a bug appears later.

Why this matters

The build-run-change loop is the fundamental rhythm of app development, and getting it working on real hardware early removes a persistent source of friction.

lessons.title: 3.5 Gradle Basics
lessons.html:
📖 Gradle Basics
The build system that turns your source into an installable app.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Gradle Basics

Gradle Basics is the focus of this Android Studio Basics lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

IDE

Software that combines code editing, building, running, and debugging tools.

Android SDK

Libraries and tools used to compile, test, and package Android applications.

Gradle

The build system that manages dependencies and produces Android app packages.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

// Module-level build.gradle.kts
dependencies {
    implementation("androidx.core:core-ktx:1.13.1")
}
// Sync the project, then Build > Make Project

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Android Studio Basics. For Gradle Basics, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Gradle compiles your code, merges resources, downloads dependencies and packages everything into an APK or AAB. You configure it in build.gradle files: one for the project, one for each module.

The module-level file is the one you edit most. It declares minSdk, targetSdk, the version name, and the dependencies block where every library you add appears as one line.

Key points

  • Project-level build.gradle configures plugins and repositories.
  • Module-level build.gradle holds SDK versions and dependencies.
  • Adding a library means one line in dependencies plus a Gradle sync.
  • versionCode is an integer Play uses; versionName is what users see.
  • Gradle caches dependencies, so only the first build is slow.
  • A failed sync blocks everything — read the Build panel message.

Example

Adding implementation("com.squareup.retrofit2:retrofit:2.9.0") and syncing is the whole process for pulling in the networking library used in Module 9.

Why this matters

Almost every capability you add to an app in this course begins with a dependency line, so being comfortable in this file matters more than it first appears.

questions.question: Which file holds an app module's dependencies?
questions.explanation: Dependencies are declared in the dependencies block of the module-level build.gradle.

questions.question: What is versionCode used for?
options: An integer Google Play uses to order releases
questions.explanation: versionCode is an internal integer; versionName is the human-readable string.

questions.question: Why is the first build much slower than later ones?
questions.explanation: Dependencies are fetched once and then served from the local cache.

lessons.title: 3.6 Android Manifest
lessons.html:
📖 Android Manifest
The declaration file Android reads before your code runs.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Android Manifest

Android Manifest is the focus of this Android Studio Basics lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

IDE

Software that combines code editing, building, running, and debugging tools.

Android SDK

Libraries and tools used to compile, test, and package Android applications.

Gradle

The build system that manages dependencies and produces Android app packages.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

// Module-level build.gradle.kts
dependencies {
    implementation("androidx.core:core-ktx:1.13.1")
}
// Sync the project, then Build > Make Project

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Android Studio Basics. For Android Manifest, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

AndroidManifest.xml tells the system what your app contains: its activities, its permissions, its launcher icon, and which screen starts first.

Anything not declared here does not exist as far as Android is concerned. An activity missing from the manifest crashes the app when you try to open it, with an error that names the class.

Key points

  • Every activity must be declared, or launching it crashes the app.
  • The LAUNCHER intent filter marks the screen that opens first.
  • Permissions are declared here: INTERNET, CAMERA, ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION.
  • Declaring a dangerous permission is not enough — you must also request it at runtime.
  • App name, icon and theme are set on the <application> element.
  • Request only the permissions you genuinely use; Play review checks this.

Example

Forgetting <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET"/> makes every network call fail with a security exception, which looks like a networking bug and is a manifest one.

Why this matters

The manifest is the first place to check when something works in code but fails at runtime, particularly around permissions and missing activities.

lessons.html: Quick check: Review the formal study notes, complete the coding exercises, then answer these questions to confirm you understood Android Manifest.

questions.question: What happens if an activity is not declared in the manifest?
options: The app crashes when you try to launch it
questions.explanation: Android refuses to start an undeclared activity and throws an error naming the class.

questions.question: Which permission must be declared for network access?
questions.explanation: Without the INTERNET permission all network calls fail with a security exception.

questions.question: Is declaring a dangerous permission in the manifest sufficient?
options: No, it must also be requested at runtime
questions.explanation: Dangerous permissions require an explicit runtime request in addition to the manifest entry.

lessons.title: 3.7 Logcat
lessons.html:
📖 Logcat
The running app talking to you.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Logcat

Logcat is the focus of this Android Studio Basics lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

IDE

Software that combines code editing, building, running, and debugging tools.

Android SDK

Libraries and tools used to compile, test, and package Android applications.

Gradle

The build system that manages dependencies and produces Android app packages.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

// Module-level build.gradle.kts
dependencies {
    implementation("androidx.core:core-ktx:1.13.1")
}
// Sync the project, then Build > Make Project

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Android Studio Basics. For Logcat, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Logcat streams messages from the device: your own log statements, framework messages, and the stack trace when something crashes. It is the primary debugging tool.

Log with the level that matches the message: Log.d for debugging, Log.i for information, Log.w for warnings, Log.e for errors. Filter by your tag or by package to cut the noise.

Key points

  • Log.d(TAG, "message") writes a debug line.
  • Levels: Verbose, Debug, Info, Warn, Error, Assert.
  • Filter by package or tag — unfiltered Logcat is unreadable.
  • A crash produces a stack trace; read from the top for the exception type.
  • “Caused by” lines point to the real origin.
  • Never log passwords, tokens or personal data — logs are readable on device.

Example

A crash trace beginning java.lang.NullPointerException with a “Caused by” line naming your file and line number tells you exactly where to look. The first line names the problem; the caused-by names the place.

Why this matters

Reading a stack trace is the single most useful debugging skill in this course, and it is mostly a matter of knowing which line to read first.

lessons.html: Quick check: Review the formal study notes, complete the coding exercises, then answer these questions to confirm you understood Logcat.

questions.question: Which method writes a debug message to Logcat?
questions.explanation: Log.d writes at debug level; Log.e is for errors.

questions.question: Where in a stack trace do you find the origin of a crash?
options: The 'Caused by' line naming your file
questions.explanation: The 'Caused by' section typically points to the line in your own code.

questions.question: What should never be written to Logcat?
questions.explanation: Device logs are readable by other tooling, so secrets must never be logged.

lessons.title: 3.8 Debugging Basics
lessons.html:
📖 Debugging Basics
Stop the app where it matters and look at the values.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Debugging Basics

Debugging Basics is the focus of this Android Studio Basics lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

IDE

Software that combines code editing, building, running, and debugging tools.

Android SDK

Libraries and tools used to compile, test, and package Android applications.

Gradle

The build system that manages dependencies and produces Android app packages.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

// Module-level build.gradle.kts
dependencies {
    implementation("androidx.core:core-ktx:1.13.1")
}
// Sync the project, then Build > Make Project

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Android Studio Basics. For Debugging Basics, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

A breakpoint pauses execution at a chosen line so you can inspect variables. Set one by clicking the gutter, then run with Debug rather than Run.

When paused, step over executes the current line, step into enters a function call, and the Variables panel shows every value in scope. This beats adding log statements and rebuilding.

Key points

  • Click the gutter to set a breakpoint; run with Debug.
  • Step over runs the line; step into enters the call.
  • The Variables panel shows live values at the pause point.
  • Conditional breakpoints pause only when an expression is true.
  • Debugging beats log-and-rebuild for anything non-trivial.
  • Reproduce the bug reliably before you start debugging it.

Example

For a crash that only happens on the fiftieth item, a conditional breakpoint on index == 49 pauses exactly there instead of making you step through forty-nine iterations.

Why this matters

Being able to inspect state at the moment of failure is what turns guesswork into diagnosis, and it is the skill Module 13 builds on.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Debugging Basics
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the formal study notes, complete the coding exercises, then answer these questions to confirm you understood Debugging Basics.

questions.question: What does a breakpoint do?
options: Pauses execution so you can inspect variables
questions.explanation: Breakpoints suspend the running app at a chosen line for inspection.

questions.question: What is the difference between step over and step into?
options: Step over runs the line; step into enters a function call
Step over skips the line entirely
questions.explanation: Step into descends into the called function; step over executes it and moves on.

questions.question: When is a conditional breakpoint most useful?
options: When a problem occurs only on a specific iteration or value
When the app will not compile
questions.explanation: Conditions avoid stepping through many irrelevant iterations to reach the failing case.

lessons.title: 3.9 Project Organization
lessons.html:
📖 Project Organization
Group files so the next person — usually you — can find them.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Project Organization

Project Organization is the focus of this Android Studio Basics lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

IDE

Software that combines code editing, building, running, and debugging tools.

Android SDK

Libraries and tools used to compile, test, and package Android applications.

Gradle

The build system that manages dependencies and produces Android app packages.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

// Module-level build.gradle.kts
dependencies {
    implementation("androidx.core:core-ktx:1.13.1")
}
// Sync the project, then Build > Make Project

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Android Studio Basics. For Project Organization, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

As an app grows past a handful of files, put related classes into packages: ui, data, model, network, util. The alternative is one flat folder of forty files.

Naming conventions matter for the same reason. Activities end in Activity, layouts are named after what they lay out, and resource ids describe the element rather than its position.

Key points

  • Package by role: ui, data, model, network, util.
  • Classes are PascalCase; functions and variables are camelCase.
  • Layout files are lowercase with underscores: activity_main.xml.
  • Resource ids describe purpose: btnSubmit, not button2.
  • Keep one class per file, named after the class.
  • Delete unused files; dead code is read as if it were live.

Example

button2 tells you nothing six weeks later, and nothing at all to a client's next developer. btnSubmitOrder costs the same to type and explains itself.

Why this matters

Freelance work in Module 16 often means reading someone else's project. Organisation is what determines whether that takes an hour or a week — and yours will be read the same way.

lessons.html: Quick check: Review the formal study notes, complete the coding exercises, then answer these questions to confirm you understood Project Organization.

questions.question: How should resource ids be named?
questions.explanation: Purpose-based names remain meaningful as the layout changes.

questions.question: What is the convention for layout file names?
questions.explanation: Android resource files use lowercase with underscores, such as activity_main.xml.

questions.question: Why does project organisation matter for freelance work?
options: You will often read and extend other people's projects, and they yours
questions.explanation: Maintenance work depends on being able to find things quickly in an unfamiliar codebase.

lessons.title: 3.10 Best Practices
lessons.html:
📖 Best Practices
Habits that keep an app maintainable as it grows.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Best Practices

Best Practices is the focus of this Android Studio Basics lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

IDE

Software that combines code editing, building, running, and debugging tools.

Android SDK

Libraries and tools used to compile, test, and package Android applications.

Gradle

The build system that manages dependencies and produces Android app packages.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

// Module-level build.gradle.kts
dependencies {
    implementation("androidx.core:core-ktx:1.13.1")
}
// Sync the project, then Build > Make Project

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Android Studio Basics. For Best Practices, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Most of what makes Android code good is unglamorous: keep strings in resources, keep functions short, handle errors, avoid doing work on the main thread, and do not repeat yourself.

The main-thread rule is the one with visible consequences. Any slow work — network calls, database queries, file reads — must run off the UI thread, or the app freezes and Android may kill it.

Key points

  • Never do network or disk work on the main thread.
  • Keep user-visible text in strings.xml.
  • Handle errors and show the user something useful.
  • Extract repeated code into functions; do not copy and paste.
  • Prefer val over var, and small functions over large ones.
  • Test on a low-end device and a slow connection before release.

Example

An app that freezes for four seconds during a network call is not slow, it is broken — Android shows an “application not responding” dialog and the user force-closes it. Module 9 covers doing this properly.

Why this matters

These practices are what separate an app that survives its second month from one that becomes unmaintainable, and they are what a client's reviewer looks for.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Best Practices
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the formal study notes, complete the coding exercises, then answer these questions to confirm you understood Best Practices.

questions.question: What must never run on the main thread?
questions.explanation: Slow work on the main thread freezes the interface and can trigger an ANR.

questions.question: Where should user-visible text live?
questions.explanation: Centralised strings support translation and reuse.

questions.question: What happens if the main thread is blocked too long?
options: Android shows an 'application not responding' dialog
questions.explanation: Blocking the UI thread triggers an ANR, which users experience as a frozen app.

lessons.title: 4.1 XML Layouts
lessons.html:
📖 XML Layouts
The screen described as a tree of views.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

XML Layouts

XML Layouts is the focus of this Android User Interface (UI) lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

View

A visible or interactive Android user-interface element.

layout

A container or rule system that positions views on a screen.

dp

Density-independent pixels used for consistent physical sizing across Android screens.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

<TextView
    android:id="@+id/titleText"
    android:layout_width="wrap_content"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="Welcome"
    android:textSize="24sp" />

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Android User Interface (UI). For XML Layouts, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

An Android screen is defined in XML: a root ViewGroup containing Views. Each element has attributes for size, position, appearance and an id your Kotlin code uses to find it.

Every view needs layout_width and layout_height. The three values are match_parent (fill the parent), wrap_content (fit the content), or a fixed size in dp.

Key points

  • A layout is a tree: a ViewGroup containing Views.
  • layout_width and layout_height are required on every view.
  • match_parent fills, wrap_content fits, dp fixes.
  • Use dp for sizes and sp for text, never raw pixels.
  • android:id="@+id/name" creates an id your code can find.
  • The Design and Split views help, but read the XML — it is the truth.

Example

dp scales with screen density, so a 48dp button is physically similar on a cheap phone and an expensive one. A size in pixels would be tiny on a high-density screen.

Why this matters

Every screen in the rest of this course is an XML layout, and using dp and sp correctly is what makes an app usable across the range of devices your users actually have.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: XML Layouts
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the formal study notes, complete the coding exercises, then answer these questions to confirm you understood XML Layouts.

questions.question: Which unit should be used for text size?
questions.explanation: sp scales with both density and the user's font size preference, which dp does not.

questions.question: What does layout_width="wrap_content" do?
options: Sizes the view to fit its content
questions.explanation: wrap_content sizes the view to exactly what it contains.

questions.question: Why use dp rather than px?
options: dp scales with screen density so sizes look consistent
questions.explanation: Density-independent pixels keep physical size consistent across different screen densities.

lessons.title: 4.2 TextView
lessons.html:
📖 TextView
Display text — the most used view in Android.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

TextView

TextView is the focus of this Android User Interface (UI) lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

View

A visible or interactive Android user-interface element.

layout

A container or rule system that positions views on a screen.

dp

Density-independent pixels used for consistent physical sizing across Android screens.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

<TextView
    android:id="@+id/titleText"
    android:layout_width="wrap_content"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="Welcome"
    android:textSize="24sp" />

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Android User Interface (UI). For TextView, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

A TextView shows text the user cannot edit. Its key attributes are text, textSize, textColor, textStyle and gravity.

Set the text from Kotlin with textView.text = "...". Reference strings from resources rather than hard-coding them, so the app can be translated.

Key points

  • android:text="@string/greeting" pulls from strings.xml.
  • In Kotlin: binding.tvGreeting.text = "Hello".
  • textSize in sp; textColor from a colour resource.
  • maxLines with ellipsize truncates long text cleanly.
  • gravity positions text inside the view; layout_gravity positions the view.
  • Long text without maxLines will push the rest of your layout off screen.

Example

A product name of unknown length in a list item needs android:maxLines="1" and android:ellipsize="end", or one long name breaks the alignment of every row.

Why this matters

Text that varies in length is the commonest cause of layouts that look right in the editor and wrong with real data.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: TextView
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the formal study notes, complete the coding exercises, then answer these questions to confirm you understood TextView.

questions.question: How do you set a TextView's text from Kotlin?
questions.explanation: Kotlin property syntax assigns directly to text.

questions.question: What prevents long text from breaking a row layout?
questions.explanation: Limiting lines and ellipsizing keeps the view a predictable height and width.

questions.question: What is the difference between gravity and layout_gravity?
options: gravity positions content inside the view; layout_gravity positions the view in its parent
questions.explanation: One aligns content within a view, the other aligns the view within its parent.

lessons.title: 4.3 EditText
lessons.html:
📖 EditText
Where the user types, and where validation begins.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

EditText

EditText is the focus of this Android User Interface (UI) lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

View

A visible or interactive Android user-interface element.

layout

A container or rule system that positions views on a screen.

dp

Density-independent pixels used for consistent physical sizing across Android screens.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

<TextView
    android:id="@+id/titleText"
    android:layout_width="wrap_content"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="Welcome"
    android:textSize="24sp" />

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Android User Interface (UI). For EditText, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

An EditText accepts typed input. Set hint rather than text so the field shows guidance that disappears when typing starts, and set inputType so the right keyboard appears.

Read it with editText.text.toString(). The value is always a String, so convert deliberately — and safely — before using it as a number.

Key points

  • hint shows guidance; text pre-fills the field.
  • inputType: text, number, textEmailAddress, textPassword.
  • Read with .text.toString(), then trim().
  • Convert with toIntOrNull(), never bare toInt().
  • Set error on the field to show inline validation messages.
  • Never store a password in plain text or log its value.

Example

Setting inputType="number" gives a numeric keyboard, which reduces mistyping. It does not prevent invalid input — the user can still paste text — so server-side or code validation is still required.

Why this matters

Input validation in the next lesson depends entirely on reading and converting these values safely.

options: No, it only changes the keyboard; validation is still needed

lessons.title: 4.4 Button
lessons.html:
📖 Button
The control that makes something happen.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Button

Button is the focus of this Android User Interface (UI) lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

View

A visible or interactive Android user-interface element.

layout

A container or rule system that positions views on a screen.

dp

Density-independent pixels used for consistent physical sizing across Android screens.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

<TextView
    android:id="@+id/titleText"
    android:layout_width="wrap_content"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="Welcome"
    android:textSize="24sp" />

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Android User Interface (UI). For Button, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

A Button is a clickable view. Give it an id, set its text, and attach a click listener in Kotlin with setOnClickListener { }.

Keep the listener short. It should read the input, call a function that does the work, and update the interface — not contain the logic itself, which is far harder to test.

Key points

  • btn.setOnClickListener { doThing() } attaches the handler.
  • Give buttons a minimum touch target of 48dp.
  • Disable the button while a slow operation runs, to prevent double submission.
  • Label the action, not the mechanism: Save order, not Submit.
  • Keep listener bodies short; delegate to named functions.
  • isEnabled and visibility control availability and presence separately.

Example

A submit button left enabled during a network call gets tapped three times on a slow connection, sending three orders. Disabling it on the first tap and re-enabling on completion prevents that entirely.

Why this matters

Double submission is one of the most common real bugs in field-tested apps, and it appears precisely on the slow connections your users have.
