lessons.html: Quick check: Review the formal study notes, complete the coding exercises, then answer these questions to confirm you understood Button.

questions.question: What is the recommended minimum touch target size?
questions.explanation: 48dp is the accessibility guideline for reliably tappable targets.

questions.question: How should a button behave during a slow network call?
options: Be disabled until the operation completes
questions.explanation: Disabling prevents repeated taps from submitting the same action multiple times.

questions.question: What belongs inside setOnClickListener?
options: A short call to a named function that does the work
questions.explanation: Short listeners that delegate are easier to read and to test.

lessons.title: 4.5 ImageView
lessons.html:
📖 ImageView
Show a picture, and keep it from destroying your memory budget.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

ImageView

ImageView is the focus of this Android User Interface (UI) lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

View

A visible or interactive Android user-interface element.

layout

A container or rule system that positions views on a screen.

dp

Density-independent pixels used for consistent physical sizing across Android screens.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

<TextView
    android:id="@+id/titleText"
    android:layout_width="wrap_content"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="Welcome"
    android:textSize="24sp" />

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Android User Interface (UI). For ImageView, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

An ImageView displays an image from resources (@drawable/logo), from a file, or from the network. scaleType controls how the image fits the view.

Large images are a leading cause of crashes. A photo straight from a camera can be several megapixels; loading it at full size into a small view exhausts memory. Use an image library, which handles resizing and caching for you.

Key points

  • scaleType: centerCrop fills and crops, fitCenter fits inside.
  • src sets the image; contentDescription is required for accessibility.
  • Loading a full-resolution photo into a small view can crash the app.
  • Use a library (Glide, Coil) for network images — it resizes and caches.
  • Provide a placeholder and an error image for network loads.
  • Keep bundled images modest; they inflate the app's download size.

Example

Coil in one line — imageView.load(url) — handles downloading, resizing, caching and cancellation. Doing it by hand correctly is considerably more code and usually gets the memory part wrong.

Why this matters

Image handling is where apps most often crash on low-memory devices, which is exactly the hardware much of the audience for these apps is using.

questions.question: Why can loading a full-resolution photo crash an app?
options: It can exhaust the memory available to the app
questions.explanation: Decoding a multi-megapixel image into memory can exceed the app's heap.

questions.question: What does scaleType="centerCrop" do?
options: Fits the whole image inside the view
Fills the view, cropping the overflow
questions.explanation: centerCrop scales to fill and crops whatever does not fit.

questions.question: Why use a library such as Glide or Coil for network images?
options: It removes the need for internet permission
It handles downloading, resizing and caching correctly
questions.explanation: These libraries solve resizing, caching and lifecycle cancellation, which are easy to get wrong by hand.

lessons.title: 4.6 RecyclerView
lessons.html:
📖 RecyclerView
Show a long list without holding every row in memory.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

RecyclerView

RecyclerView is the focus of this Android User Interface (UI) lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

View

A visible or interactive Android user-interface element.

layout

A container or rule system that positions views on a screen.

dp

Density-independent pixels used for consistent physical sizing across Android screens.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

<TextView
    android:id="@+id/titleText"
    android:layout_width="wrap_content"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="Welcome"
    android:textSize="24sp" />

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Android User Interface (UI). For RecyclerView, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

A RecyclerView displays a scrolling list by recycling a small number of row views as the user scrolls. A thousand-item list keeps only the visible rows plus a few, rather than a thousand views.

Three pieces are required: a layout for one row, an Adapter that binds data to that row, and a LayoutManager that decides the arrangement.

Key points

  • Needs a row layout, an Adapter and a LayoutManager.
  • ViewHolder caches the row's view references so lookup happens once.
  • onCreateViewHolder inflates a row; onBindViewHolder fills it with data.
  • getItemCount() must return the data size, or rows go missing.
  • Call notifyDataSetChanged() — or better, DiffUtil — after data changes.
  • Never do slow work inside onBindViewHolder; it runs during scrolling.

Example

A list that stutters while scrolling almost always has slow work in onBindViewHolder — loading an image synchronously, formatting a date, or querying a database. That method runs for every row that scrolls into view.

Why this matters

RecyclerView appears in nearly every app you will build from here on, and it is the single most asked-about component in Android interviews.

lessons.html: Quick check: Review the formal study notes, complete the coding exercises, then answer these questions to confirm you understood RecyclerView.

questions.question: Why is RecyclerView efficient for long lists?
options: It loads all rows at once
It recycles a small number of row views as you scroll
questions.explanation: Only visible rows plus a small buffer exist at any time, regardless of data size.

questions.question: What does onBindViewHolder do?
options: Fills an existing row view with data for a position
questions.explanation: onCreateViewHolder inflates; onBindViewHolder populates a recycled view.

questions.question: What causes stuttering while scrolling a RecyclerView?
questions.explanation: That method runs for every row scrolling into view, so anything slow there is felt directly.

lessons.title: 4.7 ScrollView
lessons.html:
📖 ScrollView
Let content taller than the screen be reached.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

ScrollView

ScrollView is the focus of this Android User Interface (UI) lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

View

A visible or interactive Android user-interface element.

layout

A container or rule system that positions views on a screen.

dp

Density-independent pixels used for consistent physical sizing across Android screens.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

<TextView
    android:id="@+id/titleText"
    android:layout_width="wrap_content"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="Welcome"
    android:textSize="24sp" />

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Android User Interface (UI). For ScrollView, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

A ScrollView makes its contents scrollable vertically. It takes exactly one direct child, so wrap everything in a LinearLayout or ConstraintLayout first.

Never put a RecyclerView inside a ScrollView. Both scroll, and nesting them destroys RecyclerView's recycling — every row is created at once, which is the problem RecyclerView exists to solve.

Key points

  • A ScrollView takes exactly one direct child.
  • Wrap multiple views in a LinearLayout inside it.
  • HorizontalScrollView scrolls sideways.
  • Never nest a RecyclerView inside a ScrollView.
  • Use NestedScrollView when working with Material scrolling behaviours.
  • Long forms need one; on a small screen the last field is otherwise unreachable.

Example

A registration form with eight fields fits on a large phone and not on a small one. Without a ScrollView the submit button is simply unreachable for those users, and the form cannot be completed at all.

Why this matters

This is a common accessibility failure that never shows up in development if you only test on one large device.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: ScrollView
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the formal study notes, complete the coding exercises, then answer these questions to confirm you understood ScrollView.

questions.question: How many direct children can a ScrollView have?
questions.explanation: A ScrollView takes a single child, which is usually a layout containing the rest.

questions.question: Why should a RecyclerView not be nested in a ScrollView?
options: It is not allowed to compile
It defeats recycling, so all rows are created at once
questions.explanation: Nesting forces the RecyclerView to full height, eliminating the view recycling it depends on.

questions.question: What problem does a missing ScrollView cause on small screens?
options: Content below the fold is unreachable
questions.explanation: Without scrolling, fields and buttons beyond the screen height cannot be reached.

lessons.title: 4.8 ConstraintLayout
lessons.html:
📖 ConstraintLayout
Position views by relationship, in one flat layout.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

ConstraintLayout

ConstraintLayout is the focus of this Android User Interface (UI) lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

View

A visible or interactive Android user-interface element.

layout

A container or rule system that positions views on a screen.

dp

Density-independent pixels used for consistent physical sizing across Android screens.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

<TextView
    android:id="@+id/titleText"
    android:layout_width="wrap_content"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="Welcome"
    android:textSize="24sp" />

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Android User Interface (UI). For ConstraintLayout, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

ConstraintLayout positions each view by constraining its edges to the parent or to other views. It replaces deeply nested layouts with a single flat one, which is both easier to read and faster to draw.

Every view needs at least one horizontal and one vertical constraint. A view without them compiles and then renders at the top-left corner at runtime, which is the most common ConstraintLayout surprise.

Key points

  • Constrain each view horizontally and vertically, or it lands at 0,0.
  • Constrain to the parent or to another view's edge.
  • 0dp width with both side constraints means “match constraints”.
  • Guidelines position at a percentage; chains distribute a group.
  • Barriers track the largest of several views.
  • Flat beats nested: fewer levels means faster layout passes.

Example

A view that looks correct in the Design editor but appears at the top-left when you run the app is missing a constraint. The editor shows your intent; the device shows the constraints you actually declared.

Why this matters

ConstraintLayout is the default for new Android layouts, and the missing-constraint symptom is worth recognising immediately because it is so common.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: ConstraintLayout
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the formal study notes, complete the coding exercises, then answer these questions to confirm you understood ConstraintLayout.

questions.question: What happens to a view with no constraints at runtime?
options: It appears at the top-left corner
questions.explanation: Unconstrained views default to position 0,0 when the layout is actually rendered.

questions.question: What does a width of 0dp mean in ConstraintLayout?
options: Match constraints, filling the space between them
questions.explanation: 0dp tells the layout to size the view to its constraints.

questions.question: What is the main advantage over nested layouts?
options: A flat hierarchy that is easier to read and faster to draw
questions.explanation: Fewer nesting levels means fewer layout passes and clearer structure.

lessons.title: 4.9 LinearLayout
lessons.html:
📖 LinearLayout
Stack views in a row or a column.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

LinearLayout

LinearLayout is the focus of this Android User Interface (UI) lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

View

A visible or interactive Android user-interface element.

layout

A container or rule system that positions views on a screen.

dp

Density-independent pixels used for consistent physical sizing across Android screens.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

<TextView
    android:id="@+id/titleText"
    android:layout_width="wrap_content"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="Welcome"
    android:textSize="24sp" />

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Android User Interface (UI). For LinearLayout, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

A LinearLayout arranges children in a single direction, set by orientation: vertical or horizontal. It is the simplest layout and remains useful for genuinely linear arrangements.

layout_weight distributes leftover space proportionally. Two children with weight 1 each take half the remaining space, which is how you split a row evenly without hard-coding widths.

Key points

  • orientation is required: vertical or horizontal.
  • layout_weight divides remaining space proportionally.
  • Set the dimension along the axis to 0dp when using weight.
  • Simple and readable, but nesting several is slow — prefer ConstraintLayout then.
  • gravity aligns children; layout_gravity aligns this view in its parent.
  • Good for toolbars, form rows and short vertical stacks.

Example

Two buttons side by side, each half the width: put them in a horizontal LinearLayout with layout_width="0dp" and layout_weight="1" on both. No fixed widths, so it adapts to any screen.

Why this matters

LinearLayout is still the right tool for simple rows and columns; the mistake is nesting four of them where one ConstraintLayout would do.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: LinearLayout
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the formal study notes, complete the coding exercises, then answer these questions to confirm you understood LinearLayout.

questions.question: What must be set alongside layout_weight for horizontal distribution?
questions.explanation: Setting the axis dimension to 0dp lets weight control the distribution.

questions.question: Two children with layout_weight="1" each receive:
questions.explanation: Equal weights divide the leftover space equally.

questions.question: When should you prefer ConstraintLayout over LinearLayout?
options: When the arrangement would require several nested LinearLayouts
questions.explanation: Deep nesting is where LinearLayout becomes slow and hard to read.

lessons.title: 4.10 RelativeLayout
lessons.html:
📖 RelativeLayout
Position views relative to each other — largely superseded.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

RelativeLayout

RelativeLayout is the focus of this Android User Interface (UI) lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

View

A visible or interactive Android user-interface element.

layout

A container or rule system that positions views on a screen.

dp

Density-independent pixels used for consistent physical sizing across Android screens.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

<TextView
    android:id="@+id/titleText"
    android:layout_width="wrap_content"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="Welcome"
    android:textSize="24sp" />

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Android User Interface (UI). For RelativeLayout, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

A RelativeLayout places each child relative to the parent or to a sibling: below this, to the right of that, aligned with the other. It was the standard before ConstraintLayout.

You will meet it in existing projects, which matters for the maintenance work in Module 16. For new layouts, ConstraintLayout does the same job with more capability and better performance.

Key points

  • Position with layout_below, layout_toRightOf, layout_alignParentTop.
  • Referenced siblings need ids.
  • Circular references cause a runtime exception, not a compile error.
  • Largely replaced by ConstraintLayout for new work.
  • Still common in older codebases you may be asked to maintain.
  • Converting to ConstraintLayout is offered by right-clicking the root in the editor.

Example

Two views each positioned below the other is a circular dependency. It compiles cleanly and throws at runtime, which is a good illustration of why ConstraintLayout's editor-time constraint checking is an improvement.

Why this matters

Recognising RelativeLayout is a practical necessity for freelance maintenance work, even though you are unlikely to write a new one.

questions.question: How does RelativeLayout position a child?
options: Relative to the parent or a sibling view
questions.explanation: Children are placed using relationships such as below, or aligned to the parent.

questions.question: What happens with a circular positioning reference?
options: It is caught at compile time
questions.explanation: RelativeLayout cannot resolve circular dependencies and raises a runtime exception.

questions.question: Why learn RelativeLayout at all?
options: It appears in existing projects you may maintain
questions.explanation: Maintenance work frequently involves older layouts written before ConstraintLayout.

lessons.title: 4.11 CardView
lessons.html:
📖 CardView
A raised, rounded container that groups related content.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

CardView

CardView is the focus of this Android User Interface (UI) lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

View

A visible or interactive Android user-interface element.

layout

A container or rule system that positions views on a screen.

dp

Density-independent pixels used for consistent physical sizing across Android screens.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

<TextView
    android:id="@+id/titleText"
    android:layout_width="wrap_content"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="Welcome"
    android:textSize="24sp" />

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Android User Interface (UI). For CardView, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

A CardView draws its children on a rounded, elevated surface. It is the standard way to present a discrete item — a product, a message, a summary — particularly as a RecyclerView row.

cardElevation controls the shadow, cardCornerRadius the rounding, and cardBackgroundColor the surface. Keep elevation modest; every card competing for prominence achieves none.

Key points

  • cardElevation sets the shadow depth.
  • cardCornerRadius rounds the corners.
  • Commonly used as the root of a RecyclerView row layout.
  • Add internal padding — content touching the card edge looks unfinished.
  • Keep elevation consistent; varied depths look accidental.
  • MaterialCardView adds theming and a checked state.

Example

A product list where each row is a CardView with an image, a name and a price reads as a set of distinct items. The same content in a plain LinearLayout reads as an undifferentiated wall of text.

Why this matters

Grouping related content visually is what makes a dense list scannable, and it is the most visible difference between an app that looks finished and one that does not.

questions.question: What does cardElevation control?
questions.explanation: Elevation determines how raised the card appears via its shadow.

questions.question: Where is CardView most commonly used?
options: As the root of a RecyclerView row
questions.explanation: Cards are the standard container for a discrete list item.

questions.question: What is a common mistake when using CardView?
options: Omitting internal padding so content touches the edge
questions.explanation: Without padding the content looks cramped against the card boundary.

lessons.title: 4.12 Material Design Components
lessons.html:
📖 M4:Material Design Components
Google's component library, so you are not building buttons from scratch.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Material Design Components

Material Design Components is the focus of this Android User Interface (UI) lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

View

A visible or interactive Android user-interface element.

layout

A container or rule system that positions views on a screen.

dp

Density-independent pixels used for consistent physical sizing across Android screens.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

<TextView
    android:id="@+id/titleText"
    android:layout_width="wrap_content"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="Welcome"
    android:textSize="24sp" />

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Android User Interface (UI). For Material Design Components, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Material Components provide ready-made, themed widgets: MaterialButton, TextInputLayout, MaterialCardView, FloatingActionButton, Chip, BottomNavigationView.

The practical benefit is TextInputLayout, which wraps an EditText and provides a floating label, helper text, character counter and an error slot — all things you would otherwise implement by hand and worse.

Key points

  • Add the Material dependency and use a Material theme.
  • TextInputLayout gives floating labels, helper text and error display.
  • MaterialButton supports filled, outlined and text styles.
  • FloatingActionButton marks the screen's primary action.
  • Components pick up colours from the theme — define them once.
  • Consistent components make an app look professional at very little cost.

Example

Showing a validation error with TextInputLayout is one line: tilEmail.error = "Enter a valid email". It renders in the right place, in the right colour, and clears itself when the user corrects the field.

Why this matters

Using the component library rather than styling raw views by hand is the fastest way to make an app look like it was built by someone who knew what they were doing.

questions.question: What does TextInputLayout add to an EditText?

questions.question: Which component marks a screen's primary action?
questions.explanation: The FAB is Material's convention for the single most important action on a screen.

lessons.title: 5.1 Click Events
lessons.html:
📖 Click Events
Connecting a tap to the code that should run.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Click Events

Click Events is the focus of this User Interaction lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

event listener

Code registered to run when a user or system event occurs.

input validation

Checking that entered data is present, correctly formatted, and acceptable.

Intent

An Android message used to request an action or open another component.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

binding.saveButton.setOnClickListener {
    val name = binding.nameInput.text.toString().trim()
    if (name.isBlank()) binding.nameInput.error = "Name is required"
    else Toast.makeText(this, "Saved", Toast.LENGTH_SHORT).show()
}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in User Interaction. For Click Events, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

A click listener is a function attached to a view that runs when the user taps it. In Kotlin: view.setOnClickListener { }.

Modern projects reach views through ViewBinding rather than findViewById. Binding is generated from the layout, so a missing or misspelled id is a compile error rather than a null at runtime.

Key points

  • setOnClickListener { } attaches a handler.
  • ViewBinding is type-safe; findViewById is not.
  • setOnLongClickListener handles a long press and must return a Boolean.
  • Attach listeners in onCreate, after the layout is set.
  • Debounce or disable during slow work to prevent double taps.
  • Keep the body short; call a named function.

Example

With ViewBinding, binding.btnSave.setOnClickListener { save() } fails to compile if the id changes. The findViewById equivalent compiles and crashes when the screen opens.

Why this matters

Every interactive screen in the rest of the course is built from listeners, and ViewBinding is what stops layout changes becoming runtime crashes.

lessons.title: 📝 Practice: Click Events
lessons.html: Quick check: Review the formal study notes, complete the coding exercises, then answer these questions to confirm you understood Click Events.

questions.question: What is the advantage of ViewBinding over findViewById?
options: It is type-safe, so a wrong id fails at compile time
It removes the need for ids
It is shorter to type only
questions.explanation: Binding classes are generated from the layout, so mismatches surface during compilation.

questions.question: Where should click listeners normally be attached?
options: In onCreate, after setting the layout
questions.explanation: Listeners are attached once the view hierarchy exists, which is after setContentView.

questions.question: What must setOnLongClickListener return?
options: A Boolean indicating whether the event was consumed
questions.explanation: Returning true consumes the long-press event; false lets it propagate.

lessons.title: 5.2 Input Validation
lessons.html:
📖 Input Validation
Check before you act, and tell the user exactly what is wrong.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Input Validation

Input Validation is the focus of this User Interaction lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

event listener

Code registered to run when a user or system event occurs.

input validation

Checking that entered data is present, correctly formatted, and acceptable.

Intent

An Android message used to request an action or open another component.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

binding.saveButton.setOnClickListener {
    val name = binding.nameInput.text.toString().trim()
    if (name.isBlank()) binding.nameInput.error = "Name is required"
    else Toast.makeText(this, "Saved", Toast.LENGTH_SHORT).show()
}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in User Interaction. For Input Validation, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Validation confirms input is present, correctly formed and within range before the app uses it. Do it as the user leaves a field or on submit, not silently at the end.

Error messages should say what to do. “Invalid input” leaves the user guessing; “Enter a phone number starting 077” does not.

Key points

  • Check for empty first, then format, then range.
  • trim() before checking — a space is not input.
  • Show errors on the field itself with TextInputLayout.error.
  • Say what to do, not merely that something is wrong.
  • Convert with toIntOrNull() and treat null as a validation failure.
  • Client-side validation is for usability; never rely on it for security.

Example

if (email.trim().isEmpty()) { tilEmail.error = "Enter your email address"; return } stops the submission, points at the field, and tells the user the fix.

Why this matters

Validation is what stops bad data reaching your storage and network layers in Modules 7 to 9, where the failures are much harder to diagnose.

📖 Toast Messages
A brief message that needs no response.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Toast Messages

Toast Messages is the focus of this User Interaction lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

event listener

Code registered to run when a user or system event occurs.

input validation

Checking that entered data is present, correctly formatted, and acceptable.

Intent

An Android message used to request an action or open another component.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

binding.saveButton.setOnClickListener {
    val name = binding.nameInput.text.toString().trim()
    if (name.isBlank()) binding.nameInput.error = "Name is required"
    else Toast.makeText(this, "Saved", Toast.LENGTH_SHORT).show()
}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in User Interaction. For Toast Messages, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

A Toast shows a short message that fades away on its own. It is right for confirmations — “Saved”, “Copied” — and wrong for anything the user must act on.

On newer Android versions toasts from a background app are restricted, and they are easy to miss. For anything important, a Snackbar is better: it sits in the layout, lasts longer and can carry an action such as Undo.

Key points

  • Toast.makeText(context, "Saved", Toast.LENGTH_SHORT).show().
  • Forgetting .show() is the classic mistake — nothing appears, no error.
  • Use for confirmations, not for errors requiring action.
  • Snackbar supports an action button and respects the layout.
  • Do not stack toasts; they queue and outlast their context.
  • Never put critical information only in a toast — it is easily missed.

Example

A delete action is better served by a Snackbar reading “Item deleted” with an Undo button than by a toast saying “Deleted”. The first is recoverable; the second is a notification of loss.

Why this matters

Choosing the right feedback mechanism is a large part of what makes an app feel considered rather than merely functional.

questions.question: What should never be communicated only by a Toast?
options: Critical information the user must act on
questions.explanation: Toasts fade quickly and are easily missed, so important messages need a persistent surface.

An AlertDialog presents a message with buttons and blocks interaction until dismissed. It suits confirmations of destructive actions and choices the app genuinely cannot proceed without.

Use MaterialAlertDialogBuilder for correct theming. Label the buttons with verbs — Delete and Cancel — rather than Yes and No, which force the user to re-read the question.

Key points

  • MaterialAlertDialogBuilder(context) then .setTitle(), .setMessage(), .show().
  • Label buttons with the action: Delete, not Yes.
  • Confirm destructive actions; do not confirm routine ones.
  • setCancelable(false) forces a choice — use sparingly.
  • A dialog holds a reference to its context; dismiss it before the screen goes.
  • For a set of options, a bottom sheet is often less disruptive.

Example

“Delete this order? [Delete] [Cancel]” is answerable at a glance. “Are you sure? [Yes] [No]” requires reading the title again to know what Yes means.

Why this matters

Dialogs interrupt by design, so the cost of an unnecessary one is real. Reserve them for actions that cannot be undone.

A menu holds actions that do not warrant a permanent button: refresh, settings, share, sort. Define the items in an XML menu resource, inflate them in onCreateOptionsMenu, and handle taps in onOptionsItemSelected.

showAsAction controls whether an item appears as an icon in the toolbar or inside the overflow menu. Reserve toolbar space for the one or two actions used most.

Key points

  • Menu items are defined in res/menu/ XML.
  • Inflate in onCreateOptionsMenu; handle in onOptionsItemSelected.
  • showAsAction="ifRoom" promotes an item to the toolbar.
  • Items in the toolbar need a contentDescription for accessibility.
  • Context menus appear on long press of a specific item.
  • Return true when you handle an item, or the event continues.

Example

A list screen typically promotes Search to the toolbar and leaves Sort, Filter and Settings in the overflow. Promoting all four leaves no room for the screen title.

Why this matters

Menus are how an app offers depth without cluttering the screen, and they appear in almost every app built in Modules 17 and 18.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Navigation Drawer

input validation

    else Toast.makeText(this, "Saved", Toast.LENGTH_SHORT).show()
}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in User Interaction. For Navigation Drawer, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

A navigation drawer slides in from the edge and lists the app's main sections. It suits apps with five or more top-level destinations, or destinations that do not fit a bottom bar.

It is less discoverable than bottom navigation, because the contents are hidden until opened. For three to five destinations, a bottom bar is usually the better choice.

Key points

  • DrawerLayout containing the content and a NavigationView.
  • Menu items come from an XML menu resource.
  • Suits five or more top-level destinations.
  • Less discoverable than a bottom bar — the contents are hidden.
  • Pair with the toolbar hamburger via ActionBarDrawerToggle.
  • Handle the back button so it closes the drawer before leaving the screen.

Example

An app with three main sections does not need a drawer. Putting them in a bottom bar makes all three visible at all times, and users find features they would never have opened a drawer to discover.

Why this matters

Choosing the navigation pattern to match the number of destinations is one of the clearest signals of a considered app, and it is judged immediately.

}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in User Interaction. For Bottom Navigation, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

A BottomNavigationView shows the app's main sections as tabs along the bottom edge. Because they are always visible, users find them without exploring.

It is designed for three to five destinations. Fewer than three wastes the bar; more than five crowds it and the labels stop fitting.

Key points

  • Suits three to five top-level destinations.
  • Items come from an XML menu resource, with an icon and a title each.
  • Reachable with a thumb, unlike a top toolbar on a large phone.
  • Each tab should keep its own back stack where possible.
  • Do not use it for actions — only for navigation between sections.
  • Pairs naturally with the Navigation Component in Module 6.

Example

Putting Home, Orders and Profile in a bottom bar means a user discovers all three in the first second. The same three in a drawer are found only by users who go looking.

Why this matters

Bottom navigation is the default choice for most small apps, and it is what the portfolio projects in Module 17 will mostly use.

📖 Intents
The message that starts a screen, or hands work to another app.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Intents

Intents is the focus of this User Interaction lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

event listener

Code registered to run when a user or system event occurs.

input validation

Checking that entered data is present, correctly formatted, and acceptable.

Intent

An Android message used to request an action or open another component.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

binding.saveButton.setOnClickListener {
    val name = binding.nameInput.text.toString().trim()
    if (name.isBlank()) binding.nameInput.error = "Name is required"
    else Toast.makeText(this, "Saved", Toast.LENGTH_SHORT).show()
}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in User Interaction. For Intents, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

An explicit intent names the component to start: Intent(this, DetailActivity::class.java). An implicit intent describes an action and lets Android choose an app that can handle it — sharing, dialling, opening a map.

Attach data with putExtra and read it in the destination with intent.getStringExtra. Keep extras small; they are not a data transfer mechanism for large objects.

Key points

  • Explicit: names the target component, used within your app.
  • Implicit: describes an action, handled by whichever app can.
  • putExtra(key, value) attaches data; read it with the matching getter.
  • Define extra keys as constants — a typo silently yields null.
  • Check an implicit intent can be handled before starting it.
  • Keep extras small; pass an id and re-load rather than a large object.

Example

Sharing text is an implicit intent with ACTION_SEND, and Android offers every messaging app installed. You did not integrate with any of them — the system did.

Why this matters

Intents are how Android apps cooperate, and they are the mechanism behind sharing, camera capture and opening links in the modules ahead.

questions.question: Why should large objects not be passed as intent extras?
options: Extras have a size limit and are not a data transfer mechanism
questions.explanation: Pass an identifier and re-load the data at the destination instead.

📖 Activities
One screen, one Activity — and one place where state is lost.

Tap a word to open its definition.

Activities

Activities is the focus of this User Interaction lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

event listener

Code registered to run when a user or system event occurs.

input validation

Checking that entered data is present, correctly formatted, and acceptable.

Intent

An Android message used to request an action or open another component.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

binding.saveButton.setOnClickListener {
    val name = binding.nameInput.text.toString().trim()
    if (name.isBlank()) binding.nameInput.error = "Name is required"
    else Toast.makeText(this, "Saved", Toast.LENGTH_SHORT).show()
}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in User Interaction. For Activities, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

An Activity represents a single screen with a user interface. It has a lifecycle Android drives, and a manifest entry declaring it exists.

The critical fact is that Android can destroy and recreate an activity at any time — on rotation, on low memory, on a language change. Any state held only in fields is lost when that happens.

Key points

  • Each Activity is one screen and must be declared in the manifest.
  • onCreate sets the layout and initialises the screen.
  • Android may destroy and recreate an activity at any point.
  • Rotation is the everyday case — test it deliberately.
  • Save transient state in onSaveInstanceState; keep real data elsewhere.
  • Modern apps favour one activity hosting several fragments.

Example

Type into a form, rotate the phone, and the fields empty: the activity was destroyed and recreated. It is not a bug in your code so much as a lifecycle fact your code has to accommodate.

Why this matters

Rotation loss is the single most common beginner bug in Android, and understanding why it happens is what Module 6's lifecycle lesson builds on.

questions.question: What is the modern structural preference?

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in User Interaction. For Fragments, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

A Fragment is a portion of a user interface hosted inside an activity. It has its own layout, its own lifecycle, and can be swapped without leaving the screen.

Fragments are the building blocks of single-activity apps. The Navigation Component in Module 6 moves between fragments rather than activities, which is why they matter more than their name suggests.

Key points

  • A fragment has its own layout and lifecycle, hosted by an activity.
  • Inflate the layout in onCreateView; wire views in onViewCreated.
  • The fragment's view is destroyed before the fragment itself.
  • Null the ViewBinding reference in onDestroyView to avoid a leak.
  • Communicate through a shared ViewModel, not direct references.
  • Fragments are the destinations the Navigation Component moves between.

Example

Holding a ViewBinding in a fragment field without clearing it in onDestroyView leaks the whole view hierarchy each time the fragment's view is recreated — a classic and easily missed Android memory leak.

Why this matters

Almost every screen you build from Module 6 onward is a fragment, so the view-lifecycle distinction is worth getting right now.

lessons.title: 6.1 Activity Lifecycle

📖 Activity Lifecycle
Six callbacks that describe a screen coming and going.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Activity Lifecycle

Activity Lifecycle is the focus of this App Navigation lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

lifecycle

The defined states through which an Android component moves as it is created, shown, paused, and destroyed.

back stack

The ordered history Android uses when the user moves backward through screens.

deep link

A URL or intent that opens a specific destination inside an app.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

findNavController().navigate(
    R.id.action_listFragment_to_detailFragment,
    bundleOf("itemId" to selectedId)
)

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in App Navigation. For Activity Lifecycle, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Android calls onCreate, onStart, onResume as a screen appears, and onPause, onStop, onDestroy as it goes. Each has a defined job.

The pairing matters: what you start in onStart you stop in onStop; what you register in onResume you unregister in onPause. Unpaired work is how apps leak memory and drain batteries in the background.

Key points

  • onCreate once per instance: set layout, initialise.
  • onStart / onStop: the screen becomes visible / hidden.
  • onResume / onPause: the screen gains / loses focus.
  • onDestroy: final cleanup, and not always called.
  • Pair every acquisition with its release in the matching callback.
  • Never assume onDestroy will run — the process can be killed.

Example

Starting location updates in onResume and forgetting to stop them in onPause keeps the GPS running while the user is in another app. The battery drain is blamed on your app, correctly.

Why this matters

Lifecycle-aware behaviour is what separates an app that behaves well in the background from one users uninstall for draining the phone.

questions.explanation: Android can terminate the process without calling onDestroy, so critical cleanup cannot depend on it.

questions.question: What is the consequence of unpaired lifecycle work?
options: Memory leaks and battery drain when the app is backgrounded
questions.explanation: Resources acquired and never released continue consuming memory and power.

Like an activity's, plus a separate life for the view.

Tap a word to open its definition.

Fragment Lifecycle

Fragment Lifecycle is the focus of this App Navigation lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

lifecycle

The defined states through which an Android component moves as it is created, shown, paused, and destroyed.

back stack

The ordered history Android uses when the user moves backward through screens.

deep link

A URL or intent that opens a specific destination inside an app.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

findNavController().navigate(
    R.id.action_listFragment_to_detailFragment,
    bundleOf("itemId" to selectedId)
)

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in App Navigation. For Fragment Lifecycle, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

A fragment has the activity callbacks plus view-specific ones: onCreateView, onViewCreated, onDestroyView. The fragment instance can outlive its view.

That separation is the source of most fragment bugs. A reference held to a view after onDestroyView either leaks or crashes when the fragment's view is recreated.

Key points

  • onCreateView inflates; onViewCreated wires up the views.
  • onDestroyView destroys the view while the fragment survives.
  • Clear view references in onDestroyView, always.
  • Use viewLifecycleOwner, not this, when observing LiveData.
  • Arguments are passed via a Bundle, ideally through Safe Args.
  • A ViewModel scoped to the fragment survives the view, not the fragment.

Example

Observing LiveData with this instead of viewLifecycleOwner means the observer outlives the view and updates a destroyed hierarchy — a crash that appears only after navigating back and forth.

Why this matters

This distinction accounts for a large share of the crashes in real fragment-based apps, and it is invisible until you navigate away and return.

lessons.title: 6.3 Navigation Component
lessons.html:
📖 Navigation Component
One graph describing every route through the app.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Navigation Component

Navigation Component is the focus of this App Navigation lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

lifecycle

The defined states through which an Android component moves as it is created, shown, paused, and destroyed.

back stack

The ordered history Android uses when the user moves backward through screens.

deep link

A URL or intent that opens a specific destination inside an app.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

findNavController().navigate(
    R.id.action_listFragment_to_detailFragment,
    bundleOf("itemId" to selectedId)
)

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in App Navigation. For Navigation Component, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

The Navigation Component holds your destinations and the actions between them in a single XML graph. A NavHostFragment hosts the current destination and a NavController moves between them.

The benefit is that navigation stops being scattered across activities. The graph is a diagram of the app you can read, and the back stack is handled for you rather than by hand.

Key points

  • A nav graph declares destinations and the actions joining them.
  • NavHostFragment hosts destinations; NavController navigates.
  • findNavController().navigate(R.id.action_list_to_detail).
  • The back stack is managed for you.
  • Wire it to a bottom bar with setupWithNavController.
  • The graph is a readable diagram of the whole app.

Example

Adding a screen means adding a destination and an action to the graph. Without the component, the same change touches every activity that could reach it, and the back stack must be reasoned about manually.

Why this matters

Every multi-screen app from here on uses this, and it is what makes single-activity architecture practical.

lessons.title: 6.4 Passing Data Between Screens
lessons.html:
📖 Passing Data Between Screens
Safe Args turns a runtime typo into a compile error.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Passing Data Between Screens

Passing Data Between Screens is the focus of this App Navigation lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

lifecycle

The defined states through which an Android component moves as it is created, shown, paused, and destroyed.

back stack

The ordered history Android uses when the user moves backward through screens.

deep link

A URL or intent that opens a specific destination inside an app.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

findNavController().navigate(
    R.id.action_listFragment_to_detailFragment,
    bundleOf("itemId" to selectedId)
)

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in App Navigation. For Passing Data Between Screens, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Destinations can declare arguments in the nav graph. The Safe Args plugin generates typed classes from those declarations, so passing and reading data is checked by the compiler.

The alternative — a Bundle with string keys — compiles regardless of typos and yields null at runtime. Safe Args removes that whole class of bug.

Key points

  • Declare arguments on the destination in the nav graph.
  • Safe Args generates typed Directions and Args classes.
  • ListFragmentDirections.actionToDetail(id) is checked at compile time.
  • Read with by navArgs() in the destination.
  • Pass identifiers, not large objects — re-load at the destination.
  • A shared ViewModel suits data two screens both need.

Example

bundle.getString("userId") returns null forever if the key was written "userID" when it was put in. The Safe Args equivalent does not compile.

Why this matters

Argument mismatches are among the most common and most frustrating bugs in fragment navigation, and this removes them entirely.

questions.question: What problem does Safe Args solve?

questions.explanation: Arguments have size limits and large payloads are fragile across process death.

questions.question: How are arguments read in the destination fragment?
questions.explanation: The generated Args class is retrieved with the navArgs delegate.

📖 Deep Links
A URL that opens a specific screen inside your app.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Deep Links

Deep Links is the focus of this App Navigation lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

lifecycle

The defined states through which an Android component moves as it is created, shown, paused, and destroyed.

back stack

The ordered history Android uses when the user moves backward through screens.

deep link

A URL or intent that opens a specific destination inside an app.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

findNavController().navigate(
    R.id.action_listFragment_to_detailFragment,
    bundleOf("itemId" to selectedId)
)

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in App Navigation. For Deep Links, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

A deep link maps a URL or notification to a particular destination. Tapping a link to an order takes the user to that order, not to the home screen.

The subtlety is the back stack. A user arriving from outside should still be able to press back and reach a sensible parent screen rather than being ejected from the app.

Key points

  • Declare <deepLink> on a destination in the nav graph.
  • The Navigation Component builds a synthetic back stack for you.
  • App Links are verified deep links that skip the chooser dialog.
  • Verification requires a file hosted on your domain.
  • Always validate parameters — a deep link is untrusted input.
  • Test with adb shell am start -W -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d "...".

Example

A notification for a new message should open that conversation. Opening the app's home screen instead forces the user to find it again, which is the difference between a notification that works and one that gets disabled.

Why this matters

Deep links are what make notifications and shared links useful, and they are expected in any app that sends either.

lessons.title: 6.6 Back Stack Management
lessons.html:
📖 Back Stack Management
Back should undo the last navigation, and nothing more surprising.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Back Stack Management

Back Stack Management is the focus of this App Navigation lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

lifecycle

The defined states through which an Android component moves as it is created, shown, paused, and destroyed.

back stack

The ordered history Android uses when the user moves backward through screens.

deep link

A URL or intent that opens a specific destination inside an app.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

findNavController().navigate(
    R.id.action_listFragment_to_detailFragment,
    bundleOf("itemId" to selectedId)
)

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in App Navigation. For Back Stack Management, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

The back stack records the destinations visited. Pressing back pops the top entry. Most problems arise when the stack accumulates entries it should not.

The common case is a login screen. After signing in, the user should not be able to press back into it, so that destination is popped rather than left on the stack.

Key points

  • Back pops the top destination; the stack records the path taken.
  • Use popUpTo with inclusive to remove destinations behind you.
  • Pop the login screen after a successful sign-in.
  • Avoid loops — A to B to A grows the stack indefinitely.
  • Each bottom-navigation tab should keep its own stack.
  • Test back from every screen, including after a deep link.

Example

Without popUpTo, signing in leaves Login on the stack. The user presses back from Home and is looking at the login form again while signed in — confusing, and a common review complaint.

Why this matters

Back behaviour is one of the first things a user notices when it is wrong, and one of the least noticed when it is right.

questions.question: What should happen to the login screen after a successful sign-in?
options: Be popped so back does not return to it
questions.explanation: popUpTo with inclusive removes it, so back from Home behaves sensibly.

questions.question: What causes a back stack to grow indefinitely?
options: Navigation loops such as A to B to A
questions.explanation: Each traversal adds an entry unless the previous one is popped.

questions.question: How should bottom-navigation tabs handle the back stack?
questions.explanation: Per-tab stacks preserve each section's position when switching between them.

📖 Navigation Best Practices
One graph, typed arguments, predictable back behaviour.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Navigation Best Practices

Navigation Best Practices is the focus of this App Navigation lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

lifecycle

The defined states through which an Android component moves as it is created, shown, paused, and destroyed.

back stack

The ordered history Android uses when the user moves backward through screens.

deep link

A URL or intent that opens a specific destination inside an app.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

findNavController().navigate(
    R.id.action_listFragment_to_detailFragment,
    bundleOf("itemId" to selectedId)
)

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in App Navigation. For Navigation Best Practices, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Good navigation is mostly a matter of a few consistent decisions: a single activity, fragments as destinations, Safe Args for data, and a back stack that behaves the same everywhere.

The test is whether a new developer can read the nav graph and understand how the app fits together. If routes are scattered across activities and manual transactions, they cannot.

Key points

  • Prefer one activity hosting a graph of fragment destinations.
  • Use Safe Args for every argument — no raw Bundle keys.
  • Pop screens the user should not return to.
  • Keep the graph readable; split into nested graphs by feature when it grows.
  • Handle deep links and their back stacks explicitly.
  • Test back from every destination, including after configuration change.

Example

A readable nav graph is documentation that cannot go stale, because it is the thing the app actually runs on. A diagram in a wiki is neither.

Why this matters

Navigation structure is one of the first things reviewed in a code interview, because it reveals whether an app was designed or accumulated.

lessons.title: 7.1 SharedPreferences
lessons.html:
📖 SharedPreferences
Small key-value settings, and nothing more.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

SharedPreferences

SharedPreferences is the focus of this Data Storage lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

persistence

Keeping data available after a screen closes or the app restarts.

Room

Android Jetpack’s abstraction layer for working safely with SQLite databases.

CRUD

The four core data operations: create, read, update, and delete.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

@Entity
data class Note(
    @PrimaryKey(autoGenerate = true) val id: Int = 0,
    val text: String
)
@Dao interface NoteDao {
    @Query("SELECT * FROM Note") suspend fun getAll(): List<Note>
}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Data Storage. For SharedPreferences, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

SharedPreferences stores small primitives — a theme choice, a boolean flag, a user id — as key-value pairs that survive restarts.

It is the wrong tool for anything structured or large. Storing a serialised list in it is a common beginner mistake that becomes unworkable as the data grows, and it offers no querying at all.

Key points

  • Stores primitives: Boolean, Int, Long, Float, String, Set<String>.
  • apply() writes asynchronously; commit() blocks and returns a result.
  • Prefer apply() on the main thread.
  • Not for structured data — use a database.
  • Not secure — use EncryptedSharedPreferences for anything sensitive.
  • Jetpack DataStore is the modern replacement.

Example

Storing a JSON list of orders in SharedPreferences works with five orders and fails with five hundred: every read parses the whole string, and there is no way to query or update one record.

Why this matters

Knowing where the boundary lies — settings here, data in Room — avoids a rewrite later in the project.

📖 Internal Storage
Private files only your app can read.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Internal Storage

Internal Storage is the focus of this Data Storage lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

persistence

Keeping data available after a screen closes or the app restarts.

Room

Android Jetpack’s abstraction layer for working safely with SQLite databases.

CRUD

The four core data operations: create, read, update, and delete.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

@Entity
data class Note(
    @PrimaryKey(autoGenerate = true) val id: Int = 0,
    val text: String
)
@Dao interface NoteDao {
    @Query("SELECT * FROM Note") suspend fun getAll(): List<Note>
}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Data Storage. For Internal Storage, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Internal storage is a directory belonging to your app. No other app can read it, no permission is required, and Android deletes it when your app is uninstalled.

Use it for files that are private to the app: a cached response, a generated report, a downloaded document the user does not need in their gallery.

Key points

  • Private to your app; no permission needed.
  • context.filesDir for persistent files, cacheDir for disposable ones.
  • Deleted automatically when the app is uninstalled.
  • Android may clear cacheDir under storage pressure — never rely on it.
  • Do file work off the main thread.
  • Space is limited; check before writing large files.

Example

A cached API response belongs in cacheDir: if Android reclaims it, the app re-fetches. The same file in filesDir is never reclaimed and grows without bound.

Why this matters

Choosing the right directory decides whether your app handles low storage gracefully or is the reason the device runs out.

📖 External Storage
Shared media, and the scoped-storage rules that now govern it.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

External Storage

External Storage is the focus of this Data Storage lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

persistence

Keeping data available after a screen closes or the app restarts.

Room

Android Jetpack’s abstraction layer for working safely with SQLite databases.

CRUD

The four core data operations: create, read, update, and delete.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

@Entity
data class Note(
    @PrimaryKey(autoGenerate = true) val id: Int = 0,
    val text: String
)
@Dao interface NoteDao {
    @Query("SELECT * FROM Note") suspend fun getAll(): List<Note>
}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Data Storage. For External Storage, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

External storage holds files the user or other apps may see: photos, downloads, documents. Since Android 10, scoped storage restricts direct filesystem access.

Apps now write media through MediaStore and let the user choose locations through the Storage Access Framework, rather than writing wherever they like. Broad file permissions are largely gone.

Key points

  • Scoped storage applies from Android 10 onward.
  • Write media through MediaStore, not raw paths.
  • Use the Storage Access Framework to let the user pick a location.
  • App-specific external directories need no permission.
  • MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE is restricted and rejected by Play without justification.
  • Media written via MediaStore appears in the gallery automatically.

Example

An app saving a photo to a hard-coded path worked on Android 9 and fails on Android 10 and later. The MediaStore equivalent works on both and puts the photo in the gallery without extra code.

Why this matters

Storage is one of the areas where Android changed most, and code copied from older tutorials fails on every current device.

lessons.title: 7.4 SQLite Database
lessons.html:
📖 SQLite Database
The relational database built into every Android device.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

SQLite Database

SQLite Database is the focus of this Data Storage lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

persistence

Keeping data available after a screen closes or the app restarts.

Room

Android Jetpack’s abstraction layer for working safely with SQLite databases.

CRUD

The four core data operations: create, read, update, and delete.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

@Entity
data class Note(
    @PrimaryKey(autoGenerate = true) val id: Int = 0,
    val text: String
)
@Dao interface NoteDao {
    @Query("SELECT * FROM Note") suspend fun getAll(): List<Note>
}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Data Storage. For SQLite Database, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

SQLite is an embedded relational database, present on every Android device, storing the whole database in a single file. It supports normal SQL: tables, queries, joins, transactions.

You will rarely use its raw API. Understanding it still matters, because Room is a layer over SQLite and its errors, migrations and query semantics are SQLite's.

Key points

  • Embedded, file-based, requires no server.
  • Standard SQL: CREATE TABLE, SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE.
  • Every table should have a primary key.
  • Index columns you filter or join on.
  • Use transactions for multi-statement writes.
  • Room generates SQLite code, so its errors are SQLite errors.

Example

A slow list is often a missing index rather than a slow device. Adding an index on the column being filtered can turn a visible pause into an instant result on the same data.

Why this matters

Room hides the syntax but not the semantics; knowing SQLite is what lets you read the query Room generates and understand why it is slow.

lessons.title: 7.5 Room Database
lessons.html:
📖 Room Database
A compile-time-checked layer over SQLite.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Room Database

Room Database is the focus of this Data Storage lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

persistence

Keeping data available after a screen closes or the app restarts.

Room

Android Jetpack’s abstraction layer for working safely with SQLite databases.

CRUD

The four core data operations: create, read, update, and delete.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

@Entity
data class Note(
    @PrimaryKey(autoGenerate = true) val id: Int = 0,
    val text: String
)
@Dao interface NoteDao {
    @Query("SELECT * FROM Note") suspend fun getAll(): List<Note>
}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Data Storage. For Room Database, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Room has three parts: an Entity describing a table, a DAO declaring queries, and a Database class tying them together.

Its main advantage is that it verifies your SQL at compile time. A misspelled column or a query returning the wrong shape fails the build rather than crashing on a user's device.

Key points

  • @Entity defines a table; @Dao declares queries; @Database ties them together.
  • SQL in @Query is verified at compile time.
  • Return Flow or LiveData for queries that should update automatically.
  • Suspend functions keep writes off the main thread.
  • Migrations are required when the schema changes.
  • Room is the recommended local persistence library.

Example

A typo in a column name inside @Query fails the build with a clear message. The same typo in raw SQLite throws at runtime, on a device, in front of a user.

Why this matters

Room is the standard for local storage in modern Android, and its compile-time checking removes an entire category of production crash.

Create, read, update, delete — the four things every data app does.

CRUD Operations

CRUD Operations is the focus of this Data Storage lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

persistence

Keeping data available after a screen closes or the app restarts.

Room

Android Jetpack’s abstraction layer for working safely with SQLite databases.

CRUD

The four core data operations: create, read, update, and delete.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

@Entity
data class Note(
    @PrimaryKey(autoGenerate = true) val id: Int = 0,
    val text: String
)
@Dao interface NoteDao {
    @Query("SELECT * FROM Note") suspend fun getAll(): List<Note>
}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Data Storage. For CRUD Operations, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Room provides annotations for three of them: @Insert, @Update, @Delete. Reads use @Query with your own SQL.

Writes must not run on the main thread. Mark DAO write functions suspend and call them from a coroutine, or Room will throw.

Key points

  • @Insert, @Update, @Delete generate the SQL for you.
  • @Query for reads and anything conditional.
  • Mark write functions suspend — Room rejects main-thread writes.
  • OnConflictStrategy.REPLACE handles inserting an existing key.
  • Reads returning Flow update the UI automatically on change.
  • Wrap multi-step writes in a transaction.

Example

Calling a blocking DAO write from the main thread throws IllegalStateException immediately. That is deliberate: Room fails loudly rather than letting the app freeze under load.

Why this matters

CRUD through a DAO is the backbone of the offline-capable apps built in Modules 17 and 18.

lessons.title: 7.7 Data Persistence

📖 Data Persistence
Choosing where each kind of data belongs.

Key Words & Meanings

Keeping data available after a screen closes or the app restarts.

Room

Android Jetpack’s abstraction layer for working safely with SQLite databases.

CRUD

The four core data operations: create, read, update, and delete.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

@Entity
data class Note(
    @PrimaryKey(autoGenerate = true) val id: Int = 0,
    val text: String
)
@Dao interface NoteDao {
    @Query("SELECT * FROM Note") suspend fun getAll(): List<Note>
}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Data Storage. For Data Persistence, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Android offers several stores and each has one job. Settings go in DataStore or SharedPreferences. Structured records go in Room. Files go in internal or external storage. Remote data lives on a server and is cached locally.

Most persistence problems come from using the wrong one — usually a list squeezed into preferences, or images stored as rows in a database.

Key points

  • Settings and flags → DataStore or SharedPreferences.
  • Structured records → Room.
  • Files and images → internal or external storage; store the path in Room.
  • Remote data → server, cached locally for offline use.
  • Never store large binaries as database rows.
  • Decide once, early — migrating later is expensive.

Example

Storing photos as byte arrays in a Room table makes every query slow and the database enormous. Storing the file on disk and its path in the table keeps queries fast and the file manageable.

Why this matters

These choices are made in the first hour of a project and are painful to reverse, which is why they are worth deliberate thought.

questions.explanation: Data already written in the wrong place must be migrated, which is far more work than choosing correctly.

Offline-capable apps read from a local database and treat the network as a way to refresh it. The screen renders from Room; a sync updates Room; the UI follows.

This matters particularly for learners here, where connections are intermittent. An app that shows a spinner whenever the signal drops is unusable; one that shows yesterday's data and syncs later is not.

Key points

  • Read from the local database; treat the network as a refresh mechanism.
  • Cache responses on success so the last good data is always available.
  • Show cached data with a quiet indicator rather than a blocking spinner.
  • Queue writes made offline and send them when connectivity returns.
  • WorkManager handles deferred sync that survives restarts.
  • Decide a conflict rule before you need one.

Example

A market-price app that caches yesterday's prices is useful on a weak connection. The same app showing only a spinner is uninstalled the first time it is opened in a village.

Why this matters

Offline-first is not an optimisation in this context; it is the difference between an app people keep and one they delete.

questions.explanation: Queuing lets the user keep working and syncs when the network is available.

lessons.html:
📖 Introduction to Firebase
A hosted backend for developers who do not want to run one.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Introduction to Firebase

Introduction to Firebase is the focus of this Firebase Integration lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

Firebase

Google’s platform of hosted backend services for mobile and web applications.

Firestore

A cloud NoSQL document database with real-time synchronisation.

Cloud Messaging

Firebase service used to deliver push notifications to applications.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

val db = Firebase.firestore
val learner = hashMapOf("name" to "Samuel", "active" to true)
db.collection("learners").add(learner)
    .addOnSuccessListener { document -> Log.d("DB", document.id) }
    .addOnFailureListener { error -> Log.e("DB", "Save failed", error) }

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Firebase Integration. For Introduction to Firebase, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Firebase is Google's backend platform: authentication, databases, file storage, push notifications, analytics and crash reporting, all consumed from the app through SDKs.

For a solo developer or a small team it removes the need to build and operate a server. The trade-offs are vendor lock-in and cost at scale, but for a first commercial app they are usually acceptable.

Key points

  • Provides auth, databases, storage, messaging, analytics and crash reporting.
  • Removes the need to run your own server.
  • Configured with a google-services.json file in the app module.
  • The free tier covers development and small production apps.
  • Costs scale with reads, writes and storage — model this before launch.
  • Never commit API keys or service accounts to a public repository.

Example

An app with authentication, a synced database and push notifications can be built in a weekend on Firebase. The same stack self-hosted is weeks of work plus ongoing operations.

Why this matters

Firebase is what makes a complete, cloud-backed app realistic for the portfolio projects in this course.

lessons.title: 8.2 Firebase Authentication
lessons.html:
📖 Firebase Authentication
Sign-in handled by someone who has thought about it more than you have.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Firebase Authentication

Firebase Authentication is the focus of this Firebase Integration lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

Firebase

Google’s platform of hosted backend services for mobile and web applications.

Firestore

A cloud NoSQL document database with real-time synchronisation.

Cloud Messaging

Firebase service used to deliver push notifications to applications.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

val db = Firebase.firestore
val learner = hashMapOf("name" to "Samuel", "active" to true)
db.collection("learners").add(learner)
    .addOnSuccessListener { document -> Log.d("DB", document.id) }
    .addOnFailureListener { error -> Log.e("DB", "Save failed", error) }

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Firebase Integration. For Firebase Authentication, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Firebase Authentication provides email/password, phone, Google, and other sign-in methods, plus password reset, email verification and session handling.

Building this yourself means implementing secure password storage, reset flows, rate limiting and session expiry — each of which is a well-known source of vulnerabilities.

Key points

  • Supports email/password, phone, Google and federated providers.
  • Handles hashing, reset flows, verification and sessions for you.
  • FirebaseAuth.getInstance().currentUser gives the signed-in user or null.
  • The UID is the stable key to link user data to.
  • Security rules on the database check the authenticated user, not the app.
  • Phone sign-in suits regions where email is less common.

Example

A password reset flow you build yourself must generate an unguessable single-use token, expire it, and avoid revealing whether an account exists. Getting any of those wrong is an account-takeover vulnerability.

Why this matters

Authentication is exactly the kind of security-critical code worth delegating, and every app in Module 12 uses it.
