lessons.title: 8.3 Firestore Database
lessons.html:
📖 Firestore Database
A document database that syncs and works offline.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Firestore Database

Firestore Database is the focus of this Firebase Integration lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

Firebase

Google’s platform of hosted backend services for mobile and web applications.

Firestore

A cloud NoSQL document database with real-time synchronisation.

Cloud Messaging

Firebase service used to deliver push notifications to applications.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

val db = Firebase.firestore
val learner = hashMapOf("name" to "Samuel", "active" to true)
db.collection("learners").add(learner)
    .addOnSuccessListener { document -> Log.d("DB", document.id) }
    .addOnFailureListener { error -> Log.e("DB", "Save failed", error) }

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Firebase Integration. For Firestore Database, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Firestore stores data as documents grouped into collections. It syncs across devices in real time and caches locally, so an app keeps working without a connection.

Its pricing model shapes its data modelling: you pay per document read. Structures that require reading many documents to render one screen become expensive in a way that a relational database would not.

Key points

  • Data is documents inside collections; documents can hold subcollections.
  • Real-time listeners push changes as they happen.
  • Offline caching is enabled by default on Android.
  • You pay per document read, so model to minimise reads.
  • Denormalise deliberately — duplication is often cheaper than joins.
  • Security rules are the only thing protecting the data.

Example

Rendering a feed that needs one read per item costs a hundred reads for a hundred items. Storing a summary document containing what the feed needs costs one, and duplication is the accepted trade.

Why this matters

Firestore's cost model rewards data modelling decisions that a relational background would consider wrong, which is the main adjustment when learning it.

lessons.title: 8.4 Firebase Realtime Database
lessons.html:
📖 Firebase Realtime Database
The older sibling: one JSON tree, very fast, less queryable.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Firebase Realtime Database

Firebase Realtime Database is the focus of this Firebase Integration lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

Firebase

Google’s platform of hosted backend services for mobile and web applications.

Firestore

A cloud NoSQL document database with real-time synchronisation.

Cloud Messaging

Firebase service used to deliver push notifications to applications.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

val db = Firebase.firestore
val learner = hashMapOf("name" to "Samuel", "active" to true)
db.collection("learners").add(learner)
    .addOnSuccessListener { document -> Log.d("DB", document.id) }
    .addOnFailureListener { error -> Log.e("DB", "Save failed", error) }

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Firebase Integration. For Firebase Realtime Database, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

The Realtime Database stores everything as a single large JSON tree and synchronises changes with very low latency. It predates Firestore and is still used where speed matters more than querying.

Its limitation is querying. There is no equivalent of Firestore's compound queries, so complex filtering means restructuring the tree or filtering on the client.

Key points

  • One JSON tree rather than documents and collections.
  • Lower latency; well suited to chat and presence.
  • Querying is limited compared with Firestore.
  • Deep nesting is a trap — fetching a node fetches everything under it.
  • Keep the tree shallow and denormalised.
  • Firestore is the default choice for new apps.

Example

Reading a node in the Realtime Database downloads the entire subtree beneath it. A deeply nested structure means fetching a user's name can pull down all their messages too.

Why this matters

Knowing which database to choose — and why nesting is dangerous in one of them — is a common interview question and a common early mistake.

questions.explanation: Firestore offers better querying and scaling for most new applications.

📖 Firebase Storage
Somewhere to put files that a database should not hold.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Firebase Storage

Firebase Storage is the focus of this Firebase Integration lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

Firebase

Google’s platform of hosted backend services for mobile and web applications.

Firestore

A cloud NoSQL document database with real-time synchronisation.

Cloud Messaging

Firebase service used to deliver push notifications to applications.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

val db = Firebase.firestore
val learner = hashMapOf("name" to "Samuel", "active" to true)
db.collection("learners").add(learner)
    .addOnSuccessListener { document -> Log.d("DB", document.id) }
    .addOnFailureListener { error -> Log.e("DB", "Save failed", error) }

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Firebase Integration. For Firebase Storage, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Firebase Storage holds files — images, audio, documents — and returns a URL. The usual pattern is to upload the file, store its URL in Firestore, and load it in the app with an image library.

Uploads must be constrained. Without limits on size and type, a single user can upload gigabytes, and the bill is yours.

Key points

  • Stores files and returns a download URL.
  • Store the URL in the database, never the file itself.
  • Security rules restrict who can upload and download.
  • Limit file size and type in the rules, not only in the app.
  • Compress images before upload — a phone camera file is large.
  • Load images with Coil or Glide, which cache for you.

Example

Uploading a full-resolution camera photo sends several megabytes for an image displayed at 200 pixels. Resizing before upload cuts storage cost, transfer time and the user's data bill at once.

Why this matters

Image handling is where a beginner app most often becomes slow and expensive, and both are avoidable at the point of upload.

lessons.title: 8.6 Cloud Messaging (Push Notifications)
lessons.html:
📖 Cloud Messaging (Push Notifications)
Reaching a user who does not currently have your app open.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Cloud Messaging (Push Notifications)

Cloud Messaging (Push Notifications) is the focus of this Firebase Integration lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

Firebase

Google’s platform of hosted backend services for mobile and web applications.

Firestore

A cloud NoSQL document database with real-time synchronisation.

Cloud Messaging

Firebase service used to deliver push notifications to applications.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

val db = Firebase.firestore
val learner = hashMapOf("name" to "Samuel", "active" to true)
db.collection("learners").add(learner)
    .addOnSuccessListener { document -> Log.d("DB", document.id) }
    .addOnFailureListener { error -> Log.e("DB", "Save failed", error) }

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Firebase Integration. For Cloud Messaging (Push Notifications), identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Firebase Cloud Messaging delivers messages to a device even when the app is closed. Each installation has a token; you send to that token, or to a topic many devices subscribe to.

Since Android 13, notifications require the POST_NOTIFICATIONS runtime permission. Asking for it the moment the app opens, with no context, is the surest way to be refused.

Key points

  • Each install has an FCM token; store it against the user.
  • Topics let many devices subscribe to one broadcast.
  • Android 13+ requires the POST_NOTIFICATIONS runtime permission.
  • Ask for permission when the value is obvious, not at first launch.
  • Notifications must open the relevant screen via a deep link.
  • Tokens rotate — handle onNewToken and update the server.

Example

A notification that opens the app's home screen wastes the interruption. One that opens the specific order it referred to is the reason the user allowed notifications at all.

Why this matters

Notifications are the most easily abused channel an app has, and permission, once refused, is rarely granted again.

lessons.title: 8.7 Firebase Analytics
lessons.html:
📖 Firebase Analytics
Measuring what users actually do, rather than what you assume.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Firebase Analytics

Firebase Analytics is the focus of this Firebase Integration lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

Firebase

Google’s platform of hosted backend services for mobile and web applications.

Firestore

A cloud NoSQL document database with real-time synchronisation.

Cloud Messaging

Firebase service used to deliver push notifications to applications.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

val db = Firebase.firestore
val learner = hashMapOf("name" to "Samuel", "active" to true)
db.collection("learners").add(learner)
    .addOnSuccessListener { document -> Log.d("DB", document.id) }
    .addOnFailureListener { error -> Log.e("DB", "Save failed", error) }

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Firebase Integration. For Firebase Analytics, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Analytics records events — screens viewed, buttons pressed, purchases completed — and reports them. It answers questions such as where users abandon a signup flow.

Log a small number of meaningful events rather than everything. A hundred event types nobody reads is worse than five that drive decisions, and each one carries a privacy obligation.

Key points

  • Log meaningful events, not every interaction.
  • Name events consistently — inconsistent names cannot be compared.
  • Never log personal data: names, emails, phone numbers, locations.
  • Funnels reveal where users drop out of a flow.
  • Disclose analytics in your privacy policy; Play requires it.
  • Crashlytics covers stability; Analytics covers behaviour.

Example

Discovering that 70% of users abandon signup at the phone-verification step is actionable. Knowing that a button was tapped 4,000 times is not, unless you know what it was competing with.

Why this matters

Analytics is how you decide what to build next with evidence rather than instinct, and it is expected in any commercial app.

📖 Firebase Hosting Overview
Serving the web side of a mobile product.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Firebase Hosting Overview

Firebase Hosting Overview is the focus of this Firebase Integration lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

Firebase

Google’s platform of hosted backend services for mobile and web applications.

Firestore

A cloud NoSQL document database with real-time synchronisation.

Cloud Messaging

Firebase service used to deliver push notifications to applications.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

val db = Firebase.firestore
val learner = hashMapOf("name" to "Samuel", "active" to true)

    .addOnSuccessListener { document -> Log.d("DB", document.id) }
    .addOnFailureListener { error -> Log.e("DB", "Save failed", error) }

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Firebase Integration. For Firebase Hosting Overview, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Firebase Hosting serves static web content over HTTPS from a global CDN. For an Android developer it is where the pieces that must live on the web go: a privacy policy, a landing page, and the assetlinks file that verifies App Links.

Google Play requires a publicly reachable privacy policy URL for any app that handles user data, which in practice is nearly every app.

Key points

  • Static hosting over HTTPS with a free subdomain.
  • Hosts the privacy policy Play requires.
  • Hosts /.well-known/assetlinks.json to verify App Links.
  • Deploy with the Firebase CLI: firebase deploy.
  • Supports custom domains with automatic certificates.
  • Useful for a simple landing page for your app.

Example

App Links verification fails without assetlinks.json served over HTTPS from your domain. Firebase Hosting provides that in a few minutes, and it is the same place the privacy policy can live.

Why this matters

These are small requirements that block a Play release entirely, which is why they belong in the publishing preparation rather than being discovered at submission.

lessons.title: 9.1 Introduction to REST APIs
lessons.html:
📖 Introduction to REST APIs
How an app asks a server for data.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Introduction to REST APIs

Introduction to REST APIs is the focus of this Networking & APIs lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

REST API

A web interface that exposes resources through HTTP methods and URLs.

JSON

A text format used to exchange structured data.

Retrofit

A type-safe HTTP client commonly used for Android networking.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

interface CourseApi {
    @GET("courses")
    suspend fun courses(): List<Course>
}
viewModelScope.launch {
    runCatching { api.courses() }
        .onSuccess { courses.value = it }
        .onFailure { error.value = it.message }
}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Networking & APIs. For Introduction to REST APIs, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

A REST API exposes resources at URLs and uses HTTP verbs: GET to read, POST to create, PUT or PATCH to update, DELETE to remove.

The status code tells you what happened, and each class means something different for your error handling: 2xx succeeded, 4xx you sent something wrong, 5xx the server failed.

Key points

  • GET read, POST create, PUT/PATCH update, DELETE remove.
  • 2xx success, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
  • 401 means not authenticated; 403 means not permitted.
  • 429 means rate limited — back off rather than retrying immediately.
  • Requests must use HTTPS.
  • Never place a secret in a URL; it is logged along the way.

Example

Retrying a 400 is pointless — the request itself was wrong and will be wrong again. Retrying a 503 with a delay is sensible, because the server may simply have been busy.

Why this matters

Distinguishing these classes is what separates sensible error handling from a retry loop that hammers a server and drains a battery.

questions.question: What does a 4xx status code indicate?
options: A problem with the request the client sent
questions.explanation: 4xx means the client's request was invalid, so retrying it unchanged will fail again.

questions.question: What is the correct response to a 429?
questions.explanation: 429 signals rate limiting, so the client must slow down.

questions.question: Why should a secret never appear in a URL?
options: URLs are logged by servers and proxies along the way
questions.explanation: Query strings appear in access logs and browser history, exposing the secret.

lessons.title: 9.2 JSON
lessons.html:
📖 JSON
The format almost every API speaks.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

JSON

JSON is the focus of this Networking & APIs lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

REST API

A web interface that exposes resources through HTTP methods and URLs.

JSON

A text format used to exchange structured data.

Retrofit

A type-safe HTTP client commonly used for Android networking.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

interface CourseApi {
    @GET("courses")
    suspend fun courses(): List<Course>
}
viewModelScope.launch {
    runCatching { api.courses() }
        .onSuccess { courses.value = it }
        .onFailure { error.value = it.message }
}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Networking & APIs. For JSON, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

JSON represents data as objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null. It is the standard payload format for REST APIs and maps cleanly onto Kotlin data classes.

In practice you rarely parse it by hand. A serialisation library converts JSON into typed objects, and the important discipline is declaring optional fields as nullable so a missing value does not crash the app.

Key points

  • Objects {}, arrays [], strings, numbers, booleans, null.
  • Maps directly onto Kotlin data classes.
  • Declare optional fields nullable — APIs omit fields.
  • Use @SerializedName or @SerialName when names differ.
  • Never assume a field is present because it was yesterday.
  • Malformed JSON must be handled, not allowed to crash.

Example

A non-nullable Kotlin field for a value the API sometimes omits produces a crash on exactly the records that omit it — often the older ones, so the app works in testing and fails in production.

Why this matters

Nullability discipline at the boundary is what keeps API changes from becoming crash reports.

A type-safe HTTP client commonly used for Android networking.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

interface CourseApi {
    @GET("courses")
    suspend fun courses(): List<Course>
}
viewModelScope.launch {
    runCatching { api.courses() }
        .onSuccess { courses.value = it }
        .onFailure { error.value = it.message }
}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Networking & APIs. For Retrofit, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Retrofit turns an annotated Kotlin interface into a working HTTP client. You declare the endpoint, the verb and the return type; Retrofit generates the call and a converter turns JSON into your data classes.

Made suspend, the functions integrate directly with coroutines, so a network call reads like a normal function call while running off the main thread.

Key points

  • Annotate an interface: @GET, @POST, @Path, @Query, @Body.
  • A converter (Gson, Moshi, kotlinx.serialization) handles JSON.
  • suspend functions integrate with coroutines.
  • Return Response<T> when you need the status code.
  • Add an OkHttp interceptor for auth headers and logging.
  • Never log full request bodies in a release build.

Example

@GET("orders/{id}") suspend fun getOrder(@Path("id") id: String): Order is the whole client for that endpoint. Retrofit writes the request, parses the response and hands back a typed object.

Why this matters

Retrofit with coroutines is the standard networking stack in modern Android, and it appears in every app that touches a server.

lessons.title: 9.4 Fetching Data
lessons.html:
📖 Fetching Data
Load, show progress, handle failure — every screen, every time.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Fetching Data

Fetching Data is the focus of this Networking & APIs lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

REST API

A web interface that exposes resources through HTTP methods and URLs.

JSON

A text format used to exchange structured data.

Retrofit

A type-safe HTTP client commonly used for Android networking.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

interface CourseApi {
    @GET("courses")
    suspend fun courses(): List<Course>
}
viewModelScope.launch {
    runCatching { api.courses() }
        .onSuccess { courses.value = it }
        .onFailure { error.value = it.message }
}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Networking & APIs. For Fetching Data, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

A fetch has three outcomes the UI must represent: loading, success and error. Screens that only handle success show a blank page when the network fails, which users read as a broken app.

The usual pattern is a sealed class or state object exposed by a ViewModel, with the fragment rendering whichever state arrives.

Key points

  • Model three states explicitly: loading, success, error.
  • Fetch in the ViewModel, not the fragment, so rotation does not refetch.
  • Use viewModelScope so the call is cancelled with the ViewModel.
  • Show cached data while refreshing, rather than a blank screen.
  • An empty result is a fourth state and needs its own message.
  • Never block the main thread waiting for a response.

Example

A list screen with no empty state shows nothing when the query returns zero results, and the user cannot tell whether it is loading, broken, or genuinely empty. All three look identical.

Why this matters

State modelling is what makes an app feel reliable on a weak connection, which is the normal condition for most users here.

lessons.title: 9.5 Sending Data
lessons.html:
📖 Sending Data
Writes are riskier than reads, because they can happen twice.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Sending Data

Sending Data is the focus of this Networking & APIs lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

REST API

A web interface that exposes resources through HTTP methods and URLs.

JSON

A text format used to exchange structured data.

Retrofit

A type-safe HTTP client commonly used for Android networking.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

interface CourseApi {
    @GET("courses")
    suspend fun courses(): List<Course>
}
viewModelScope.launch {
    runCatching { api.courses() }
        .onSuccess { courses.value = it }
        .onFailure { error.value = it.message }
}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Networking & APIs. For Sending Data, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Sending data uses POST, PUT or PATCH with a body. The complications are validation before sending, disabling the control so the user cannot submit twice, and deciding what a timeout means.

A timeout is genuinely ambiguous: the request may have succeeded and the response lost. Blind retries can create a duplicate record, which is why servers use idempotency keys.

Key points

  • Validate before sending; do not rely on the server to reject bad input.
  • Disable the submit control while the request is in flight.
  • A timeout is ambiguous — the write may have succeeded.
  • Use an idempotency key when the server supports it.
  • Show a clear result: success confirmation or an actionable error.
  • Queue offline writes rather than failing them outright.

Example

Tapping Pay twice because the first tap showed no feedback creates two payments. Disabling the button on the first tap is a one-line change that prevents a real financial error.

Why this matters

Duplicate writes are among the most damaging bugs in a small app, because they are invisible to the developer and expensive for the user.

Tell the user what happened and what they can do.

A web interface that exposes resources through HTTP methods and URLs.

JSON

A text format used to exchange structured data.

Retrofit

A type-safe HTTP client commonly used for Android networking.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

interface CourseApi {
    @GET("courses")
    suspend fun courses(): List<Course>
}
viewModelScope.launch {
    runCatching { api.courses() }
        .onSuccess { courses.value = it }
        .onFailure { error.value = it.message }
}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Networking & APIs. For Error Handling, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Network calls fail in distinct ways: no connectivity, timeout, 4xx, 5xx, malformed response. Each deserves a different message, and only some are worth retrying.

Never show a raw exception. “UnknownHostException” means nothing to a user; “No internet connection — check your data and try again” tells them exactly what to do.

Key points

  • Distinguish no connectivity, timeout, 4xx, 5xx and parse failure.
  • Retry 5xx and timeouts with backoff; never retry 4xx unchanged.
  • Never surface a raw exception message to a user.
  • Offer a retry action where retrying could help.
  • Log the technical detail; show the human explanation.
  • Failing silently is worse than failing visibly.

Example

A screen that silently shows nothing when a request fails is the hardest kind of bug to report, because the user cannot describe what went wrong. A visible error with a Retry button is both usable and diagnosable.

Why this matters

Error handling is where an app either earns trust on a poor connection or loses it, and this is the condition most learners here are building for.

📖 API Authentication
Proving who is calling, without shipping the secret.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

API Authentication

API Authentication is the focus of this Networking & APIs lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

REST API

A web interface that exposes resources through HTTP methods and URLs.

JSON

A text format used to exchange structured data.

Retrofit

A type-safe HTTP client commonly used for Android networking.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

interface CourseApi {
    @GET("courses")
    suspend fun courses(): List<Course>
}
viewModelScope.launch {
    runCatching { api.courses() }
        .onSuccess { courses.value = it }
        .onFailure { error.value = it.message }
}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Networking & APIs. For API Authentication, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Most APIs authenticate with a token sent in a header, usually Authorization: Bearer <token>. An OkHttp interceptor adds it to every request in one place rather than at each call site.

Anything compiled into the app can be extracted. Treat a key in the APK as public: restrict it by package and signature at the provider, and keep genuinely secret operations on a server you control.

Key points

  • Send tokens in the Authorization header, not in the URL.
  • Add them with an OkHttp interceptor, once.
  • Anything in the APK can be extracted — assume keys are public.
  • Restrict keys by package name and signing certificate.
  • Store tokens in EncryptedSharedPreferences.
  • Handle 401 by refreshing the token or signing the user out.

Example

A key hard-coded in an app is recoverable from the APK in minutes. Restricting it to your package and signature at the provider means the extracted key is useless in anyone else's app.

Why this matters

Believing that compiled code hides a secret is the most common security misconception among new mobile developers, and it is expensive when the bill arrives.

Consuming Third-Party APIs is the focus of this Networking & APIs lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

A web interface that exposes resources through HTTP methods and URLs.

JSON

A text format used to exchange structured data.

Retrofit

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

interface CourseApi {
    @GET("courses")
    suspend fun courses(): List<Course>
}

    runCatching { api.courses() }
        .onSuccess { courses.value = it }

}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Networking & APIs. For Consuming Third-Party APIs, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Third-party APIs bring capability you could not build: maps, payments, weather, currency rates. They also bring dependency — on their uptime, their pricing and their versioning.

Read the terms before designing around one. Rate limits, attribution requirements and pricing changes have all forced apps to be rewritten after launch.

Key points

  • Check rate limits, pricing and terms before designing around an API.
  • Cache responses to stay within limits and work offline.
  • Handle 429 by backing off, not by retrying immediately.
  • Wrap the API behind your own interface so it can be replaced.
  • Never expose a paid key in a public repository.
  • Have a plan for the API disappearing or changing its terms.

Example

Calling a weather API on every screen open exhausts a free tier by mid-morning. Caching for an hour serves the same user need with a fraction of the calls, and keeps the app inside the free plan.

Why this matters

Wrapping a third-party service behind your own interface is what makes replacing it a day's work rather than a rewrite.

lessons.title: 10.1 Camera Integration
lessons.html:
📖 Camera Integration
Taking a photo without writing a camera.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Camera Integration

Camera Integration is the focus of this Media & Device Features lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

runtime permission

User approval requested while the app is running for protected device data or features.

sensor

Hardware that measures device or environmental information.

location service

A system service that estimates the device’s geographic position.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

private val permission = registerForActivityResult(
    ActivityResultContracts.RequestPermission()
) { granted ->
    if (granted) openCamera() else showPermissionReason()
}
permission.launch(Manifest.permission.CAMERA)

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Media & Device Features. For Camera Integration, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

The simplest approach uses ActivityResultContracts.TakePicture, which hands the work to the device's camera app and returns to you when it is done. It requires no camera permission, because the user is operating their own camera app.

CameraX is the alternative when you need a preview inside your app, custom controls or image analysis. It is more code and requires the camera permission.

Key points

  • ActivityResultContracts.TakePicture delegates to the camera app.
  • Delegating needs no camera permission.
  • CameraX for in-app preview, custom capture or analysis.
  • CameraX requires the CAMERA permission at runtime.
  • Use a FileProvider to share the output file safely.
  • Test on a low-end device — camera behaviour varies widely.

Example

If the app only needs a profile photo, delegating to the camera app is a few lines and no permission prompt. Building the same thing with CameraX is a preview surface, lifecycle binding, a permission request and considerably more that can go wrong.

Why this matters

Choosing the simpler path when it suffices is a recurring judgement in Android, and the camera is where it makes the biggest difference.

📖 Photo Capture
What to do with the image once you have it.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Photo Capture

Photo Capture is the focus of this Media & Device Features lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

runtime permission

User approval requested while the app is running for protected device data or features.

sensor

Hardware that measures device or environmental information.

location service

A system service that estimates the device’s geographic position.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

private val permission = registerForActivityResult(
    ActivityResultContracts.RequestPermission()
) { granted ->
    if (granted) openCamera() else showPermissionReason()
}
permission.launch(Manifest.permission.CAMERA)

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Media & Device Features. For Photo Capture, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

A camera photo is large — several megabytes and thousands of pixels wide. Displaying it directly in a small view wastes memory, and uploading it directly wastes the user's data.

Resize and compress before storing or sending. Store the file on disk and keep only its path in the database, and load it with a library that handles scaling and caching for you.

Key points

  • Resize and compress before storing or uploading.
  • Store the file on disk; keep the path in the database.
  • Load with Coil or Glide — they scale and cache.
  • Loading a full-size bitmap into a small view risks OutOfMemoryError.
  • Strip EXIF location data before sharing a photo.
  • Respect the image's rotation flag or portraits appear sideways.

Example

A photo taken in portrait often displays sideways because the file is stored landscape with a rotation flag. Ignoring that flag is why so many first apps show every portrait photo on its side.

Why this matters

Image handling is the most common source of memory crashes in beginner Android apps, and every one of these points prevents a specific failure.

The Photo Picker is the modern way to let a user choose an image. It shows a system picker, returns only what the user selected, and requires no storage permission at all.

The older approach requested broad media permissions to browse the gallery yourself. That is now discouraged, and Play scrutinises apps that request it.

Key points

  • ActivityResultContracts.PickVisualMedia is the Photo Picker.
  • Requires no storage permission.
  • Returns a URI for only the item the user chose.
  • Take a persistable permission if you need the URI after a restart.
  • Load the URI with Coil or Glide.
  • Broad media permissions are discouraged and scrutinised by Play.

Example

Requesting READ_MEDIA_IMAGES to let a user choose one profile picture asks for access to every photo on the device. The Photo Picker asks for nothing and returns exactly the one they picked.

Why this matters

Requesting the narrowest access that does the job is both a privacy principle and a practical requirement for passing Play review.

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Media & Device Features. For Audio Playback, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

MediaPlayer covers simple playback; ExoPlayer (Media3) handles streaming, formats and buffering properly and is the standard choice for anything substantial.

The part beginners miss is audio focus. Your app must stop or duck when something more important plays — a phone call, a navigation instruction — and resume afterwards if appropriate.

Key points

  • MediaPlayer for simple clips; ExoPlayer for streaming.
  • Request and respect audio focus.
  • Duck or pause when another app takes focus; resume when appropriate.
  • Release the player in onStop — it holds significant resources.
  • Use a foreground service for playback that continues in the background.
  • Show a media notification with transport controls.

Example

An app that keeps playing through an incoming call is the fastest route to a one-star review. Handling audio focus is a short callback and it is what users notice only when it is missing.

Why this matters

Media resources are among the heaviest an app holds, and failing to release them is a common cause of battery complaints.

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Media & Device Features. For Video Playback, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

ExoPlayer is the standard video player. It handles streaming formats, adaptive bitrate, subtitles and buffering — all things that are painful to implement on MediaPlayer.

Adaptive streaming matters here. It adjusts quality to the available bandwidth, so a video plays at a lower resolution rather than stalling on a weak connection.

Key points

  • ExoPlayer (Media3) is the standard for video.
  • Adaptive bitrate adjusts quality to bandwidth rather than stalling.
  • Release the player in onStop; recreate in onStart.
  • Keep the screen on during playback, and let it sleep afterwards.
  • Warn before large downloads on a metered connection.
  • Provide captions where you can — many users watch without sound.

Example

A fixed high-resolution stream stalls repeatedly on a slow connection and the user gives up. An adaptive stream drops to a lower resolution and keeps playing, which is almost always the better outcome.

Why this matters

Video is the heaviest thing most apps do to a user's data plan, and adaptive streaming is what makes it viable on the connections common here.

The FusedLocationProviderClient combines GPS, network and sensor data to give a location efficiently. You request coarse or fine accuracy, and the user grants or refuses at runtime.

Since Android 10 there is a separate permission for background location, and Play requires a strong justification for it. Most apps genuinely need location only while in use.

Key points

  • FusedLocationProviderClient is the recommended API.
  • ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION for approximate, ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION for precise.
  • Request the coarsest accuracy that does the job.
  • Background location is a separate permission requiring Play justification.
  • Users can grant approximate location only — handle that.
  • Stop location updates when the screen stops.

Example

A shop-finder needs approximate location. Requesting fine, continuous, background location for it prompts users to refuse and invites a Play policy rejection, for accuracy the feature never uses.

Why this matters

Location is the permission users refuse most readily, so asking for the minimum with a clear reason is what determines whether the feature works at all.

lessons.title: 10.7 Maps Integration
lessons.html:
📖 Maps Integration
Showing location in a way people can read.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Maps Integration

Maps Integration is the focus of this Media & Device Features lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

runtime permission

User approval requested while the app is running for protected device data or features.

sensor

Hardware that measures device or environmental information.

location service

A system service that estimates the device’s geographic position.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

private val permission = registerForActivityResult(
    ActivityResultContracts.RequestPermission()
) { granted ->
    if (granted) openCamera() else showPermissionReason()
}
permission.launch(Manifest.permission.CAMERA)

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Media & Device Features. For Maps Integration, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

The Google Maps SDK provides a MapView or SupportMapFragment, markers, camera control and overlays. It requires an API key restricted to your package and signing certificate.

Maps are heavy: they consume memory, network and battery. Their lifecycle callbacks must be forwarded, and large numbers of markers need clustering rather than being added individually.

Key points

  • Requires an API key restricted by package and signing certificate.
  • SupportMapFragment handles most lifecycle forwarding for you.
  • Cluster markers — hundreds of individual ones will stall the map.
  • Maps cost memory, network and battery; release them properly.
  • Consider a static map image where interaction is not needed.
  • Cache tiles where the licence permits, for weak connections.

Example

Adding four hundred markers individually makes the map unusable. Clustering them into grouped pins that expand on zoom keeps it responsive with the same data.

Why this matters

Maps are one of the most expensive components an app can include, so using a static image where a live map is not needed is often the better engineering choice.

questions.explanation: Clustering keeps rendering responsive as the number of points grows.

questions.explanation: A static image avoids the memory, battery and network cost of a live map.

lessons.title: 10.8 Sensors
lessons.html:
📖 Sensors
Reading the device's own measurements.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Sensors

Sensors is the focus of this Media & Device Features lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

runtime permission

User approval requested while the app is running for protected device data or features.

sensor

Hardware that measures device or environmental information.

location service

A system service that estimates the device’s geographic position.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

private val permission = registerForActivityResult(
    ActivityResultContracts.RequestPermission()
) { granted ->
    if (granted) openCamera() else showPermissionReason()
}
permission.launch(Manifest.permission.CAMERA)

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Media & Device Features. For Sensors, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Android exposes sensors through SensorManager: accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer, light, proximity, step counter. You register a listener, receive events, and unregister when done.

Sensors deliver events continuously and quickly. Registering one and forgetting to unregister keeps the CPU awake and drains the battery, which is the commonest sensor bug.

Key points

  • Access via SensorManager; register and unregister a listener.
  • Always unregister in onPause or onStop.
  • Choose the slowest delay that works — delay affects battery directly.
  • Not every device has every sensor; check availability first.
  • Raw values are noisy and usually need smoothing.
  • The step counter needs ACTIVITY_RECOGNITION permission.

Example

A registered accelerometer listener that is never unregistered keeps delivering events while the user is in another app. The battery drain is real and is attributed to your app in the system's battery screen.

Why this matters

Sensor lifecycle is a specific instance of the general Android rule that everything acquired must be released, and here the cost of forgetting is immediately visible to the user.

questions.explanation: More frequent events mean more CPU wake-ups and more power used.

lessons.title: 10.9 Permissions Management
lessons.html:
📖 Permissions Management
Ask at the right moment, for the least you need, and handle refusal.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Permissions Management

Permissions Management is the focus of this Media & Device Features lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

runtime permission

User approval requested while the app is running for protected device data or features.

sensor

Hardware that measures device or environmental information.

location service

A system service that estimates the device’s geographic position.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

private val permission = registerForActivityResult(
    ActivityResultContracts.RequestPermission()
) { granted ->
    if (granted) openCamera() else showPermissionReason()
}
permission.launch(Manifest.permission.CAMERA)

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Media & Device Features. For Permissions Management, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Dangerous permissions are requested at runtime with ActivityResultContracts.RequestPermission. The user may grant, deny, or deny permanently, and your app must work in all three cases.

Timing decides the answer. A permission requested at first launch, before the user knows what the app does, is usually refused. The same request made when the user taps a feature that obviously needs it is usually granted.

Key points

  • Request at the moment the feature is used, not at launch.
  • Explain why before prompting if the reason is not obvious.
  • Handle three outcomes: granted, denied, permanently denied.
  • On permanent denial, direct the user to Settings — you cannot re-prompt.
  • Request the narrowest permission that works.
  • Every permission must be declared in the manifest as well.

Example

Asking for camera access the moment the app opens gets refused by most users. Asking when they tap “Add photo” gets granted by most, because the reason is self-evident at that moment.

Why this matters

Permissions are the clearest example in Android of user experience and technical outcome being the same thing: a badly timed request means the feature simply does not work.

options: When the user activates the feature that needs it
questions.explanation: Context makes the reason obvious, which markedly increases grant rates.

questions.explanation: Permanent denial cannot be re-prompted and requires directing the user to Settings.

questions.question: What must accompany every runtime permission request?
questions.explanation: Undeclared permissions cannot be granted regardless of the runtime request.

lessons.title: 11.1 Material Design Principles
lessons.html:
📖 Material Design Principles
A system that makes an unfamiliar app immediately usable.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Material Design Principles

Material Design Principles is the focus of this Material Design lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

Material Design

Google’s design system for consistent, usable digital interfaces.

theme

A named collection of colours, typography, shapes, and component styles.

component

A reusable interface element with defined appearance and behaviour.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

<com.google.android.material.button.MaterialButton
    android:id="@+id/continueButton"
    style="@style/Widget.Material3.Button"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="Continue" />

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Material Design. For Material Design Principles, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Material Design is Google's design system: components, spacing, elevation, motion and colour that behave consistently. Following it means users already know how your app works before they open it.

Material 3 introduces dynamic colour, which derives the palette from the user's wallpaper. Adopting the components rather than styling views individually is what makes theming and dark mode work at all.

Key points

  • A consistent system of components, spacing, elevation and motion.
  • Material 3 supports dynamic colour from the user's wallpaper.
  • Use Material components, not hand-styled generic views.
  • Keep spacing on a consistent scale — typically multiples of 8dp.
  • Elevation conveys hierarchy; motion conveys causality.
  • Following the system makes accessibility easier by default.

Example

An app built from Material components inherits correct touch targets, ripple feedback, dark mode and dynamic colour without extra work. The same screens built from hand-styled views need each of those implemented individually.

Why this matters

Design systems are labour-saving before they are aesthetic: consistency is what lets a solo developer ship a coherent app.

options: Correct touch targets, ripple feedback and theme support
questions.explanation: The components implement the system's behaviour, including accessibility basics.

questions.question: What is dynamic colour in Material 3?
options: A palette derived from the user's wallpaper
questions.explanation: Dynamic colour personalises the app palette from the system wallpaper.

questions.question: What spacing scale does Material typically use?
questions.explanation: An 8dp grid keeps spacing consistent across components and screens.

lessons.title: 11.2 Themes
lessons.html:
📖 Themes
Define appearance once, apply it everywhere.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Themes

Themes is the focus of this Material Design lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

Material Design

Google’s design system for consistent, usable digital interfaces.

theme

A named collection of colours, typography, shapes, and component styles.

component

A reusable interface element with defined appearance and behaviour.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

<com.google.android.material.button.MaterialButton
    android:id="@+id/continueButton"
    style="@style/Widget.Material3.Button"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="Continue" />

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Material Design. For Themes, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

A theme is a collection of attributes — colours, typography, shapes — applied to the whole app or an activity. Views reference theme attributes rather than fixed values.

That indirection is what makes dark mode work. A view that references ?attr/colorSurface changes automatically when the theme changes; one with a hard-coded white background does not.

Key points

  • Themes are declared in themes.xml and applied in the manifest.
  • Reference attributes (?attr/colorPrimary), not literal colours.
  • values-night/ supplies the dark variant.
  • A hard-coded colour is invisible until dark mode is switched on.
  • Theme overlays restyle one part of the screen.
  • Changing the theme should require no changes to layouts.

Example

One hard-coded #FFFFFF background produces a white panel in an otherwise dark app. It is invisible during development and obvious to every user who prefers dark mode.

Why this matters

Theming discipline is what makes dark mode a configuration change rather than a second design pass across every screen.

options: So the appearance changes with the theme, including dark mode
questions.explanation: Attribute references resolve per theme; literals never change.

questions.explanation: Resource qualifiers supply the night-mode variants automatically.

questions.question: What is the visible symptom of a hard-coded colour?
options: A panel that stays light in dark mode
questions.explanation: It does not respond to the theme change, so it stands out once dark mode is on.

lessons.title: 11.3 Colors
lessons.html:
📖 Colors
A small palette, used consistently, with enough contrast.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Colors

Colors is the focus of this Material Design lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

Material Design

Google’s design system for consistent, usable digital interfaces.

theme

A named collection of colours, typography, shapes, and component styles.

component

A reusable interface element with defined appearance and behaviour.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

<com.google.android.material.button.MaterialButton
    android:id="@+id/continueButton"
    style="@style/Widget.Material3.Button"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="Continue" />

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Material Design. For Colors, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Material defines colour roles rather than a list of colours: primary, secondary, surface, background, error, and an “on” colour for content drawn on each. Assigning roles rather than picking colours per screen is what produces consistency.

Contrast is a requirement, not a preference. Body text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 against its background, and a great deal of attractive-looking design fails that test.

Key points

  • Material 3 uses colour roles: primary, secondary, surface, error.
  • Each role has an “on” colour for content drawn on it.
  • Body text needs at least 4.5:1 contrast.
  • Never rely on colour alone to convey meaning.
  • Define colours once in colors.xml and reference them.
  • Check the palette in both light and dark themes.

Example

Light grey text on a white card looks refined and is unreadable outdoors on a phone at midday — which is exactly where many users here will be reading it.

Why this matters

Contrast is one of the few design rules with a measurable pass mark, and failing it excludes users rather than merely displeasing them.

questions.explanation: WCAG requires at least 4.5:1 for normal-sized body text.

options: Roles such as primary, surface and error
questions.explanation: Roles let the same semantic colour adapt across themes.

questions.question: Why should colour alone never convey meaning?
options: Users with colour vision deficiency cannot perceive the distinction
questions.explanation: Meaning must also be carried by text, shape or icon.

lessons.title: 11.4 Typography
lessons.html:
📖 Typography
Readable text, in a small number of consistent styles.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Typography

Typography is the focus of this Material Design lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

Material Design

Google’s design system for consistent, usable digital interfaces.

theme

A named collection of colours, typography, shapes, and component styles.

component

A reusable interface element with defined appearance and behaviour.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

<com.google.android.material.button.MaterialButton
    android:id="@+id/continueButton"
    style="@style/Widget.Material3.Button"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="Continue" />

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Material Design. For Typography, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Material defines a type scale — display, headline, title, body, label — each with a defined size and weight. Using the scale rather than setting sizes per view keeps a screen coherent.

Text sizes must be specified in sp, not dp. Only sp respects the user's font-size setting, and ignoring it makes an app unusable for anyone who has enlarged their text.

Key points

  • Use the Material type scale rather than ad-hoc sizes.
  • Text in sp; everything else in dp.
  • sp respects the user's accessibility font-size setting.
  • Two font families at most; one is usually enough.
  • Body text below 14sp is difficult to read on a phone.
  • Test at the largest system font size — layouts must not break.

Example

An app that sets text in dp looks identical for every user, including one who enlarged their system font because they cannot read the default. For that user the app is simply unusable.

Why this matters

Respecting the user's font setting is the single most impactful accessibility decision in a mobile layout, and it costs one letter.

lessons.html: Quick check: Review the formal study notes, complete the coding exercises, then answer these questions to confirm you understood Typography.

questions.question: Which unit should text sizes use?
questions.explanation: Only sp scales with the user's accessibility font-size preference.

questions.question: What is the consequence of setting text in dp?
options: The app ignores the user's font-size setting
questions.explanation: Users who enlarged their system font see no change, which can make the app unusable.

questions.question: How many font families should a typical app use?
options: As many as the design needs
questions.explanation: Restraint in type families is what keeps an interface coherent.

lessons.title: 11.5 Buttons
lessons.html:
📖 M11:Buttons
The right button style for the weight of the action.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Buttons

Buttons is the focus of this Material Design lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

Material Design

Google’s design system for consistent, usable digital interfaces.

theme

A named collection of colours, typography, shapes, and component styles.

component

A reusable interface element with defined appearance and behaviour.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

<com.google.android.material.button.MaterialButton
    android:id="@+id/continueButton"
    style="@style/Widget.Material3.Button"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="Continue" />

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Material Design. For Buttons, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Material provides several button styles and each signals importance: filled for the primary action, tonal or outlined for secondary, text for tertiary, and the FAB for a screen's single most important action.

One filled button per screen is the guideline. Two compete, and the user must read both to decide, which is precisely what visual hierarchy exists to avoid.

Key points

  • Filled for the primary action — one per screen.
  • Outlined or tonal for secondary actions.
  • Text buttons for low-emphasis actions such as Cancel.
  • The FAB is for the screen's single most important action.
  • Minimum touch target 48dp, whatever the visual size.
  • Label with a verb: Save, not OK.

Example

A dialog with two filled buttons makes Delete and Cancel look equally intended. Making Delete filled and Cancel a text button tells the user which one the screen expects without them reading a word.

Why this matters

Button hierarchy is the cheapest form of guidance an interface has, and getting it wrong causes destructive taps.

lessons.title: 11.6 Cards
lessons.html:
📖 Cards
Grouping related content into a tappable unit.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Cards

Cards is the focus of this Material Design lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

Material Design

Google’s design system for consistent, usable digital interfaces.

theme

A named collection of colours, typography, shapes, and component styles.

component

A reusable interface element with defined appearance and behaviour.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

<com.google.android.material.button.MaterialButton
    android:id="@+id/continueButton"
    style="@style/Widget.Material3.Button"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="Continue" />

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Material Design. For Cards, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

A MaterialCardView groups related information into a single surface with elevation and rounded corners. Cards work well for list items containing several pieces of data.

The common mistake is treating a card as decoration. If everything on a screen is a card, nothing is grouped, and the elevation that was meant to convey hierarchy conveys nothing.

Key points

  • Group related content into one surface.
  • Elevation implies the card sits above the background.
  • Make the whole card clickable if it represents one thing.
  • Do not nest cards — the hierarchy becomes meaningless.
  • Keep consistent corner radius and elevation across the app.
  • A card is not a substitute for spacing.

Example

A list where each item is a card, inside a card, on a card background produces three levels of elevation that mean nothing. Removing two of them makes the remaining one informative.

Why this matters

Cards are the most over-used Material component, and restraint with them is what makes the ones that remain read as meaningful groupings.

lessons.title: 11.7 Animations
lessons.html:
📖 Animations
Motion that explains what just happened.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Animations

Animations is the focus of this Material Design lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

Material Design

Google’s design system for consistent, usable digital interfaces.

theme

A named collection of colours, typography, shapes, and component styles.

component

A reusable interface element with defined appearance and behaviour.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

<com.google.android.material.button.MaterialButton
    android:id="@+id/continueButton"
    style="@style/Widget.Material3.Button"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="Continue" />

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Material Design. For Animations, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Animation should communicate causality: where a new screen came from, what a tap affected, that a list changed. Motion for its own sake slows the app and irritates users who use it daily.

Keep durations short — roughly 200 to 300 milliseconds for most transitions. Anything longer feels sluggish once the novelty has worn off.

Key points

  • Motion should explain a change, not decorate it.
  • Typical durations: 200-300ms; longer feels slow with repeated use.
  • MotionLayout handles complex coordinated transitions.
  • DiffUtil gives RecyclerView correct item animations.
  • Respect the system's reduce motion accessibility setting.
  • Never block interaction while an animation plays.

Example

A 600ms transition is charming the first time and tedious the fiftieth. Users open their most-used screens dozens of times a day, and every one of those waits is real.

Why this matters

Animation is the clearest case where a designer's first impression and a daily user's experience diverge, and the daily user should win.

questions.explanation: Short transitions read as responsive; longer ones become tedious with repetition.

options: What changed and where it came from
questions.explanation: Motion is most valuable when it explains a change in state.

questions.question: Which accessibility setting must animations respect?
questions.explanation: Some users experience discomfort from motion and disable it system-wide.

lessons.title: 11.8 Responsive Layouts
lessons.html:
📖 Responsive Layouts
One app, many screen sizes and orientations.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Responsive Layouts

Responsive Layouts is the focus of this Material Design lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

Material Design

Google’s design system for consistent, usable digital interfaces.

theme

A named collection of colours, typography, shapes, and component styles.

component

A reusable interface element with defined appearance and behaviour.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

<com.google.android.material.button.MaterialButton
    android:id="@+id/continueButton"
    style="@style/Widget.Material3.Button"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="Continue" />

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Material Design. For Responsive Layouts, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Android runs on small phones, large phones, foldables and tablets. ConstraintLayout with match-constraints and guidelines adapts far better than fixed sizes.

Resource qualifiers supply alternatives: layout-sw600dp for larger screens, layout-land for landscape. The goal is not a separate design per device but a layout that does not break.

Key points

  • Use ConstraintLayout with match-constraints, not fixed widths.
  • sw600dp targets larger screens; -land targets landscape.
  • Never assume a fixed screen width in code.
  • Test the smallest supported device and the largest.
  • Foldables change size at runtime — handle configuration changes.
  • Long text in another language will be longer than your English draft.

Example

A layout designed on a large test phone often clips its own text on a small budget device — which is the device most of the intended users actually own.

Why this matters

Testing on the cheapest device you support is the fastest way to find layout problems that a flagship emulator hides.

lessons.title: 11.9 Dark Mode
lessons.html:
📖 Dark Mode
A second theme that costs nothing if the first was built properly.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Dark Mode

Dark Mode is the focus of this Material Design lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

Material Design

Google’s design system for consistent, usable digital interfaces.

theme

A named collection of colours, typography, shapes, and component styles.

component

A reusable interface element with defined appearance and behaviour.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

<com.google.android.material.button.MaterialButton
    android:id="@+id/continueButton"
    style="@style/Widget.Material3.Button"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="Continue" />

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Material Design. For Dark Mode, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Dark mode follows the system setting through values-night/ resources. If the app themes correctly — attributes rather than literals — supporting it is largely a matter of supplying the night palette.

Dark mode is not simply inverted colours. Pure black with pure white text is harsh; Material uses dark greys with slightly desaturated accents, because saturated colours vibrate against dark backgrounds.

Key points

  • Supplied through values-night/ resources, following the system setting.
  • Requires theme attributes rather than hard-coded colours.
  • Not an inversion — use dark greys, not pure black.
  • Desaturate accent colours slightly for dark surfaces.
  • Elevation is expressed by lighter surfaces, not stronger shadows.
  • Check every screen, including dialogs and empty states.

Example

Pure white text on pure black is uncomfortable to read for long, and saturated accents appear to vibrate. Material's dark palette uses off-black surfaces and muted accents for exactly that reason.

Why this matters

Dark mode is expected rather than optional now, and it is a direct test of whether the theming in Module 11 was done properly.

questions.question: What makes dark mode straightforward to add?
options: Having themed with attributes rather than literal colours

questions.question: Why is pure black with pure white text avoided?
options: It is harsh to read and makes accents appear to vibrate
questions.explanation: Material uses dark greys and muted accents for visual comfort.

questions.question: How is elevation expressed in dark mode?
questions.explanation: Shadows are ineffective on dark backgrounds, so elevated surfaces are lightened.

lessons.title: 12.1 User Registration
lessons.html:
📖 User Registration
Collecting an account without collecting problems.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

User Registration

User Registration is the focus of this Authentication & Security lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

authentication

Verifying the identity of a user or system.

authorization

Deciding what an authenticated identity is permitted to do.

encryption

Transforming readable data so only authorised parties can restore it.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

Firebase.auth.signInWithEmailAndPassword(email, password)
    .addOnSuccessListener { openDashboard() }
    .addOnFailureListener { showError("Unable to sign in") }
// Never store the user password yourself.

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Authentication & Security. For User Registration, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Registration should ask for the minimum needed, validate as the user types, and explain any password requirement before it is broken rather than after.

Never store a password yourself. Delegate to Firebase Authentication or an equivalent, which handles hashing, verification and reset flows that are easy to implement insecurely.

Key points

  • Ask for the minimum — every extra field loses registrations.
  • Validate inline and explain requirements before submission.
  • Never store passwords — delegate to an auth provider.
  • Verify email or phone before granting full access where it matters.
  • Handle the already-registered case with a route to sign in.
  • Support phone sign-in where email is less common.

Example

Telling a user their password is invalid only after they submit, without saying why, is the most common cause of abandoned registration. Stating the rule beside the field costs nothing.

Why this matters

Registration is the first thing a user does and the easiest place to lose them, which is why its details matter more than their size suggests.

lessons.html: Quick check: Review the formal study notes, complete the coding exercises, then answer these questions to confirm you understood User Registration.

questions.question: Where should password requirements be communicated?
questions.explanation: Stating the rule up front prevents the failure rather than explaining it.

questions.question: Why should an app never store passwords itself?
options: Secure hashing, reset and verification are easy to implement insecurely
questions.explanation: Delegating to an auth provider avoids a well-known class of vulnerability.

questions.question: What is the effect of extra registration fields?
questions.explanation: Each additional field increases abandonment, so ask only for what is needed.

lessons.title: 12.2 Login System
lessons.html:
📖 Login System
Signing in reliably, and staying signed in.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Login System

Login System is the focus of this Authentication & Security lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

authentication

Verifying the identity of a user or system.

authorization

Deciding what an authenticated identity is permitted to do.

encryption

Transforming readable data so only authorised parties can restore it.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

Firebase.auth.signInWithEmailAndPassword(email, password)
    .addOnSuccessListener { openDashboard() }
    .addOnFailureListener { showError("Unable to sign in") }
// Never store the user password yourself.

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Authentication & Security. For Login System, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

A login screen collects credentials, calls the auth provider, and routes to the app on success. The details that matter are session persistence, error messages that do not leak information, and popping the login screen from the back stack.

Users should not have to sign in every time they open the app. Firebase persists the session automatically; check for a current user at startup and skip the login screen when one exists.

Key points

  • Check for an existing session at startup and skip login if present.
  • Return the same message for wrong email and wrong password.
  • Pop the login destination so back does not return to it.
  • Rate limit attempts; the provider usually does this for you.
  • Offer password reset from the login screen itself.
  • Show a clear loading state — auth calls are not instant.

Example

“No account with that email” tells an attacker which addresses are registered. “Email or password is incorrect” tells the legitimate user everything they need and the attacker nothing.

Why this matters

Login is the most attacked screen in most apps, and these are the details that decide whether attacks are cheap or expensive.

lessons.html: Quick check: Review the formal study notes, complete the coding exercises, then answer these questions to confirm you understood Login System.

questions.question: Why should login errors not distinguish wrong email from wrong password?
options: Distinct messages let an attacker enumerate registered accounts
questions.explanation: Identical messages prevent account enumeration.

questions.question: What should happen to the login screen after a successful sign-in?
options: Be popped from the back stack
questions.explanation: Otherwise back returns the signed-in user to the login form.

questions.question: Why check for an existing session at startup?
options: So returning users are not forced to sign in again
questions.explanation: Persisted sessions are the difference between a usable app and an irritating one.

lessons.title: 12.3 Password Security
lessons.html:
📖 M12:Password Security
What the app must do, and what it must not attempt.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Password Security

Password Security is the focus of this Authentication & Security lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

authentication

Verifying the identity of a user or system.

authorization

Deciding what an authenticated identity is permitted to do.

encryption

Transforming readable data so only authorised parties can restore it.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

Firebase.auth.signInWithEmailAndPassword(email, password)
    .addOnSuccessListener { openDashboard() }
    .addOnFailureListener { showError("Unable to sign in") }
// Never store the user password yourself.

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Authentication & Security. For Password Security, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

The app's job is to enforce a sensible minimum length, avoid obstructing password managers, and transmit over HTTPS. Hashing and storage belong to the auth provider.

Length matters far more than composition rules. Forcing symbols and monthly rotation produces predictable variations written on paper, which is a worse outcome than a long passphrase.

Key points

  • Enforce a minimum length; composition rules add little.
  • Never store or log a password, even during debugging.
  • Do not block paste — it breaks password managers.
  • Always transmit over HTTPS.
  • Offer a reveal toggle; hidden typing causes errors.
  • Delegate hashing and storage to the auth provider.

Example

Blocking paste on a password field, intended as a security measure, prevents password managers from working and pushes users toward short passwords they can type. It makes things worse.

Why this matters

Several long-standing password “best practices” have been withdrawn by standards bodies, and repeating them now actively reduces security.
