lessons.html: Quick check: Review the formal study notes, complete the coding exercises, then answer these questions to confirm you understood Password Security.

questions.question: What matters most in password strength?
questions.explanation: Length and unpredictability resist guessing far better than composition rules.

questions.question: Why should paste not be blocked on a password field?
options: It prevents password managers from working, encouraging weaker passwords
questions.explanation: Blocking paste pushes users toward passwords short enough to type by hand.

questions.question: Who should be responsible for hashing passwords?
questions.explanation: Client-side hashing does not substitute for correct server-side storage.

lessons.title: 12.4 Biometric Authentication
lessons.html:
📖 Biometric Authentication
Fingerprint and face unlock as convenience, with a fallback.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Biometric Authentication

Biometric Authentication is the focus of this Authentication & Security lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

authentication

Verifying the identity of a user or system.

authorization

Deciding what an authenticated identity is permitted to do.

encryption

Transforming readable data so only authorised parties can restore it.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

Firebase.auth.signInWithEmailAndPassword(email, password)
    .addOnSuccessListener { openDashboard() }
    .addOnFailureListener { showError("Unable to sign in") }
// Never store the user password yourself.

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Authentication & Security. For Biometric Authentication, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

The BiometricPrompt API presents the system biometric dialog and reports success or failure. It is used to unlock an existing session quickly, not usually as the primary credential.

There must always be a fallback. Sensors fail with wet hands, some devices have none, and users can remove their enrolment — so a PIN, pattern or password path must remain.

Key points

  • BiometricPrompt shows the system dialog and returns the result.
  • Check availability with BiometricManager before offering it.
  • Always provide a fallback: device credential or password.
  • Biometric data never leaves the device and your app never sees it.
  • Use it to unlock a session, not to replace authentication entirely.
  • Re-authenticate before genuinely sensitive actions.

Example

An app that offers only fingerprint unlock locks out a user whose sensor fails, or who is working with wet hands. The fallback is not an optional extra; it is what makes the feature safe to offer.

Why this matters

Biometrics are convenience layered on authentication, and treating them as a replacement for it produces apps people cannot get into.

questions.question: What must always accompany biometric authentication?
options: A fallback such as device credential or password
questions.explanation: Sensors fail and enrolments change, so an alternative path is required.

questions.question: What does the app receive from BiometricPrompt?
options: A success or failure result only
questions.explanation: Biometric data stays in secure hardware; the app only learns the outcome.

questions.question: What is biometric unlock best used for?
questions.explanation: It is a convenience layer over an already-established identity.

lessons.title: 12.5 Secure Data Storage
lessons.html:
📖 Secure Data Storage
Assume the device may be lost or compromised.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Secure Data Storage

Secure Data Storage is the focus of this Authentication & Security lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

authentication

Verifying the identity of a user or system.

authorization

Deciding what an authenticated identity is permitted to do.

encryption

Transforming readable data so only authorised parties can restore it.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

Firebase.auth.signInWithEmailAndPassword(email, password)
    .addOnSuccessListener { openDashboard() }
    .addOnFailureListener { showError("Unable to sign in") }
// Never store the user password yourself.

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Authentication & Security. For Secure Data Storage, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Sensitive values — tokens, keys, personal data — should be stored with EncryptedSharedPreferences or an encrypted Room database, backed by the Android Keystore.

Plain SharedPreferences and unencrypted databases are readable on a rooted or compromised device. The question is not whether that will happen but what is exposed when it does.

Key points

  • EncryptedSharedPreferences for sensitive key-value data.
  • SQLCipher or equivalent for an encrypted database.
  • The Android Keystore holds keys in hardware where available.
  • Never log tokens or personal data.
  • Exclude sensitive files from automatic backup.
  • Store the minimum — data you do not hold cannot leak.

Example

A session token in plain SharedPreferences is readable on a rooted device and grants full account access. The same token encrypted with a Keystore-backed key is not usable off the device.

Why this matters

Storing less is the strongest control available, and it is the one most often skipped in favour of caching everything just in case.

lessons.html: Quick check: Review the formal study notes, complete the coding exercises, then answer these questions to confirm you understood Secure Data Storage.

questions.question: What should be used for storing a session token?
questions.explanation: Encrypted storage with a Keystore-backed key protects the token if the device is compromised.

questions.question: What is the strongest available data-protection measure?
options: Not storing the data at all
questions.explanation: Data that is never stored cannot be exposed.

questions.question: What should be excluded from automatic backup?
questions.explanation: Backups can carry sensitive data off the device unless explicitly excluded.

lessons.title: 12.6 App Permissions
lessons.html:
📖 M12:App Permissions
Every permission you request is a claim you must justify.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

App Permissions

App Permissions is the focus of this Authentication & Security lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

authentication

Verifying the identity of a user or system.

authorization

Deciding what an authenticated identity is permitted to do.

encryption

Transforming readable data so only authorised parties can restore it.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

Firebase.auth.signInWithEmailAndPassword(email, password)
    .addOnSuccessListener { openDashboard() }
    .addOnFailureListener { showError("Unable to sign in") }
// Never store the user password yourself.

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Authentication & Security. For App Permissions, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Each permission in the manifest is visible on the store listing and reviewed by Play. Requesting more than the app uses reduces installs and invites rejection.

Audit the manifest before release. Permissions accumulate during development — added to try something, never removed — and each one that remains is a promise about behaviour.

Key points

  • Every manifest permission appears on the store listing.
  • Audit and remove unused permissions before release.
  • Prefer approaches that need no permission at all.
  • Sensitive permissions require a Play declaration and justification.
  • Explain the reason at the point of request.
  • The app must remain usable when a permission is refused.

Example

The Photo Picker replaces a broad media permission entirely. Choosing it means one fewer permission on the listing, no prompt, and no Play declaration to justify.

Why this matters

Permission minimalism is simultaneously a privacy practice, a conversion optimisation and a store-compliance requirement.

questions.question: What is preferable to requesting a permission?

questions.explanation: System pickers and delegation avoid the permission entirely.

lessons.title: 12.7 Security Best Practices
lessons.html:
📖 M12:Security Best Practices
A short checklist that covers most mobile security failures.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Security Best Practices

Security Best Practices is the focus of this Authentication & Security lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

authentication

Verifying the identity of a user or system.

authorization

Deciding what an authenticated identity is permitted to do.

encryption

Transforming readable data so only authorised parties can restore it.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

Firebase.auth.signInWithEmailAndPassword(email, password)
    .addOnSuccessListener { openDashboard() }
    .addOnFailureListener { showError("Unable to sign in") }
// Never store the user password yourself.

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Authentication & Security. For Security Best Practices, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Most app compromises come from a small set of mistakes: secrets in the APK, data stored unencrypted, traffic not properly protected, and trusting the client.

The governing principle is that the device is not trusted. Anything shipped in the app can be read, and anything the app enforces can be bypassed — so the server must enforce it too.

Key points

  • Assume the APK can be read; ship no meaningful secrets in it.
  • Use HTTPS everywhere and do not disable certificate validation.
  • Encrypt sensitive local storage; store as little as possible.
  • Validate on the server — client checks are advisory.
  • Keep dependencies current; most vulnerabilities arrive through them.
  • Enable code shrinking and obfuscation, but do not rely on them.

Example

Disabling certificate validation to silence an error during development, and shipping that, exposes every user's traffic to interception. It is a one-line change and one of the most damaging mistakes a mobile developer can make.

Why this matters

These few rules cover the majority of real mobile security incidents, and none of them requires specialist knowledge to follow.

lessons.html: Quick check: Review the formal study notes, complete the coding exercises, then answer these questions to confirm you understood Security Best Practices.

questions.question: What should be assumed about code shipped in an APK?
options: It is signed and therefore private
It can be decompiled and read
questions.explanation: Anything in the package is recoverable, so it can hold no meaningful secret.

questions.question: Why must validation be repeated on the server?
options: Client-side checks can be bypassed by a modified app
questions.explanation: The client is under the user's control and cannot be trusted to enforce rules.

questions.question: What is the most common route by which vulnerabilities enter an app?
questions.explanation: Most application code comes from libraries, and their flaws are inherited.

lessons.title: 13.1 Debugging Apps
lessons.html:
📖 Debugging Apps
Find the cause, rather than changing things until it stops.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Debugging Apps

Debugging Apps is the focus of this Testing & Debugging lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

unit test

An automated test of a small isolated piece of program behaviour.

UI test

An automated check that interacts with the application interface like a user.

Logcat

Android Studio’s stream of application and system log messages.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

@Test
fun total_isPriceTimesQuantity() {
    val result = total(price = 5.0, quantity = 3)
    assertEquals(15.0, result, 0.0)
}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Testing & Debugging. For Debugging Apps, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Android Studio's debugger sets breakpoints, steps through code and inspects variables. Logcat shows system and app logs, filtered by tag and level.

The habit that matters is reading the stack trace properly. The first line names the exception, and the first frame in your package is almost always where the problem is — not the framework frames above it.

Key points

  • Breakpoints and stepping beat scattering log statements.
  • In a stack trace, find the first frame in your package.
  • Caused by: lines at the bottom usually hold the real cause.
  • Filter Logcat by tag and level; unfiltered output is unreadable.
  • Use Log.d for development and remove it before release.
  • Reproduce reliably before attempting a fix.

Example

A NullPointerException stack trace lists twenty framework frames before yours. Scrolling to the first line mentioning your package names the file and line that actually failed.

Why this matters

Debugging skill is what turns an unexplained crash report into a fix, and it is the difference between hours and minutes on the same bug.

questions.explanation: Framework frames are the path; your frame is where the fault occurred.

questions.question: Where is the underlying cause of a wrapped exception usually found?
questions.explanation: Caused-by chains reveal the original exception beneath the wrapper.

questions.question: What should be done before attempting a fix?
questions.explanation: Without reliable reproduction you cannot confirm a fix worked.

lessons.title: 13.2 Unit Testing
lessons.html:
📖 Unit Testing
Fast, isolated tests for logic that has no Android in it.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Unit Testing

Unit Testing is the focus of this Testing & Debugging lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

unit test

An automated test of a small isolated piece of program behaviour.

UI test

An automated check that interacts with the application interface like a user.

Logcat

Android Studio’s stream of application and system log messages.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

@Test
fun total_isPriceTimesQuantity() {
    val result = total(price = 5.0, quantity = 3)
    assertEquals(15.0, result, 0.0)
}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Testing & Debugging. For Unit Testing, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Unit tests run on the JVM in milliseconds and test one piece of logic in isolation: a validator, a calculation, a ViewModel's state transitions.

They only work if the logic is separated from the framework. Business rules written inside an Activity cannot be unit tested; the same rules in a plain Kotlin class can be tested exhaustively.

Key points

  • Run on the JVM under src/test/; milliseconds, no device.
  • Test one behaviour per test, with a descriptive name.
  • Arrange, act, assert is the standard structure.
  • Testability requires logic separated from Activities and Fragments.
  • Fake or mock dependencies such as network and database.
  • Cover edge cases: empty, null, zero, negative, maximum.

Example

A price calculation inside a click listener can only be tested by launching the app and tapping. The same function in a plain class can be tested against twenty inputs in under a second.

Why this matters

Testability is a design property rather than a testing activity, which is why separating logic from the framework is the prerequisite for everything in this module.

questions.explanation: JVM tests are fast because they need no Android runtime.

questions.question: What makes logic unit-testable?
options: Separating it from Activities and Fragments
questions.explanation: Framework-coupled logic cannot be exercised without a device.

questions.question: What is the standard structure of a unit test?
questions.explanation: Arrange the inputs, act on the unit, assert the outcome.

lessons.title: 13.3 UI Testing

📖 UI Testing
Driving the app the way a user would.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

UI Testing

unit test

An automated test of a small isolated piece of program behaviour.

UI test

An automated check that interacts with the application interface like a user.

Logcat

Android Studio’s stream of application and system log messages.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

@Test
fun total_isPriceTimesQuantity() {
    val result = total(price = 5.0, quantity = 3)

}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Testing & Debugging. For UI Testing, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Espresso tests run on a device or emulator, finding views, performing actions and checking results. They verify that screens are wired together correctly.

They are slower and more brittle than unit tests, so write fewer of them and aim them at critical flows: signing in, completing a purchase, submitting a form.

Key points

  • Espresso tests run on a device under src/androidTest/.
  • onView(withId(...)).perform(click()).check(matches(...)).
  • Slower and more brittle than unit tests — write fewer.
  • Target critical user journeys, not every screen.
  • Idling resources handle asynchronous work; sleeps do not.
  • Test on a small screen as well as a large one.

Example

A UI test that verifies a user can register, sign in and reach the home screen catches the wiring failures that unit tests cannot see, and it is worth more than twenty tests of individual buttons.

Why this matters

The balance — many fast unit tests, few slow UI tests on critical paths — is what keeps a test suite useful rather than a burden.

questions.explanation: UI tests are expensive, so they are best spent on flows that must not break.

questions.question: How should asynchronous work be handled in an Espresso test?
questions.explanation: Sleeps are unreliable and slow; idling resources synchronise properly.

questions.question: Where do Espresso tests live?

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Testing & Debugging. For Performance Testing, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Android Studio's Profiler shows CPU, memory, network and energy use over time. It identifies which operation is actually slow rather than which one feels slow.

The metrics that matter to users are startup time, frame rendering (jank) and battery drain. A frame must render within about 16 milliseconds to sustain 60 frames per second.

Key points

  • Profile first — assumptions about what is slow are usually wrong.
  • Startup time, jank and battery are what users notice.
  • A frame budget is roughly 16ms at 60fps.
  • Common causes: main-thread work, over-drawing, unoptimised images.
  • Test on a low-end device; a flagship hides most problems.
  • Measure again after the change to confirm it helped.

Example

Optimising a function that runs once at startup while a layout inflates on every scroll frame is effort spent where it cannot be felt. The profiler would have shown which was which in a minute.

Why this matters

Performance work without measurement is guesswork, and the guess is usually wrong — which is why profiling comes before optimising.

📖 Crash Analysis
Learning from failures on devices you will never see.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

unit test

An automated test of a small isolated piece of program behaviour.

UI test

An automated check that interacts with the application interface like a user.

Logcat

Android Studio’s stream of application and system log messages.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

@Test
fun total_isPriceTimesQuantity() {
    val result = total(price = 5.0, quantity = 3)
    assertEquals(15.0, result, 0.0)
}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Testing & Debugging. For Crash Analysis, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Firebase Crashlytics collects crashes from real users, groups them by cause, and reports how many users each affects along with the device and OS breakdown.

Prioritise by users affected rather than by total occurrences. A crash hitting one user in a loop can outnumber one hitting a thousand users once, and the second is far more important.

Key points

  • Crashlytics groups crashes and reports affected user counts.
  • Prioritise by users affected, not raw occurrence count.
  • Add custom keys — screen, user state — for context.
  • Log non-fatal exceptions for handled failures worth knowing about.
  • Upload mapping files so obfuscated traces stay readable.
  • A crash-free rate below about 99% is a serious problem.

Example

Without uploading the ProGuard mapping file, every stack trace from a release build is obfuscated class names and is effectively unreadable. The crash is reported and cannot be acted on.

Why this matters

Crash reporting is how you find the bugs that only occur on hardware and Android versions you do not own, which is most of them.

📖 Memory Management
Leaks are quiet until the app dies.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Memory Management

Memory Management is the focus of this Testing & Debugging lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

unit test

An automated test of a small isolated piece of program behaviour.

UI test

An automated check that interacts with the application interface like a user.

Logcat

Android Studio’s stream of application and system log messages.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

@Test
fun total_isPriceTimesQuantity() {
    val result = total(price = 5.0, quantity = 3)
    assertEquals(15.0, result, 0.0)
}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Testing & Debugging. For Memory Management, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

A memory leak is an object kept alive by a reference that should have been released. In Android the usual culprits are contexts, views and listeners held past their lifecycle.

LeakCanary detects leaks automatically in debug builds and reports the reference chain holding the object. It is the fastest way to find leaks you would otherwise never notice.

Key points

  • Leaks come from holding contexts, views or listeners too long.
  • Clear ViewBinding references in onDestroyView.
  • Unregister listeners and receivers in the matching callback.
  • Never hold an Activity context in a static field or singleton.
  • LeakCanary finds leaks automatically in debug builds.
  • Bitmaps dominate memory; scale before loading.

Example

A singleton holding an Activity context keeps that entire screen — every view, every bitmap — in memory for the life of the process, and a new one leaks on every rotation.

Why this matters

Memory leaks do not crash immediately; they crash later, on cheaper devices, in ways that are hard to reproduce from the report.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

@Test
fun total_isPriceTimesQuantity() {
    val result = total(price = 5.0, quantity = 3)
    assertEquals(15.0, result, 0.0)
}

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Testing & Debugging. For App Optimization, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Optimisation covers three things users feel: app size, startup time and responsiveness. Each has well-known causes and well-known fixes.

Size matters more here than in wealthier markets. A 60 MB app is a real cost on a metered connection, and users on limited storage uninstall large apps first.

Key points

  • Ship an Android App Bundle — Play serves only what each device needs.
  • Enable R8 shrinking and resource shrinking for release builds.
  • Use WebP or vector drawables instead of large PNGs.
  • Move work off the startup path; measure cold start.
  • Avoid deep view hierarchies and over-draw.
  • Batch network requests rather than polling.

Example

Switching from PNG assets to WebP and enabling resource shrinking routinely halves an app's download size, with no visible difference and no code changes.

Why this matters

Size and startup time are the two things a user judges before they have seen a single feature, which makes them disproportionately worth fixing.

📖 Preparing for Release
The gap between an app that runs and an app you can publish.

Preparing for Release

Preparing for Release is the focus of this Publishing Your App lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

Android App Bundle

A publishing format Google Play uses to generate optimised APKs for different devices.

signing key

A private cryptographic identity proving who published an Android app and its updates.

version code

An increasing integer Android uses to identify each release.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

android {
    defaultConfig {
        versionCode = 12
        versionName = "1.3.0"
    }
}
// Build > Generate Signed Bundle / APK

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Publishing Your App. For Preparing for Release, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Before release: remove debug logging, disable debuggable builds, enable shrinking, point at production endpoints, check every permission is used, and test a release build on a real device.

Release builds behave differently from debug builds. R8 can remove code that reflection depends on, so a release build must be tested rather than assumed equivalent.

Key points

  • Remove debug logging and any test endpoints.
  • Enable R8 shrinking and obfuscation; keep the mapping file.
  • Audit permissions — remove any not used.
  • Test the release build on a real device, not just debug.
  • Confirm the privacy policy URL is live.
  • Verify crash reporting works in the release configuration.

Example

An app that works perfectly in debug can crash in release when R8 strips a class only referenced by reflection. Testing the release build is the only way to find that before users do.

Why this matters

Release preparation is a checklist rather than a skill, and skipping it is how a working app becomes a one-star launch.

lessons.title: 14.2 App Signing
lessons.html:
📖 App Signing
The key that proves an update comes from you.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

App Signing

App Signing is the focus of this Publishing Your App lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

Android App Bundle

A publishing format Google Play uses to generate optimised APKs for different devices.

signing key

A private cryptographic identity proving who published an Android app and its updates.

version code

An increasing integer Android uses to identify each release.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

android {
    defaultConfig {
        versionCode = 12
        versionName = "1.3.0"
    }
}
// Build > Generate Signed Bundle / APK

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Publishing Your App. For App Signing, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Every APK is signed. Android accepts an update only if it is signed by the same key as the installed version, so the signing key is the identity of the app itself.

Losing the key historically meant losing the ability to update — you would have to publish a new listing. Play App Signing solves this: Google holds the app signing key and you keep an upload key that can be reset.

Key points

  • An update must be signed with the same key as the installed app.
  • Play App Signing: Google holds the app key, you hold an upload key.
  • An upload key can be reset; a lost app signing key historically could not.
  • Never commit the keystore or its passwords to a repository.
  • Back the keystore up somewhere separate from the code.
  • The signing certificate is also what restricts your API keys.

Example

Losing a keystore without Play App Signing means the app can never be updated. The published listing must be abandoned and a new one started, losing every install, rating and review.

Why this matters

This is one of the few mistakes in mobile development that is genuinely irreversible, which is why the key handling matters more than its size suggests.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

    defaultConfig {
        versionCode = 12

// Build > Generate Signed Bundle / APK

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Publishing Your App. For Versioning, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

versionCode is an integer Play uses to order releases; it must increase with every upload. versionName is the string users see and can be anything.

Semantic versioning — major.minor.patch — is the usual convention for versionName: a patch for fixes, a minor for compatible features, a major for breaking changes.

Key points

  • versionCode: an integer, must increase on every upload.
  • versionName: the human-readable string users see.
  • Semantic versioning: major.minor.patch.
  • Play rejects an upload whose versionCode is not higher.
  • Tag each release in version control to match.
  • minSdk decides which devices can install; choose it deliberately.

Example

Uploading a build with an unchanged versionCode is rejected by Play immediately. It is the most common first-upload error and takes a minute to fix once you know what it means.

Why this matters

Version discipline is what lets you tie a crash report from a user back to the exact code that produced it.

The first thing a user sees, at a very small size.

// Build > Generate Signed Bundle / APK

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Publishing Your App. For Creating App Icons, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Android uses adaptive icons: a foreground layer and a background layer that the launcher masks into whatever shape the device uses. Design both layers, and keep the important content inside the safe zone.

Icons are seen at roughly 48dp. Detail that reads on a monitor disappears at that size, which is why simple, high-contrast shapes work and detailed illustrations do not.

Key points

  • Adaptive icons: separate foreground and background layers.
  • Keep key content within the central safe zone — masks vary.
  • Design for roughly 48dp; detail disappears at that size.
  • Use Image Asset Studio in Android Studio to generate densities.
  • Provide a monochrome layer for themed icons.
  • Test on a launcher using circular and squircle masks.

Example

An icon with small text is unreadable at 48dp and appears as a grey smear. A single bold shape in two contrasting colours is recognisable on a crowded home screen, which is the actual job.

Why this matters

The icon is the app's only presence on the home screen, and it determines whether a user finds it again after installing.

Play requires a feature graphic of 1024 by 500 pixels. It appears at the top of the listing and in promotional placements, and it is the largest visual element a potential user sees.

It is often cropped and frequently displayed with an overlaid play button, so keep essential content centred and avoid placing text where it may be covered.

Key points

  • Required size: 1024 x 500 pixels, PNG or JPEG.
  • Keep essential content centred — edges may be cropped.
  • A play button may be overlaid centrally when a video is present.
  • Little text, large enough to read on a phone.
  • It must not misrepresent the app.
  • Match the visual style of the icon and screenshots.

Example

A feature graphic with a paragraph of small text is unreadable on the device where it is actually seen. One short phrase and a strong image communicates in the moment a user is scrolling past.

Why this matters

Store assets are the conversion step between being found and being installed, and they are usually the least considered part of a launch.

Play requires at least two phone screenshots and allows up to eight. Most users scroll the first two or three and decide from those, so order matters more than quantity.

Show the app doing something, with realistic content. Empty states and placeholder text tell a browsing user nothing about whether the app is worth installing.

Key points

  • Minimum two, maximum eight per device type.
  • The first two carry most of the decision — lead with the best.
  • Show real content, never empty states or lorem ipsum.
  • A short caption on each helps far more than a bare screen.
  • Provide tablet screenshots if you support tablets.
  • Update them when the interface changes.

Example

A screenshot of an empty list with “No items yet” is technically a screenshot of your app and tells a prospective user nothing. The same screen with realistic data shows them what they would get.

Why this matters

Screenshots are the highest-leverage part of a listing, and they are usually captured hurriedly on the day of submission.

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Publishing Your App. For Writing App Descriptions, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Play shows a short description of up to 80 characters and a full description of up to 4,000. The short description appears in search results and is often all a user reads.

Lead with the benefit rather than the technology. Users search for what they want to accomplish, and both the search algorithm and the reader respond to plain language over feature lists.

Key points

  • Short description: 80 characters, and often all that is read.
  • Full description: up to 4,000 characters.
  • Lead with what the app does for the user.
  • Include the words users would actually search for.
  • Do not keyword-stuff — Play penalises it.
  • Localise the listing if you target several languages.

Example

“Built with Kotlin and Firebase” describes your stack. “Track your shop's daily sales and see what sells best” describes what the user gets, and it contains the words they would search for.

Why this matters

The description is where an app is found or not found, and technology-led writing fails at both discovery and persuasion.

Publishing means creating a Play Console account, completing the store listing, filling the content rating questionnaire and data safety form, uploading a signed App Bundle, and submitting for review.

The Data safety section is where most first submissions stall. It must accurately declare what data the app collects and shares, and inaccuracy is treated as a policy violation rather than an oversight.

Key points

  • A Play Console account requires a one-off registration fee.
  • Upload an App Bundle (.aab), not an APK.
  • Complete the content rating questionnaire honestly.
  • The Data safety form must match actual behaviour.
  • A privacy policy URL is required for apps handling user data.
  • Use internal and closed testing tracks before production.

Example

Declaring that the app collects no data while an analytics SDK reports device identifiers is a policy violation. Play checks, and the app is removed rather than queried.

Why this matters

Most first-time rejections come from these declarations rather than from the code, which is why they belong in preparation and not at submission.

An increasing integer Android uses to identify each release.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

android {
    defaultConfig {
        versionCode = 12
        versionName = "1.3.0"
    }
}
// Build > Generate Signed Bundle / APK

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Publishing Your App. For App Updates, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

An update needs a higher versionCode, the same signing key, and release notes describing what changed. Staged rollouts release to a percentage of users first, so a serious problem affects few people.

Watch the crash-free rate after each release. A rollout can be halted if the new version is worse than the one it replaces, which is the whole reason to stage it.

Key points

  • Increase versionCode; sign with the same key.
  • Write release notes that describe user-visible changes.
  • Use a staged rollout — 5-10% first.
  • Watch the crash-free rate before increasing the percentage.
  • Halt the rollout if stability regresses.
  • Handle database migrations — users update from old versions.

Example

Releasing a Room schema change without a migration crashes every existing user on first launch while working perfectly on a fresh install — which is exactly what your test device is.

Why this matters

Migrations are the update failure that testing on a clean device cannot reveal, which is why they deserve deliberate attention.

lessons.title: 15.1 Using ChatGPT for Coding
lessons.html:
📖 Using ChatGPT for Coding
A fast assistant that is confidently wrong often enough to matter.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Using ChatGPT for Coding

Using ChatGPT for Coding is the focus of this AI Tools for Android Developers lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

prompt

The instruction and context supplied to an AI system.

hallucination

A confident AI response that is false, invented, or unsupported.

code review

A structured examination of code for correctness, security, clarity, and maintainability.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

// Responsible AI request
// Goal: explain the crash and propose the smallest fix.
// Context: include only the relevant Kotlin and stack trace.
// Constraints: Android version, libraries, privacy, and tests.
// Verify: run the fix and add a regression test.

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in AI Tools for Android Developers. For Using ChatGPT for Coding, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

AI assistants are effective at explaining unfamiliar code, drafting boilerplate, suggesting approaches and interpreting stack traces. They are quick and they never tire of basic questions.

They are also unreliable on specifics. Android APIs change, and an assistant will produce deprecated or invented method names with the same confidence as correct ones. Every suggestion must be compiled and tested before it is trusted.

Key points

  • Good for explanation, boilerplate, and interpreting errors.
  • Unreliable on specific APIs — Android changes faster than training data.
  • Compile and test every suggestion before trusting it.
  • Ask it to explain its code; if it cannot, do not ship it.
  • Never paste API keys, credentials or client data into it.
  • Use it to learn faster, not to avoid understanding.

Example

An assistant may suggest a method that was removed two API levels ago, with a confident explanation of what it does. It compiles nowhere, and the explanation is invented.

Why this matters

The developers who benefit most from these tools are those who can already evaluate the answer, which is the argument for learning the fundamentals in the preceding modules.

lessons.title: 15.2 GitHub Copilot

📖 GitHub Copilot
Autocomplete that finishes the thought, sometimes wrongly.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

GitHub Copilot

GitHub Copilot is the focus of this AI Tools for Android Developers lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

prompt

The instruction and context supplied to an AI system.

hallucination

A confident AI response that is false, invented, or unsupported.

code review

A structured examination of code for correctness, security, clarity, and maintainability.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

// Responsible AI request
// Goal: explain the crash and propose the smallest fix.
// Context: include only the relevant Kotlin and stack trace.
// Constraints: Android version, libraries, privacy, and tests.
// Verify: run the fix and add a regression test.

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in AI Tools for Android Developers. For GitHub Copilot, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Copilot suggests code inline as you type, using the surrounding file as context. It is strongest on repetitive, predictable code — data classes, adapters, boilerplate — where the next lines are largely determined.

It is weakest exactly where care is needed: security-sensitive code, unusual business rules, and anything requiring context from outside the current file. Accepting suggestions without reading them is how subtle bugs enter a codebase.

Key points

  • Suggests code inline from the surrounding file's context.
  • Strongest on repetitive, predictable code.
  • Weakest on security-sensitive and unusual logic.
  • Read every suggestion before accepting it.
  • It cannot see files it has not been given as context.
  • Suggested code may carry licensing implications.

Example

Copilot writes a RecyclerView adapter almost perfectly, because there are thousands of near-identical ones. It writes your particular pricing rule confidently and wrongly, because it has never seen it.

Why this matters

Knowing which category a task falls into is what makes the tool a genuine accelerator rather than a source of plausible-looking defects.

📖 Firebase AI Features
Machine learning without training a model.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Firebase AI Features is the focus of this AI Tools for Android Developers lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

prompt

The instruction and context supplied to an AI system.

hallucination

A confident AI response that is false, invented, or unsupported.

A structured examination of code for correctness, security, clarity, and maintainability.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

// Responsible AI request
// Goal: explain the crash and propose the smallest fix.
// Context: include only the relevant Kotlin and stack trace.
// Constraints: Android version, libraries, privacy, and tests.
// Verify: run the fix and add a regression test.

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in AI Tools for Android Developers. For Firebase AI Features, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Firebase ML Kit provides on-device models for common tasks: text recognition, barcode scanning, face detection, image labelling and translation. You call an API; there is no training and often no network.

On-device processing matters here for two reasons. It works without a connection, and the image never leaves the phone, which removes both a bandwidth cost and a privacy concern.

Key points

  • ML Kit offers text recognition, barcode scanning, face detection and translation.
  • On-device models work offline and keep data on the phone.
  • No training required — call the API and read the result.
  • Bundled models increase app size; downloaded models need a first connection.
  • Accuracy varies with lighting and image quality — handle failure.
  • Use it for well-defined tasks, not as a general intelligence.

Example

Scanning a receipt with on-device text recognition works in a market with no signal and sends nothing anywhere. The same feature built on a cloud API needs a connection and uploads a photograph of the receipt.

Why this matters

On-device machine learning is one of the clearest cases where the technically simpler option is also the better one for users in low-connectivity settings.

📖 AI Code Debugging
A second reader for an error you have stopped seeing.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

AI Code Debugging

AI Code Debugging is the focus of this AI Tools for Android Developers lesson. It helps the learner implement, test, and explain this Android development skill in a working application.

prompt

The instruction and context supplied to an AI system.

hallucination

A confident AI response that is false, invented, or unsupported.

code review

A structured examination of code for correctness, security, clarity, and maintainability.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

// Responsible AI request
// Goal: explain the crash and propose the smallest fix.
// Context: include only the relevant Kotlin and stack trace.
// Constraints: Android version, libraries, privacy, and tests.
// Verify: run the fix and add a regression test.

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in AI Tools for Android Developers. For AI Code Debugging, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Pasting a stack trace and the relevant code into an assistant often produces a useful hypothesis quickly, particularly for unfamiliar framework errors where the message is opaque.

Treat the answer as a hypothesis to test, not a diagnosis. The assistant cannot run your app, does not know your data, and will produce a confident explanation whether or not it is right.

Key points

  • Provide the stack trace and the relevant code, not just the message.
  • Treat the answer as a hypothesis to verify.
  • Ask it to explain why, which exposes weak reasoning.
  • Redact credentials, tokens and user data before pasting.
  • It cannot run your app or see your data.
  • If a fix works but you cannot explain why, you have not fixed it.

Example

An assistant explaining that an error comes from observing LiveData with the wrong lifecycle owner gives you something specific to check. Accepting the fix without understanding it leaves you unable to avoid the same bug next week.

Why this matters

Used as a hypothesis generator it accelerates learning; used as an oracle it prevents it.

📖 Productivity Tools
Removing the friction between having an idea and shipping it.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Productivity Tools

// Goal: explain the crash and propose the smallest fix.

// Constraints: Android version, libraries, privacy, and tests.

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in AI Tools for Android Developers. For Productivity Tools, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Beyond the IDE, a few tools save meaningful time: version control, a template project, keyboard shortcuts, a device emulator configured for your target hardware, and a build that does not take five minutes.

The most valuable habit is version control. Committing regularly means an experiment that goes wrong costs a minute rather than an afternoon.

Key points

  • Git is the single highest-value tool — commit often.
  • Learn the IDE shortcuts you use most; they compound.
  • Keep a template project with your usual dependencies configured.
  • Use Gradle build caching and configuration caching.
  • Test on one real low-end device, not only the emulator.
  • Automate anything you have done manually three times.

Example

An experiment that breaks the app costs one git checkout to undo when the work was committed, and an afternoon of trying to remember what changed when it was not.

Why this matters

Tooling discipline is what makes a solo developer productive enough to actually finish projects, which is the difference between a portfolio and a folder of half-built apps.

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in AI Tools for Android Developers. For AI-Assisted UI Design, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

AI design tools generate layout ideas, colour palettes, icons and placeholder imagery from a description. They are useful for breaking a blank-page problem and for producing variations to compare.

They do not know your users, your constraints or the platform's conventions. A generated layout frequently ignores touch target sizes, contrast requirements and Material patterns, all of which you must check.

Key points

  • Useful for exploring options and generating placeholder assets.
  • Generated layouts often ignore touch targets and contrast rules.
  • Check every output against the Material guidance from Module 11.
  • It does not know your users or their devices.
  • Verify licensing before shipping generated imagery.
  • Use it to explore, then decide deliberately.

Example

A generated layout may look striking and place 32dp tap targets in low-contrast grey. Both fail the accessibility rules from Module 11, and neither is visible in the rendering that made it look good.

Why this matters

The tools produce options; the judgement about which option is usable on a cheap phone in bright sunlight remains yours.

Evidence that you can build things, not claims that you can.

Key Words & Meanings

Building a Developer Portfolio

A portfolio is a small number of complete, working apps with source code, screenshots and a clear description of what each does and what you built. Three finished apps beat ten abandoned ones.

Complete matters more than ambitious. A simple app that handles errors, works offline, looks considered and is published demonstrates far more than an elaborate one that only runs on your machine.

Key points

  • Three complete apps beat ten unfinished ones.
  • Publish the source on GitHub with a real README.
  • Include screenshots and say what problem each app solves.
  • State clearly what you built if it was collaborative.
  • At least one app published on Play is worth several that are not.
  • Solve a problem you actually understand — local ones are strongest.

Example

An app that solves a real problem for a market trader in Monrovia is more memorable to an interviewer than another to-do list, because you can explain the requirement, the constraints and the decisions.

Why this matters

Portfolios are how developers without formal credentials get hired, and specificity is what makes them persuasive.

Android project case study

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Freelancing & Career Development. For Publishing Projects on GitHub, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

A repository needs a README that says what the app does, shows a screenshot, lists the technologies and explains how to build it. Most visitors read only that.

Never commit secrets. API keys, keystores and google-services.json belong in .gitignore, and a key committed once remains in the history even after it is deleted from the current files.

Key points

  • The README is the most important file in the repository.
  • Include a screenshot — visitors will not build the app to see it.
  • Add a .gitignore before the first commit.
  • Never commit keystores, API keys or google-services.json.
  • A committed secret stays in history; it must be rotated, not just deleted.
  • Write commit messages that explain why, not what.

Example

Deleting an API key in a later commit does not remove it from the repository's history. Anyone can retrieve it from an earlier commit, which is why the key must be revoked rather than merely deleted.

Why this matters

A public repository is often the first thing an employer looks at, and a leaked key in its history is the first thing a security-minded one will notice.

Documentation covers the README, code comments, API notes and setup instructions. Its test is whether a developer who has never seen the project can build and run it from your instructions alone.

Comments should explain why, not what. The code already states what it does; what it cannot state is the constraint or decision that made it necessary.

Key points

  • The test: can a stranger build and run it from your instructions?
  • Comment why, not what — the code states what.
  • Document setup: dependencies, keys required, build steps.
  • Note any non-obvious decision and its reason.
  • Keep documentation next to the code so it is updated with it.
  • Out-of-date documentation is worse than none.

Example

// increment i restates the code. // the API returns 1-based page numbers, unlike the rest of this client explains something the reader could not otherwise know and would otherwise 'fix'.

Why this matters

Documentation is how a solo project becomes something another developer can join, and it is a large part of what employers assess in a portfolio repository.

A developer resume needs contact details, a short summary, skills, projects with links, experience and education. Projects matter most when experience is limited, and each should say what you built and what it does.

Quantify where you can. “Built an Android app” is a claim; “Published an offline-first inventory app used by 40 market traders” is evidence, and it invites the question you want to be asked.

Key points

  • One page unless you have many years of experience.
  • Lead with projects when work experience is limited.
  • Link every project to its repository or Play listing.
  • Quantify outcomes: users, downloads, time saved.
  • Tailor the skills list to the role advertised.
  • Proofread — errors in a document about precision are costly.

Example

“Android developer familiar with Kotlin” says nothing a hundred other applicants do not say. “Published an offline-first sales tracker on Play, used daily by 40 traders” is specific, checkable and memorable.

Why this matters

For developers without formal credentials, the resume's job is to get someone to open the portfolio, which is what actually gets you hired.

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Freelancing & Career Development. For Preparing for Interviews, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Android interviews cover fundamentals — lifecycle, coroutines, architecture, memory — and almost always ask you to walk through a project you built. The second part is where most candidates underperform.

Be able to explain why you chose Room over SharedPreferences, why the app is offline-first, what you would do differently. Interviewers are assessing judgement, and “it was in the tutorial” is a poor answer.

Key points

  • Expect lifecycle, coroutines, architecture and memory questions.
  • Be ready to walk through a project and justify its decisions.
  • “I would look it up” is better than a confident wrong answer.
  • Prepare a two-minute description of your strongest project.
  • Have questions ready — it signals genuine interest.
  • Practise aloud; explaining is a separate skill from knowing.

Example

Asked why you used Room, “because the data is relational and I needed compile-time-checked queries and offline access” demonstrates judgement. “It was in the tutorial” demonstrates that you followed one.

Why this matters

Technical knowledge gets you the interview; the ability to explain decisions is what gets you the job.

Finding first clients when nobody knows your name.

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Freelancing & Career Development. For Freelancing Platforms, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Upwork, Freelancer, Fiverr and similar platforms connect developers with clients. They handle payment and provide dispute resolution, in exchange for a commission and a great deal of competition.

The first few contracts are the hardest, because ratings drive visibility and you have none. Specialising narrowly — a particular kind of app, a particular industry — is more effective than competing on price with everyone.

Key points

  • Platforms handle payment and disputes for a commission.
  • Early contracts are hardest — ratings drive visibility.
  • Specialise; competing on price against everyone is unwinnable.
  • Write proposals about the client's problem, not your CV.
  • Never work outside the platform's payment protection early on.
  • A small, well-delivered contract with a good review compounds.

Example

A proposal that begins by restating the client's problem and how you would approach it is read. One that begins “I am an experienced developer proficient in Kotlin” is one of forty identical openings.

Why this matters

Freelancing is genuinely accessible from Liberia, and the constraints are payment logistics and reputation-building rather than technical capability.

Most project failures are communication failures.

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Freelancing & Career Development. For Working with Clients, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Successful client work depends on a written scope, agreed milestones, regular visible progress and a defined process for changes. Technical skill is rarely the binding constraint.

Scope creep is the standard failure: small additions accumulate until the project is far larger than the price. The remedy is not refusal but a written change process — each addition is quoted and agreed.

Key points

  • Agree scope in writing before starting.
  • Break work into milestones with payment attached.
  • Show progress regularly; silence is read as trouble.
  • Handle changes through a written change process, not verbally.
  • Take a deposit; never deliver everything before any payment.
  • Agree who owns the source code and accounts at the outset.

Example

“Could you just add login as well?” is a week of work presented as a small favour. A change process lets you say yes, with a price, without damaging the relationship.

Why this matters

Client management is what determines whether freelancing is sustainable, and it is the part most self-taught developers have never been taught.

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Freelancing & Career Development. For Pricing Mobile App Projects, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Common models are hourly, fixed-price per project, and milestone-based. Fixed price rewards efficiency and carries the risk of underestimating; hourly is safer for vague requirements.

New freelancers underprice consistently. Estimate the work, then add margin for revisions, communication and the things you have not thought of — which on a first project is most of it.

Key points

  • Hourly suits vague scope; fixed price suits well-defined work.
  • Estimate the build, then add margin for revisions and communication.
  • Charge for maintenance and support separately.
  • Underpricing attracts the most demanding clients, not the best ones.
  • Raise rates as your portfolio and reviews grow.
  • Quote a range when scope is uncertain, and say why.

Example

A fixed price based only on coding time ignores meetings, revisions, store submission and post-launch fixes — which together are often as much work again as the build.

Why this matters

Pricing determines whether freelance work is a career or an expensive hobby, and the most common error is systematic rather than occasional.

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Real-World Projects. For Calculator App, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Build a calculator with the four basic operations, a clear button, and a display. The layout is a grid of buttons; the logic is a small state machine tracking the current entry, the pending operation and the accumulator.

The value is in the edge cases. Division by zero, repeated operators, a leading decimal point and very long numbers all have to be decided rather than ignored.

Key points

  • Layout: GridLayout or ConstraintLayout with a chain of buttons.
  • Track state: current entry, pending operation, accumulator.
  • Handle division by zero explicitly.
  • Handle repeated operator presses and multiple decimal points.
  • Preserve state across rotation.
  • Keep the calculation logic in a plain class so it can be unit tested.

Example

Deliverable: a working calculator that survives rotation and handles division by zero gracefully. Add unit tests for the calculation logic — it is the easiest thing in the course to test properly.

Why this matters

This is the first app where separating logic from the interface pays off immediately, and it makes the testing module concrete.

Build a to-do app: add tasks, mark them complete, delete them, and have them survive restarting the app. Use RecyclerView for the list and Room for storage.

This is the canonical first data app because it exercises everything at once: adapters, view holders, a database, a DAO, and the observation that keeps the list in step with the data.

Key points

  • RecyclerView with a ListAdapter and DiffUtil.
  • Room entity, DAO and database for persistence.
  • Return Flow from the DAO so the list updates automatically.
  • Handle the empty state with a message, not a blank screen.
  • Offer undo on delete via a Snackbar.
  • Confirm the data survives a full app restart.

Example

Deliverable: tasks that persist across restarts, an empty state, and undo on delete. If deleting is instant and irreversible, the app is technically complete and unpleasant to use.

Why this matters

Almost every app is a list of things you can add to and remove from, which makes this the pattern most reused in everything that follows.

Build a notes app with a list of notes, an editor screen, and search. Notes are stored in Room and edited on a second screen reached through the Navigation Component.

The requirement that distinguishes a good version is not losing work. Save drafts as the user types, or on leaving the screen — a note lost to a back press is the failure users remember.

Key points

  • Two screens: a list and an editor, joined by the Navigation Component.
  • Pass the note id as a Safe Args argument, not the whole note.
  • Auto-save or save on leaving the editor.
  • Search with a Room query filtered by title and body.
  • Show the last-modified time in the list.
  • Confirm before discarding an edited note.

Example

Deliverable: a note that survives being typed, backgrounded, rotated and returned to. Test by typing half a sentence and pressing back — if the text is gone, the app is not finished.

Why this matters

Data loss is the failure users least forgive, and designing against it is a habit worth forming on a small app.

  • Show when the data was last updated.

Deliverable: an app that shows yesterday's cached weather with a “last updated” label when offline, rather than an error. That behaviour is the difference between usable and not on a weak connection.

This is the project that turns the networking module from theory into something you have debugged yourself.

Build an expense tracker: record expenses with an amount, category and date; list them; and show totals by category and by month. Store everything in Room.

Handle money carefully. Floating-point arithmetic accumulates rounding errors, so store amounts as integer minor units — cents — and format for display rather than storing formatted strings.

Key points

  • Room entity with amount, category, date and note.
  • Store money as integer minor units, never as a float.
  • Group and total by category and by month.
  • Validate the amount before saving.
  • Show an empty state before any expense exists.
  • Format currency for display; never store the formatted string.

Example

Deliverable: monthly totals that are correct to the cent after a hundred entries. Storing amounts as doubles produces totals that drift by a few cents, which in a financial app is a defect.

Why this matters

This is the most immediately useful app in the module for a small trader, and the money-handling point applies to every financial feature you will ever build.

Image-heavy lists are where beginner apps most often become slow, and doing one properly is a portfolio piece in itself.

Build a chat app using Firebase Authentication and Firestore or the Realtime Database. Users sign in, see a list of conversations, and exchange messages that appear without refreshing.

Real-time listeners are the new idea here. The screen subscribes to a query and updates as data changes, which means you must also unsubscribe when the screen goes — a listener left attached costs reads and battery indefinitely.

Key points

  • Firebase Auth for identity; Firestore or Realtime DB for messages.
  • Real-time listeners update the screen without a refresh.
  • Detach listeners when the screen stops.
  • Order messages by timestamp; handle clock differences.
  • Security rules must restrict messages to their participants.
  • Show sending, sent and failed states for each message.

Example

Deliverable: two devices exchanging messages that appear immediately, with security rules that stop a third user reading the conversation. Test the rules by trying to read someone else's chat.

Why this matters

Multi-user apps introduce a whole class of problem — authorisation, ordering, offline conflict — that single-user apps never face.

  • Use Room relations rather than duplicating data.
  • Attendance is per student per date — enforce uniqueness.
  • Summarise: attendance percentage and average grade per student.
  • Handle a student joining or leaving mid-term.
  • Export or print a simple report.

Example

Deliverable: an attendance register a teacher could actually use for one term, with a per-student summary. This is the project most likely to become a paid commission in Liberia.

A realistic data model with relationships is the step from tutorial apps to the kind of software people commission, and it is worth the extra effort.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

Capstone release checklist
[ ] Core journey works offline or handles no connection
[ ] Input is validated and access is controlled
[ ] Data survives lifecycle changes
[ ] Tests pass on target devices
[ ] Signed release build installs
[ ] Documentation and presentation are complete

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Capstone Project. For Project Planning, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

The capstone begins with a written plan: the problem, who has it, what the app must do, and explicitly what it will not do. The last item is what keeps the project finishable.

List the screens and the data model on paper first. An hour spent here saves days of rebuilding, because a data model discovered halfway through is expensive to change.

Key points

  • State the problem and who has it, in two sentences.
  • List must-have features, then everything you are excluding.
  • Sketch the screens and how the user moves between them.
  • Draft the data model — entities and their relationships.
  • Choose the stack deliberately and record why.
  • Set a realistic scope; a finished small app beats an unfinished large one.

Example

Deliverable: a one-page plan with the problem, the must-have features, an explicit exclusion list, screen sketches and a data model. Everything after this stage refers back to it.

Why this matters

The exclusion list is the most valuable part. Without it, every good idea becomes a requirement and the project never ships.

Capstone release checklist
[ ] Core journey works offline or handles no connection
[ ] Input is validated and access is controlled
[ ] Data survives lifecycle changes
[ ] Tests pass on target devices
[ ] Signed release build installs
[ ] Documentation and presentation are complete

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Capstone Project. For UI Design, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Produce a design for every screen in the plan: layout, the Material components used, the type scale and the colour roles. Paper or a free tool is fine; the point is deciding before coding.

Check accessibility while it is still a drawing. Touch targets of at least 48dp, text contrast of at least 4.5:1, and no meaning carried by colour alone — all far cheaper to fix now than after the layouts exist.

Key points

  • Design every screen in the plan, including empty and error states.
  • Use Material components rather than inventing controls.
  • Check touch targets (48dp) and contrast (4.5:1) at design time.
  • Apply one type scale and one set of colour roles across all screens.
  • Design the dark variant alongside the light one.
  • Confirm the layout works on a small, cheap phone.

Example

Deliverable: designs for every screen including empty, loading and error states. Screens without those three states get built without them, and that is how apps end up showing blank pages.

Why this matters

Designing the failure states alongside the happy path is the single habit that most distinguishes a considered app from a demo.

[ ] Signed release build installs
[ ] Documentation and presentation are complete

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Capstone Project. For Database Design, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Define the Room entities, their fields and their relationships, then write the DAO queries each screen needs. Changing this after release means writing migrations for real users' data.

Normalise by default and denormalise only for a measured reason. Duplicated data must be updated in every copy, and missing one is how records quietly disagree with each other.

Key points

  • Define entities, primary keys and relationships explicitly.
  • Write the DAO query each screen needs, before building the screen.
  • Index the columns you filter or sort on.
  • Normalise by default; denormalise only with a reason.
  • Plan for migrations — the schema will change.
  • Decide what happens to related rows when a parent is deleted.

Example

Deliverable: a schema diagram, the entity classes, and a DAO whose queries cover every screen in the plan. If a screen needs data the schema cannot produce, that is far cheaper to discover now.

Why this matters

Schema changes after release require migrations that must work on every existing user's data, which is why an hour of design here is worth days later.

[ ] Documentation and presentation are complete

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Capstone Project. For Authentication, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Implement registration, login, logout, password reset and session persistence using Firebase Authentication. Then link the app's data to the signed-in user's UID.

The consequences reach further than the login screen. Every query becomes scoped to a user, security rules must enforce that scoping, and the app needs a sensible state for a signed-out visitor.

Key points

  • Registration, login, logout, reset and persistent sessions.
  • Scope all user data by UID.
  • Enforce the scoping in security rules, not only in queries.
  • Handle the signed-out state on every screen.
  • Pop the login destination after a successful sign-in.
  • Test that one account cannot read another's data.

Example

Deliverable: two accounts on two devices, each seeing only their own data, verified by attempting to read the other's. If the rules are missing, both will succeed — and the app looks correct until someone checks.

Why this matters

Authorisation failures are invisible from inside your own account, which is why they must be tested deliberately with a second one.

📱 Kotlin or Android pattern to study

Capstone release checklist
[ ] Core journey works offline or handles no connection
[ ] Input is validated and access is controlled
[ ] Data survives lifecycle changes
[ ] Tests pass on target devices
[ ] Signed release build installs
[ ] Documentation and presentation are complete

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Capstone Project. For API Integration, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Integrate whichever external service the capstone requires — a data API, maps, payments, notifications. Use Retrofit, handle every failure mode, and cache what you can.

Wrap the service behind your own interface. Providers change their terms, their pricing and occasionally their existence, and the abstraction is what keeps that from becoming a rewrite.

Key points

  • Use Retrofit with a typed interface and a JSON converter.
  • Handle loading, success, error and empty states on every screen.
  • Cache responses so the app works on a weak connection.
  • Keep keys out of source control and restrict them at the provider.
  • Wrap the provider behind your own interface.
  • Respect rate limits; back off rather than retrying immediately.

Example

Deliverable: the integrated feature working, and working sensibly with the network switched off. Test with aeroplane mode — if the screen goes blank, the integration is not finished.

Why this matters

Aeroplane mode is the fastest and most honest test of whether an app was built for the connections its users actually have.

Capstone release checklist
[ ] Core journey works offline or handles no connection
[ ] Input is validated and access is controlled
[ ] Data survives lifecycle changes

[ ] Signed release build installs
[ ] Documentation and presentation are complete

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Capstone Project. For Testing, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Write unit tests for the logic, a small number of UI tests for the critical journeys, and test manually on a real low-end device. Then test the release build, not just the debug one.

Test the awkward cases deliberately: no connectivity, a rotated screen, an empty database, a very long input, the largest system font. Each is a case users will reach and demos never do.

Key points

  • Unit tests for the logic separated from the framework.
  • UI tests for the critical journeys only.
  • Test manually on a real low-end device.
  • Test the release build; shrinking changes behaviour.
  • Deliberately test: offline, rotation, empty state, long input, large font.
  • Fix what you find before the presentation, or note it honestly.

Example

Deliverable: a test report listing what you tested, what passed, and what is known to be broken. An honest list of known issues is more credible than a claim that everything works.

Why this matters

Every experienced reviewer knows nothing is perfect, so a candid list of limitations reads as competence rather than weakness.

How this connects: This pattern represents the normal workflow used in Capstone Project. For Deployment, identify the input or starting state, follow the main operation, then check the visible result, saved data, log message, test, or release output.

Prepare the release: bump the version, enable shrinking, sign the bundle, write the listing, complete the data safety declaration, and publish to at least a closed testing track.

Publishing to a testing track is enough to have completed the exercise. What matters is that the app is installable by someone else, from the store, without you present.

Key points

  • Increase versionCode; sign with a keystore you have backed up.
  • Enable R8 shrinking; keep the mapping file.
  • Write the listing: short description, screenshots, feature graphic.
  • Complete the data safety declaration accurately.
  • Publish a privacy policy URL if the app handles user data.
  • Release to internal or closed testing at minimum.

Example

Deliverable: an install link a friend can use to install your app from Play without your involvement. That is the moment the project stops being a school exercise.

Why this matters

Shipping is the step most self-taught developers never complete, and having done it once is what distinguishes a portfolio from a folder of projects.
